The timeline and every list built like it (favourites, a person, a folder, the trash, a shared library, a user's public page) are read day by day. A day is not stored: a photo belongs to the day of its date taken (exif_timestamp, wall-clock time), or to the undated group when it has none. All three endpoints take the same filters, so a day's count, its pages and its layout always agree. Up to 1.5.x these were GET /api/albums/date/list/ and GET /api/albums/date/<id>/?page=N. Both still answer, read-only and deprecated, for released clients such as UhuruPhotos: they take the same filters plus last_modified, use the day ids below, and page a day by offset, which is slow on very large days. New clients use the endpoints below. Note public, hidden, in_trashcan, show_all_stack_photos and libraries are booleans: true, 1, yes or on switch them on, false, 0, no, off or a blank value leave them off, and any other value is a 400 naming the parameter. The media filters (favorite, video, photo, is_screenshot, is_document, hide_screenshots, hide_documents, archived) are tri-state: a false word turns them off, any other value on, and leaving them out applies neither. person and library must be numbers, otherwise the answer is a 400. Filters (all three endpoints):​ ?favorite=true - Favourite images only (rated at least the user's favourite rating) ?public=true&username=<name> - That user's public images; no sign-in needed. The user's public profile must be on. An owner who keeps dates to themselves shows all their public images as one undated group. ?in_trashcan=true - Images currently in the trashcan (images already marked as removed are excluded) ?hidden=true - Hidden images instead of the default non-hidden ones ?person=<id> - Images showing this person ?folder=<prefix> - Images with a file under this folder ?video=true, ?photo=true, ?media=photos|videos - Videos only, or photos only ?is_screenshot=true, ?is_document=true - Only that category (false hides it); ?hide_screenshots=true, ?hide_documents=true hide it ?archived=false - Leave archived images out (the timeline); true shows only them ?apply_default=true - Apply the user's saved timeline filter first ?library=<owner id> - The library another user shares with you, instead of yours ?libraries=true - Also the libraries you show in your timeline ?show_all_stack_photos=true - Also the photos of a stack that are not its primary ?order=oldest - Oldest day first (and each day's photos oldest first); the undated group stays last Headers:​ Authorization - Bearer <token> (not needed with public=true)

The days, newest first: {"results": [{"id", "date", "location", "numberOfItems"}]}. id is the day as YYYYMMDD, 1 for the undated group (date is null there). location is the town of the day's first located photo, when its owner shares where it was taken. Not paginated.

A page of a day's images: {"items": [...], "next": <photo id> | null}. ?after=<photo id> - The images after this one: the previous page's next, or a layout's page_after. Leave it out for the first page. A photo that is not in this day any more (deleted, hidden, moved to another day) is a 400 on after; read the day's layout again. ?limit=<n> - How many images (default 100, at most 500) Images taken in the same second keep the order of their file paths, which is how a camera numbers a burst.

What a client lays a day out with before its images load: {"id", "numberOfItems", "aspectRatios": [...], "page_after": [...]}. aspectRatios holds every image's aspect ratio in the day's order. page_after[i] is the after that opens page i + 1 of limit images (?limit=<n>, default 100), null for the first.

Fetch the days with the count of their images with GET /api/days/. Based on the number of photos per day, create a bunch of empty <div/> with the attribute isTemp, which will then be rendered by react-pig. A day of more than one page also gets its layout, which gives the placeholders their real aspect ratio. react-pig calculates the height for scrolling from the number of elements and their aspectRatio. When scrolling, the isTemp element is used to determine if a currently visible element is actually loaded yet or not. If not, load its page with GET /api/days/<id>/photos/?after=...: the previous page's next when that page is loaded, else the cursor from the day's layout, so the grid can jump into the middle of a 200,000-photo day.
We process media files with different libraries to convert them to a widely compatible format and to speed up previewing files.

By leveraging libvips' lightning-fast image processing capabilities and memory-efficient design, the conversion process becomes remarkably fast, ensuring optimal performance even with numerous images. Moreover, the utilization of pyvips as a Python interface facilitates seamless integration with the project libvips comes bundled with pyvips-binary; what that build cannot decode (HEIC, JPEG XL, BMP, JPEG 2000) is decoded by Pillow with pillow-heif and pillow-jxl-plugin and handed back to pyvips (api/thumbnails/decoding.py). The original is decoded once, at the big thumbnail's size; the two smaller thumbnails are resized from that image (create_static_thumbnails in api/thumbnails/render.py). Thumbnails are WebP at quality 95 and encoder effort 2, which encodes twice as fast as libwebp's default effort 4 at the same file size.

Almost every camera stores a JPEG preview it rendered itself inside the RAW file. When that preview shows the whole picture (the same aspect ratio as the sensor image) and is at least as tall as the big thumbnail, the thumbnail is made from it, in the worker (image_decoding.raw_preview). This takes a fraction of a full render, and the thumbnail looks like the camera's own JPEG. Otherwise the RAW is rendered with LibRaw through rawpy, which ships LibRaw in its wheel, and the result is resized and saved as WebP by pyvips. This runs on a separate microservice so that a decoder crash on an exotic file stays away from the API workers.

As a powerful and versatile multimedia framework, FFmpeg equips users with a comprehensive suite of tools to seamlessly convert videos in various formats. The open-source nature of FFmpeg results in continuous updates and improvements that keep pace with evolving industry standards.

Big thumbnails act as a source of truth for all subsequent processing like finding faces, calculating similarity, finding objects etc. The reason for that is twofold: First, we know that all files will be compatible with the machine learning pipelines, because it's only one format, second all file dimensions are limited to a certain format, which will prevent a possible explosion of resource use.

We also create thumbnails for previewing faces: during face extraction the face region is cropped out of the big thumbnail and stored as a JPEG under protected_media/faces, so a lot of them can be displayed quickly. User avatars are not thumbnailed by the backend — the frontend scales the chosen image to a 150x150 PNG in the browser before upload, and the backend stores that file as-is under protected_media/avatars.

Authentication These /media/... endpoints are all served by UnifiedMediaAccessView, which is declared AllowAny and authenticates with JWTCookieAuthentication plus Basic auth: an Authorization: Bearer header when there is one, otherwise the jwt cookie. When both are sent, the header wins. POST /api/auth/token/obtain/ and POST /api/auth/token/refresh/ set the jwt cookie automatically, which is how and
Gives you a large preview of the actual file. It is also an image for videos. If you want to display the video file use media/photos/<hash> instead.
Gives you a normal preview of the actual file. Can be an image or a video.
Gives you a small preview. Usually only usable with a blur to indicate loading. Could be replaced by blur hash.
Return the actual image or video from the server.

Returns the cropped face image for a photo. The file is created as <hash>_<face_number>.jpg, but Django's default storage appends a random uniqueness suffix when that name is already taken (for example bb6685821c52c994cf7bbe9ebfd5eb7e1_2_fpZqB0S.jpg), so do not construct the name yourself — use the face_url value returned by the faces or persons endpoints.

Returns the avatar for a given user. The frontend uploads it as <first_name>avatar.png (there is no hash component on the first upload); the same random uniqueness suffix is appended on re-upload. Use the avatar_url field from the user endpoints rather than building the name.

Returns the embedded video track of a motion photo (Samsung or Google) as video/mp4. The path segment accepts either the photo UUID (36 characters with 4 hyphens) or the legacy image hash, and returns 404 if the photo has no embedded media file. Used by the frontend lightbox to play the motion-photo clip. Unlike the other endpoints this one does not hard-require the cookie: an unauthenticated request is limited to public photos, and it narrows to the owner's photos when the request is authenticated (bearer header, jwt cookie or Basic auth).

Serves a bulk-download archive as application/x-zip-compressed. The path segment is a filename prefix, not the full filename — the backend appends the requesting user's id and .zip, so a user can only retrieve their own archive. Requires authentication (bearer header or jwt cookie); returns 403 Forbidden otherwise.

Checks if a file exists on the server. The hash is calculated by md5 + user_id Answers {"exists": true, "photo_id": "<uuid>"} for a file you already have, and {"exists": false, "photo_id": null} otherwise; only your own photos count. The photo_id lets a client add a file it already has to the album it is uploading into. New in 1.4.0 Older servers send only exists. Headers:​ Authorization - Bearer <token>

Uploads a file in chunks. On the first chunk leave upload_id empty, you will get a response with the upload_id in the body, which you need to send with the next chunk Form Data:​ file - The chunk of the file, name is blob upload_id - The id of the upload offset - The byte offset of the chunk (sent by the web client, but ignored by the server — see the note below) md5 - The md5 hash of the chunk (not used yet, you can leave it empty) Headers:​ Content-Type - multipart/form-data Authorization - Bearer <access token> (or Cookie - jwt=<access token> as a fallback) Content-Range - bytes <start>-<end>/<total> The server derives the chunk position from the Content-Range header only, not from the offset form field. If the header is omitted it assumes the chunk starts at byte 0, so any upload of more than one chunk must send Content-Range or the second chunk fails with 400 "Offsets do not match". The response body returns the server's authoritative offset (alongside upload_id and expires); use it as the start of the next chunk. Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) An upload expires CHUNKED_UPLOAD_EXPIRATION_DELTA (a day) after its last chunk or completion attempt, and both endpoints answer 410 "Upload has expired" after that; up to 1.6.0 it expired a day after its first chunk and completion did not check it. Two chunks sent for the same offset at once are written once: the second answers 400 "Offsets do not match".

Assembles the uploaded chunks into a single file and imports it. Form Data:​ upload_id - The id of the upload md5 - Just the md5 hash of whole file filename - The original filename device_created_at (optional) - When the device says the photo was taken, used as its date only when the file carries none (screenshots, images saved from messengers). Epoch milliseconds (an integer of at least 11 digits) or ISO 8601. An ISO value keeps its wall-clock time: 2025-10-11T21:30:00-07:00 is stored as 21:30 on 11 October, like a camera's local DateTimeOriginal. device_modified_at (optional) - The same, used when device_created_at is missing or unusable. album_id (optional) - New in 1.4.0 One of your own albums to add the photo to. It is checked before the file is saved: an id that is not one of your albums (someone else's, or deleted) answers 400 with code album_not_found, a locked album 400 with code album_locked, and a value that is not an id 400 with code invalid, in the API's error format (field is album_id). The staged upload is kept after such a refusal, so the same upload_id can be completed again without album_id to put the file in the library only. device_tz_offset (optional) - The device's UTC offset in minutes east of UTC at that moment (-420 for UTC-7; the opposite sign of JavaScript's getTimezoneOffset()). Epoch milliseconds carry no time zone: they are shown at this offset, or in the owner's default time zone when it is not sent. A shorter number or a value that does not parse is ignored. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, epoch milliseconds were stored as UTC time and ISO values as their UTC instant, so these photos could land on the wrong day. Headers:​ Content-Type - multipart/form-data Authorization - Bearer <access token> (or Cookie - jwt=<access token> as a fallback) On completion:​ On success the server: Writes the assembled file to <upload root>/web/<sanitized filename>. The upload root is the user's upload folder when an admin set one, otherwise <scan_directory>/uploads (User.upload_root()). The web/ subfolder is created if missing; web is currently hardcoded as the origin device, so mobile backups land there too. Creates the photo (create_new_image) and queues one background task (django-q), import_uploaded_photo in api/jobs/upload_import.py, that processes it: thumbnails and metadata, then add_photo_to_user_album when album_id was sent (it checks again that the album is still yours and unlocked, and skips it otherwise), the device date fallback, tags, geolocation with the day album's place, and face extraction. A step that fails does not stop the others. Because of this, clients do not need to call /api/scanuploadedphotos/ afterwards; the upload is already imported. New in 1.5.0 Counts the upload in your Import Uploads job (job type 20), opening one when you have none. You have at most one open import job: every upload adds one to its progress_target, and the task adds one to its progress_current once all its steps ran. The job finishes when it is sealed (see POST /api/upload/seal/ below) and every counted upload was processed. A file that makes no photo (a sidecar, embedded media) is not counted, and neither is a duplicate. When the import job finishes, requests your upload follow-ups (api/jobs/upload_followups.py). New in 1.5.0 They run the library-level steps a scan's follow-ups run: search embeddings for photos that have none (with tagging off the per-photo steps store none), a rebuild of the similarity index so new photos show up in semantic and similar-photo search, and encodings for faces that have none (faces read from XMP regions). Then cluster_new_faces queues Find Similar Faces (cluster_all_faces, which queues Train Faces) when the gates in api/faces/clustering_gate.py allow it: at least MIN_NEW_FACES (20) faces past the face watermark and NEW_FACE_SHARE (2 %) of the user's faces, the last clustering at least CLUSTER_INTERVAL (1 h) ago, the last uploaded file UPLOAD_QUIET (30 min) and the last face labelling LABEL_QUIET (15 min) ago, and no scan, face scan, clustering, training or upload import of the user's running. When there are enough faces but a gate holds it back, the run re-arms itself for the earliest allowed time. Every clustering records the highest face id it saw and when it ran (UploadFollowupState.face_watermark, last_clustered_at), and every face labelling, delete or restore stamps last_face_label_at. Requests are debounced per user: the run starts at most two minutes after the first request, so several import jobs in a row get one run, and a request during a run makes it go round once more. The run takes a per-user lease (UploadFollowupState), so two workers never run it at once. Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) A run that finds the lease held looks again when it expires, so the work of a worker that died mid-run is picked up instead of waiting for the next upload. Up to 1.4.0, uploaded photos stayed out of semantic search until the next scan or restart. Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) Deletes the staged upload last. Any failure before that (a full disk while copying, a database error while making the photo or queuing its task) removes the copy, takes back the photo and the job count, and leaves the upload completable: retry /api/upload/complete/ with the same upload_id. Up to 1.6.0 only some failures did, and the others left the upload id answering 400 "Upload has already been marked as complete" or 404. A second completion of the same upload while the first runs answers 400 "Upload has already been marked as complete". Deduplicates by hash: if a Photo with the same hash already exists, or a same-named file in the upload folder has the same hash, the file is not copied and no new import is performed (the endpoint still returns 200); with album_id, the photo you already have is added to that album. If a same-named file exists with a different hash, the image hash is appended to the basename. Response:​ New in 1.5.0 {"job_id": "<uuid>", "photo_id": "<uuid>"}: the import job counting the upload and the photo it made, both null when the file made no photo. A duplicate answers {"detail": "Photo duplicated. No new import performed.", "photo_id": "<uuid>"}, with the photo you already have (null when the identical file is in the upload folder but not in your library yet). Up to 1.4.0, every completion answered {}. The job is a normal job row (GET /api/jobs/), so a client can follow the processing: progress_target: the uploads counted so far, progress_current: those processed, done or failed. Show at most the target: a task that runs after the job was finished as lost can count past it. result.stages: per step (media, album, date, tags, places, faces), how many photos went through it without an error; a step with nothing to do counts as done. result.failed_files: the last 100 photos with an error, {"photo_id", "file", "stage", "error"}, where stage is the first step that failed and photo_id is what this endpoint answered. result.error_count, result.errors, result.status: as for every job. result.lost: uploads that were never processed, when the job was finished as lost (below). result.followups_requested: true once the job finished and requested the follow-ups. The job counts every upload of the user, from the web app, the mobile app or another client, so a client shows it as "your uploads", not as its own files. It does not mark the job queue busy (GET /api/rqavailable/ ignores it), and it cannot be cancelled or removed while it runs (409, code upload_import_running). Error responses: 400 if the user has no configured scan directory, or the configured directory does not exist on disk. 400 "File type not allowed" if the file fails the media-type check (is_valid_media); the chunked-upload record is deleted. Authentication for the upload endpoints Unlike the other endpoints, /api/upload/ and /api/upload/complete/ are plain Django views rather than DRF views, so DRF's authentication never runs. They call JWTCookieAuthentication.authenticate_strict themselves (authenticate_upload_request), which reads an Authorization: Bearer <access token> header first and falls back to the jwt cookie, whose value is the access token set on the response of POST /api/auth/token/obtain/ and POST /api/auth/token/refresh/. Browser clients send the cookie automatically with credentials: "include"; other clients should send the header. A request without credentials returns 403 {"detail": "Authentication credentials were not provided"}, and one with an expired or otherwise invalid token 403 {"detail": "Authentication credentials were invalid"}. A malformed header, or a token for an account that is gone or deactivated, also answers 403 {"detail": "Authentication credentials were not provided"}. Uploads must also be enabled: the endpoints check the ALLOW_UPLOAD site setting first and return 403 "Uploading is not allowed" when it is off, so that 403 is not always an authentication problem.

New in 1.5.0 Tells the server an upload run is over: the import jobs it names take no more files, and finish once their uploads are processed. A file uploaded after that opens a new job. Body (JSON):​ job_ids - The job_id values POST /api/upload/complete/ answered during the run (at most 100). Answers {"sealed_job_ids": ["<uuid>"]}, the jobs this call sealed. A job that was sealed already, has finished or is not yours is left out, not refused. Headers:​ Authorization - Bearer <access token> A client does not have to call it: a job that takes no file for 3 minutes is sealed by a sweeper that runs every minute, the path of the mobile app's backup, which uploads one file at a time with no end. The sweeper also finishes a sealed job whose uploads made no progress for 30 minutes while the job queue is empty (a worker stopped while it held them): the missing uploads count as failed (result.lost) and the follow-ups still run. The web app calls it when its upload queue drains.

New in 1.5.0 What your uploads are doing on the server, for the web app's upload card, the ring around the avatar and its Importing your uploads menu section (#2739). Everything in it is your own, staff included. Query parameters (each repeatable, at most 100):​ job_id - Import jobs POST /api/upload/complete/ answered. They are listed even once they finished, so a client sees them end. photo_id - Uploaded photos to check. Response:​ imports - Your unfinished Import Uploads jobs (from any client, the mobile app's backup included, at most 20) and the named ones, newest first, as GET /api/jobs/ lists them. Their result carries failed_files ({"photo_id", "file", "stage", "error"}, stage media meaning the file could not be read), error_count, lost and followups_requested. ready_photo_ids - The named photos that have their thumbnails, so they show in the timeline. The jobs are read before the photos: a photo whose job is listed as finished and that is not ready never will be. followups - {"state", "next_run_at"}: running while a follow-up run holds its lease, pending while one is scheduled within the next 3 minutes (a run waiting for a quiet period before face clustering is further out and counts as idle), else idle. next_run_at is the scheduled run, or null.

Alias of POST /api/fullscanphotos/ — both are handled by the same view (FullScanPhotosView). Despite the name it is not restricted to the upload folder: it queues a full rescan of the user's entire scan directory, reprocessing every file rather than only new or modified ones. Returns {"status": true, "job_id": "<uuid>", "job_ids": ["<uuid>"]} on success; the job's row exists from that moment. Without a usable scan directory it answers 400, while a scan of the user is still queued or running 409 (code job_already_running, with that scan's job_id in the entry), and when the job cannot be queued 500 (code job_start_failed), all in the API's error format. GET is still accepted but is marked deprecated in the OpenAPI schema (deprecated=True, "Use POST method instead"); new clients should use POST. You normally do not need to call this after an upload — POST /api/upload/complete/ already imports the file, including the caption, geolocation and face-extraction steps.

The deploy/ directory in the monorepo contains the Docker configuration for running LibrePhotos. This includes: deploy/compose/docker-compose.yml - Base configuration (published images), used in both dev and prod deploy/compose/docker-compose.dev.yml - Development overrides (builds from local source, hot reload) deploy/compose/docker-compose.unified.yml - Single-container image with PostgreSQL; reads the same librephotos.env as docker-compose.yml, and api/tests/infra/test_compose_files_in_sync.py keeps the backend environment of the two files equal deploy/compose/docker-compose.e2e.yml - End-to-end test stack (builds from local source) deploy/docker/backend/ - Backend Dockerfile (app layer) and entrypoint.sh, the one entrypoint of the backend and unified images. Image differences are guarded blocks in it (SERVE_FRONTEND for unified) or ENV defaults in a Dockerfile; api/tests/infra/test_deploy_images.py fails on a second copy deploy/docker/backend/base/ - Backend base image Dockerfile (system dependencies, including the Vulkan loader and Mesa's Vulkan drivers for the GPU), published separately deploy/docker/frontend/ - Frontend Dockerfiles (production and development) deploy/docker/proxy/ - Nginx reverse proxy configuration deploy/docker/unified/ - Single-container image (Single Container Deployment) with its own standalone Dockerfile; build it locally from the repo root with docker build -f deploy/docker/unified/Dockerfile .

When modifying Docker files, please ensure: Cross-platform compatibility: Test on both Linux and macOS/Windows (WSL2) ARM64 support: Images should build on both AMD64 and ARM64 (Apple Silicon, Raspberry Pi) Layer optimization: Order commands to maximize Docker layer caching Security: Don't run services as root when avoidable; use minimal base images
File Purpose docker-compose.yml Base configuration, used in both dev and prod docker-compose.dev.yml Development overrides (hot reload, mounted source, pgadmin on :3001)

The backend Dockerfile (deploy/docker/backend/Dockerfile) builds the Django application: cd librephotos/deploy/compose # Test your changes docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml build backend docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d backend # Check logs for errors docker compose logs -f backend

The backend image is built in two tiers. deploy/docker/backend/Dockerfile starts FROM reallibrephotos/librephotos-base:${BASE_TAG} (BASE_TAG defaults to dev), then pip-installs requirements.txt and copies in apps/backend/. The requirements files are copied and installed before the source, so a change that only touches Python code reuses the cached dependency layers. The only system-level dependencies are Python and perl (for the ExifTool wheel), in the separate deploy/docker/backend/base/Dockerfile; libvips, LibRaw, ExifTool, ffmpeg, libpq and OpenCV come from pip as prebuilt wheels (the ones PyPI lacks are built by .github/workflows/prebuilt-wheels.yml). There is no PyTorch: the ML models run on ONNX Runtime, which is a plain pip package in requirements.txt. The base is pulled, not built: docker compose build backend, even with --no-cache, will not rebuild it. To test a change to the base locally, build and tag it yourself first, then rebuild the backend: # from the monorepo root docker build -t reallibrephotos/librephotos-base:dev deploy/docker/backend/base # then rebuild the app layer (from deploy/compose/) docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml build backend The base image is published to Docker Hub by .github/workflows/image-backend-base.yml, which runs only on pushes to dev that touch deploy/docker/backend/base/**. The unified image (deploy/docker/unified/) also builds FROM this base, so a base change affects it too. A release does not rebuild the base: it promotes the current :dev to :<release-tag>, and the release builds of the backend and unified images pass BASE_TAG=<release-tag>, so a published release keeps the base it shipped with.

The frontend has two Dockerfiles: deploy/docker/frontend/Dockerfile - Production build (multi-stage: node:24-slim builds dist/, then halverneus/static-file-server serves it on port 3000 behind the nginx proxy) deploy/docker/frontend/Dockerfile.dev - Development build (hot reload)

The proxy configuration is in deploy/docker/proxy/nginx.conf. After changes: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml build proxy docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d proxy

Environment variables are loaded from the .env file. Key variables for Docker: Variable Purpose Default tag Docker image tag to use latest httpPort Host port for the application 3000 scanDirectory Path to photo library - data Path to persistent data - The dev overlay bind-mounts apps/backend, apps/frontend and packages (the frontend compiles the shared packages/api-client from source) by path relative to deploy/compose/, so there is no environment variable for the source-code location.

Before submitting a PR, from deploy/compose/. Include the dev overlay on every command — the base docker-compose.yml uses published images and defines no build: sections, so docker compose build on its own rebuilds nothing and starts the images pulled from Docker Hub instead of your change: Clean build: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml build --no-cache (this does not refresh the base image — see Modifying the Backend Base Image) Fresh start: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml down -v && docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d Check all services: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml ps (all should be "healthy" or "running") Test basic functionality: Upload a photo, trigger a scan, verify it works Note On a fresh stack, uploads are off by default: librephotos.env ships without an allowUpload entry, so docker-compose.yml passes ALLOW_UPLOAD=false and the upload button is hidden in the UI entirely. Enable it by adding allowUpload=true to your .env before the first start, or by turning on Allow uploads under the app's Admin → Site Settings.

New in 1.5.0 There is no separate GPU image. The backend and unified images ship ONNX Runtime's WebGPU plugin (onnxruntime-ep-webgpu in apps/backend/requirements.txt), and their base image installs libvulkan1 and mesa-vulkan-drivers. apps/backend/service/onnx_session.py puts every model on the GPU when the plugin finds one, and on the CPU otherwise. To try a GPU, give the backend service /dev/dri (Intel, AMD) or an NVIDIA device reservation with NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=compute,utility,graphics, as Utilizing GPU Acceleration shows. The base image change only reaches a local build after you rebuild the base (see Modifying the Backend Base Image). Up to 1.4.0, deploy/docker/backend-gpu/ built a separate NVIDIA-only image, reallibrephotos/librephotos-gpu, on CUDA 12.1.1 and Ubuntu 22.04 (Python 3.10). It is gone, and so is the Python 3.10 floor it set.
Keep images small by: Using multi-stage builds Cleaning apt/pip caches in the same layer Using .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files
Order Dockerfile commands from least to most frequently changed Copy dependency files before source code for better caching Use --parallel flag for multi-service builds

If you encounter permission issues with mounted volumes on Linux: # Check the UID/GID of files in the container docker exec -it backend ls -la /data # You may need to adjust ownership sudo chown -R $(id -u):$(id -g) ./librephotos/data

The frontend is a React 18 single-page app, written in TypeScript and built with Vite. Mantine provides the UI components, TanStack Router handles routing, and TanStack Query handles server state. The full tech stack, the development commands (yarn start, yarn test, yarn build) and the code style conventions are documented in apps/frontend/README.md, which lives next to the code. Please read that first — this page only covers what it does not: debugging, and how the source tree is laid out.

We use ESLint and Prettier to keep our code tidy. Before you commit, run yarn lint:error to check your changes and yarn lint:error:fix to apply the automatic fixes — the ESLint config enforces Prettier through the prettier/prettier rule, so linting also flags unformatted code. The lint-frontend CI workflow runs the lint, test and build steps on every pull request that touches apps/frontend and fails on anything unclean, so nothing un-linted gets merged. yarn build does not type-check, so run yarn typecheck as well. It runs tsc --noEmit over the app and vite.config.ts. The frontend has zero type errors and no baseline: any error fails it, and so does the typecheck-frontend CI workflow. Fix the type rather than working around it. The repository ships a husky pre-commit hook (apps/frontend/.husky/pre-commit, which runs lint-staged), but it is currently inactive in the monorepo: yarn install runs the prepare script — husky — with the working directory set to apps/frontend, which has no .git of its own, so husky exits without registering the hook. Don't rely on it; lint before you commit.

apps/frontend/e2e holds a Playwright smoke suite: log in, the timeline shows photos, the lightbox opens, a favorite toggles and persists, log out. It has its own package.json, separate from the app's. The e2e workflow runs it nightly, on demand, and on pull requests labelled e2e, and uploads the Playwright report, traces and container logs when it fails. Against the Docker e2e stack (what CI does). deploy/compose/docker-compose.e2e.yml builds the proxy, frontend and backend from your checkout, creates admin/admin and scans the eight sample photos in deploy/e2e/photos: docker compose -f deploy/compose/docker-compose.e2e.yml up -d --build --wait cd apps/frontend/e2e yarn install yarn playwright install chromium yarn test # or `yarn test:ui` for the interactive runner docker compose -f ../../../deploy/compose/docker-compose.e2e.yml down -v Against a native stack (no Docker, see Native Windows Setup). Use a fresh data directory and an admin/admin account, copy deploy/e2e/photos to <DataDir>\data\e2e (it has to be inside the backend's data root), then point the suite at the Vite dev server and that folder: $env:E2E_BASE_URL = "http://localhost:3000" $env:E2E_SCAN_DIR = "C:\librephotos-devdata\data\e2e" yarn test The setup step sets the admin's scan directory and starts a scan when the account has no photos yet. A scan started this way first downloads the ML models (about 1.3 GB, once). The specs expect exactly the sample library, so run them against an account with no other photos. E2E_USERNAME and E2E_PASSWORD override the credentials.

New in 1.5.0 The same package takes the screenshots of this site and of the release posts. yarn screens takes every shot listed in e2e/screens/manifest.ts in the light and the dark theme, at 1600 × 1000 and, for the shots marked phone, on a Pixel 7. It writes <id>-<theme>.webp and <id>-phone-<theme>.webp into apps/docs/static/img/shots/ and regenerates manifest.json there, which the <Screenshot id="..." /> component and the release check read. It logs in like the smoke suite, so the same variables apply: cd apps/frontend/e2e E2E_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8080 yarn screens SHOTS=timeline,lightbox yarn screens # only these shot ids SHOTS_DIR=/tmp/shots yarn screens # somewhere else, to look before you replace the docs files yarn screens:unit # the helpers, without a running LibrePhotos Each shot waits for its screen, for the pictures and map tiles in view, and for the page to stop changing. A new shot that looks like the file it would replace (at most 0.2 % of the pixels changed) keeps the old file, so a second run changes nothing. The run says per file whether it kept or wrote it, and how much changed. Shots are WebP at quality 80, or at 70 or 60 when that is what it takes to fit the budget: a desktop shot over 200 KB or a phone shot over 120 KB even at 60 fails its test. The browser clock and the Memories strip are fixed to SHOTS_DAY (default 2026-05-12), so the memories are the same in every run. The e2e stack has the eight sample photos and no machine learning, so it has no faces, places or events: take timeline, lightbox, timeline-filter and category-badge there. The committed landing page shots come from a bigger sample library. Commit only shots made inside the Playwright Linux container (mcr.microsoft.com/playwright, the version of @playwright/test in e2e/package.json): fonts and rendering differ between operating systems, so shots from your machine would change every image. The screenshots workflow does that: started by hand on a branch (default dev) with the shot ids to take, it builds and starts the e2e stack with the sidebar showing the latest release, runs yarn screens in that container, uploads the shots as an artifact, and opens a PR "docs: refresh screenshots" with the files that changed (none changed, no PR). A PR opened by a workflow starts no checks: close and reopen it to run them.
React provides a debug tool, which you can download here.

WDYR explains to you why a component re-rendered, by logging the changed props and hooks to the browser console. It is wired up in src/wdyr.ts and only runs in development builds. Set VITE_APP_WDYR to the literal string true — any other value (True, 1, unset) leaves it off. Where you set it depends on how you run the frontend: Local dev server (yarn start) — add VITE_APP_WDYR=true to apps/frontend/.env.development. Docker dev stack — add VITE_APP_WDYR=true to deploy/compose/.env, then recreate the container so it picks up the new environment: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d frontend Either way the dev server has to be restarted. WDYR needs its own JSX transform, which vite.config.ts only selects when the variable is set at startup, so flipping it mid-session has no effect.
Our REST API is documented with Swagger and ReDoc. Once your development stack is up, both are served from the running instance — see Development Installation for the URLs.

Everything below is relative to apps/frontend/src. routes holds the pages. Routing is file-based: the path of a file determines its URL. Routes under _protected require a logged-in user, routes under public do not, and __root.tsx is the shell they all render into. routeTree.gen.ts is generated from this folder by the TanStack Router plugin — never edit it by hand. Pages should be split up into React components, which you can find in components, grouped by feature. api_client is the web side of the API layer, and every request starts there. The requests themselves live in packages/api-client, which the mobile app uses too: one endpoint function per call in src/endpoints, each parsing the answer with its zod schema from src/schemas and returning the parsed type. api.ts sets up apiClient, the shared client with the web's policy around it: it attaches the access token, refreshes it on a 401, logs out when that fails, rejects a failed request with ApiError, and shows a "please report this" notification when an answer does not match its schema. Around it, one folder per domain (photos, albums, faces, …) holds the TanStack Query hooks the components actually call (useFetch…Query, use…Mutation): each wraps an endpoints.<name>(apiClient, …) call and adds the web's cache invalidation and notifications, with keys from the domain's key factory in packages/api-client/src/hooks/queryKeys.ts, which the mobile app's hooks share. Files under /media/ (thumbnails, originals, videos) get their URLs from mediaUrl and are fetched with fetchMedia, both in api_client/media/mediaUrl.ts. A component never calls apiClient or fetch itself: when it needs a request, add the endpoint and its schema (with a fixture test) to packages/api-client, then a hook to the domain's folder. Lint enforces this: no file in api_client calls apiClient directly or defines its own zod schema (#2347). hooks and service contain cross-cutting hooks and helpers, such as authentication and notifications. locales holds the translations, set up in i18n.ts. Translations are contributed through Weblate rather than edited directly: its librephotos-frontend component translates apps/frontend/src/locales/*/translation.json against the English file, apps/frontend/src/locales/en/translation.json. English ships in the main bundle, and i18n.ts loads every other directory under locales as its own chunk, so a language Weblate adds loads without a code change. To offer it in the Profile language picker, give it an entry in components/settings/languageOptions.ts and a dayjs locale in dayjsLocaleLoaders (i18n.ts); src/i18n.test.ts fails until both are there. The names of things (the words the tagger finds, apps/backend/service/tags/tags.txt) are their own namespace, locales/<lang>/tags.json, loaded only by the pages that show things (hooks/useThingLabel.ts). locales/en/tags.json names every word as itself and is the source a Weblate component translates; src/i18n.tags.test.ts fails when it and tags.txt differ, so a word added to tags.txt goes into tags.json in the same change. Only the display is translated: links and search keep the English word. In util you can find miscellaneous functions.

You can look into the issues here, on what features are missing from the frontend. End-to-end tests live in apps/frontend/e2e. They are a Playwright smoke suite (login, timeline, lightbox, favorites, logout); see End-to-end tests for how to run them. Organizing flows such as duplicates, stacks and user settings are not covered yet, and more coverage is very welcome. You can also help by expanding the documentation.

It uses the endpoints of the backend to upload the files in chunks. The steps are: Only show button if upload is enabled in admin area Even then, the button and the dropzone stay disabled (greyed out, with a "Scan directory not configured - contact administrator" tooltip) if the logged in user has no scan directory. The backend enforces the same rule and answers complete with a 400 when the user's scan directory is unset or does not exist on disk Check if file is on the server by using the exists endpoint. If it is, don't upload it If it isn't, upload it with the upload endpoint If the upload is complete, call the complete endpoint The frontend never triggers a scan itself. While the backend handles complete, it queues a django-q Chain for that one file: handle_new_image, caption generation, geolocation, adding the location to the album dates and face extraction. Duplicates are skipped — the endpoint answers with "Photo duplicated. No new import performed." and no chain is queued. Once the last file is done, the client only invalidates its cached queries (recently added photos, date albums, the "Not in an album" list, count stats, photo month count and storage stats). New in 1.4.0 An upload can go into one of the user's albums (#612). useUploadQueue().start(files, album) gives every queued item that album: the album page's Upload to this album… item and its empty state call it through useAlbumUpload, and the album page names its album to the window-wide UploadDropTarget through useRegisterDropAlbum, so a drop there goes into the album too (a locked album's page only says the files go to the library). The queue sends album_id with complete; when the server refuses the album (album_locked, album_not_found), it completes the same upload again without it and marks the row library only. A file exists already knows is added with one PATCH /api/albums/user/edit/<id>/ per album once the queue drains, using the photo_id that exists answered. The card names the album and links to it, and the album's grid, its card and the "Not in an album" list are refreshed at the end and once more a little later, after the server's import chain has filed the last files. Note GET /api/scanuploadedphotos still exists on the backend, but it is only an alias of the same view as /api/fullscanphotos and nothing in the web frontend calls it. This is implemented in the ChunkedUploadButton component in the frontend. The progress is saved within the state of the component.

The LibrePhotos mobile app lives in apps/mobile/. It is an Expo (React Native, New Architecture) app for Android and iOS with an offline-first data model: a local SQLite mirror of the library, kept current by delta sync against the backend, plus camera-roll backup. The app README is the full developer guide, and the design documents are in plans/mobile-v2/.

You need Node.js 24, which is what CI uses. The app is an npm workspace together with the shared API client in packages/api-client, so install once from the repository root. The root package-lock.json is the only lockfile: npm ci at the repository root cd apps/mobile npx expo start --go and scan the QR code with Expo Go, or build a development build with npx expo run:android / npx expo run:ios The native android/ and ios/ folders are not committed. expo prebuild generates them from app.json.

Every pull request that touches apps/mobile/, packages/ or the root package.json / package-lock.json runs typecheck, lint and the Jest suites in CI. Run the same checks locally before pushing: npm run check --workspace apps/mobile The shared API client has its own checks: npm run test --workspace packages/api-client
English strings live in apps/mobile/src/i18n/locales/en.ts. Other languages fall back to English until translations are added.

Before you begin, ensure you have the following installed: Git - for version control Docker (v20.10+) and Docker Compose (v2.0+) 8GB+ RAM recommended for ML models Info Use absolute paths (not relative) when configuring scanDirectory in your .env file Docker Compose v2 uses docker compose (with a space) instead of docker-compose (with a hyphen)

Create a project directory and clone the LibrePhotos monorepo. All apps (backend, frontend, mobile, docs) and the deploy configs live in a single repository. Linux/macOS: export devdir=~/dev mkdir -p $devdir cd $devdir git clone https://github.com/LibrePhotos/librephotos.git cd librephotos Windows (PowerShell): $Env:devdir = "$HOME\dev" New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $Env:devdir Set-Location $Env:devdir git clone https://github.com/LibrePhotos/librephotos.git Set-Location librephotos

Navigate to the deploy/compose directory and create your environment file: cd deploy/compose cp librephotos.env .env Edit the .env file with your preferred editor and set these important variables: # Path to test photos (create a folder with some sample images) scanDirectory=/home/youruser/dev/test-photos # Internal data directory data=./librephotos/data

docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d The first startup takes 10-20 minutes: The image build downloads the base images and installs the Python dependencies. On first start the frontend container runs yarn install. It does this on every start, so the first start is the slowest. ML models are not downloaded during this step. They are fetched in the background the first time something needs them — saving ML settings, starting a photo scan, or running face recognition — and total several GB.

Once the containers are running, access the application: Application: http://localhost:3000 API Documentation (Swagger): http://localhost:3000/api/swagger API Documentation (ReDoc): http://localhost:3000/api/redoc pgAdmin (Database UI): http://localhost:3001 (user: admin@admin.com, pass: admin — override with PGADMIN_DEFAULT_EMAIL / PGADMIN_DEFAULT_PASSWORD in your .env) Create your admin account through the web interface or via command line: docker exec -it backend python manage.py createsuperuser

Requires Python 3.14 (New in 1.5.0; 3.11 up to 1.4.0) and Node 24 (the version in apps/frontend/.nvmrc); everything else, ffmpeg included, comes from pip. cd apps\backend py -3.14 -m venv .venv .\.venv\Scripts\pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements.dev.txt .\scripts\dev_windows.ps1 -DataDir C:\librephotos-devdata # API on http://localhost:8000 In a second shell: cd apps\frontend Copy-Item .env.development.example .env.development # then set VITE_BACKEND_URL=http://localhost:8000 yarn install yarn start # http://localhost:3000 Create a user with python manage.py createadmin <user> <email> in the backend venv. ML features (faces, captions, tags, semantic search) are off in this stack; see apps/backend/CLAUDE.md.

Both frontend and backend support hot reload: Frontend: Changes to React/TypeScript files automatically refresh the browser Backend: Django auto-reloads when Python files change (you may need to refresh the page)

# All containers docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml logs -f # Specific container docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml logs -f backend docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml logs -f frontend

Backend (Django): docker exec -it backend bash # Now inside the container (/code is apps/backend): python manage.py migrate python manage.py shell python manage.py test api.tests ruff check . # lint ruff format . # format CI runs ruff check apps/backend and ruff format --check apps/backend on every pull request, so run these before pushing or the required lint-backend check will fail. Frontend (Node.js): docker exec -it frontend sh # Now inside the container: yarn lint:error yarn test

Backend (requirements.txt / requirements.dev.txt) — Python packages are installed into the image at build time, so rebuild the image and recreate the container: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml build backend docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d backend A plain build already re-runs pip install, because copying the changed source invalidates the cache; add --no-cache only if you suspect a stale layer. Frontend (package.json) — no image rebuild is needed. The dev image contains no node_modules; the entrypoint runs yarn install into the bind-mounted apps/frontend every time the container starts. Just restart it: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml restart frontend

# Check container status docker compose ps # Restart a container docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml restart backend # Stop all containers docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml down # Stop containers and remove anonymous volumes. NOTE: your photos and database # live in host bind mounts (the `data` / `scanDirectory` paths in your .env) and # are NOT deleted by this — see "Database Issues" below for a real reset. docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml down -v # Access container shell docker exec -it backend bash docker exec -it frontend sh docker exec -it db psql -U docker -d librephotos

VS Code with the Remote Containers extension provides the best experience: Install extensions: Python Pylance Docker Remote - Containers ESLint Prettier Attach to the backend container: Open Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P / Cmd+Shift+P) Run "Remote-Containers: Attach to Running Container" Select the backend container Open the /code folder The repository includes VS Code settings that are automatically mounted.
Go to Settings → Project → Python Interpreter Add Interpreter → On Docker Compose Select both docker-compose.yml and docker-compose.dev.yml Choose the backend service

Using pdb: Add a breakpoint in your Python code: import pdb; pdb.set_trace() Attach to the container to use the debugger: docker attach $(docker ps --filter name=backend -q) When done, press Ctrl+P followed by Ctrl+Q to detach without stopping the container. Using Django Silk: In development mode, access /api/silk for request profiling and SQL query analysis. Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) Silk and django-extensions (shell_plus, show_urls) are in requirements.dev.txt, which the development compose build installs; the released images leave them out.

React DevTools: Install the browser extension WDYR (Why Did You Render): Set VITE_APP_WDYR=true in deploy/compose/.env to log component re-render reasons to the browser console. The value must be the lowercase string true; anything else leaves WDYR off. Recreate the frontend container to pick up the change: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d frontend

# Check logs for errors docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml logs backend # Rebuild the container docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml build --no-cache backend docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d

# Reset the database. The Postgres data is a host bind mount, not a Docker # volume, so `down -v` will NOT clear it — you must delete the directory. docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml down # Remove the DB directory under your `data` path (default ./librephotos/data, # relative to deploy/compose/). The files are root-owned, hence sudo. sudo rm -rf ./librephotos/data/db docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d # Run migrations manually docker exec -it backend python manage.py migrate

If port 3000 is in use, change httpPort in your .env file: httpPort=3080 Avoid 3001: in the dev stack that host port is already taken by the pgAdmin service, whose port is fixed and not configurable through .env.

The dev stack bind-mounts the source into the containers (../../apps/backend and ../../apps/frontend). Compose resolves those relative paths against the location of the compose files you pass to -f — not your shell's current directory — so the code that runs is whatever clone contains the deploy/compose files you launched. If your edits don't appear, make sure you're editing the same checkout you started the stack from, not a copy of it. You can check what is actually mounted with: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml config and reading the resolved volumes: source paths (or run docker inspect backend).
Read the Architecture Overview to understand the system design Check Contribution Guidelines to learn about pull requests Take a look at First Steps to set up your first scan

Several concepts go by different names in the UI, the models, the URLs and the clients. This page says which name is canonical. Name new code (variables, types, endpoints, UI strings, docs) after the term in the first column. Legacy names stay where they are because clients depend on them, but new code does not copy them. Backend paths are relative to apps/backend.

JSON keys are snake_case. api/tests/infra/test_api_naming.py fails on a camelCase serializer field, openapi.json property or dict key; the legacy keys listed there only shrink. A new route takes a photo as Photo.id in a photo_id URL argument; image_hash is for content-hash lookups. The same test fails on a new image_hash URL argument. "Tag" means the user's Tag. What OpenCLIP detects in a photo is a "thing".

Term (UI) Code API Legacy names Photo Photo (api/models/photo.py), a photo or a video; identified by id (UUID) api/photos/ url serializer field (repeats image_hash) Image hash Photo.image_hash: content MD5 plus owner id; names the thumbnail files api/photos/<image_hash>/file/<file_hash>/, main-file/ (the only routes keyed by it) File File (api/models/file.py), one file on disk, keyed by File.hash; a photo has files and a main_file file_variants on a photo File variant Another File of the same photo: RAW next to JPEG, a live photo's video file_variants, api/photos/<image_hash>/file/<file_hash>/ the raw_jpeg and live_photo stack types Embedded media File.embedded_media, a clip extracted from a motion photo embedded_media[].id (a File.hash) File copy FileCopy (api/models/file.py), another path holding the exact bytes of a File; it shares that row, and the scan treats the path as known Thumbnail Thumbnail (api/models/thumbnail.py), sizes in SQUARE_THUMBNAIL_HEIGHTS (api/thumbnails/render.py) and the BIG_THUMBNAIL_HEIGHT setting: big 1080 px by default, grid 500 px and 250 px high, aspect ratio kept (videos: short mp4, plus a WebP still of the same name beside it, the grid's poster, Thumbnail.video_poster) big_thumbnail_url, /media/ square_thumbnails, square_thumbnails_small (directories, /media/ paths), square_thumbnail_url, small_square_thumbnail_url, api-client squareThumbnailUrl, squareThumbnailSmallUrl: not square, kept so files and shipped apps keep working Stack PhotoStack (api/models/photo_stack.py): burst, exposure bracket or manual api/stacks/ Duplicate Duplicate (api/models/duplicate.py): exact copies or visual duplicates, reviewed by the user api/duplicates/ Edit PhotoEdit (api/models/photo_edit.py): a photo's non-destructive edit, one row per photo, owner only: the edit recipe, its history (history, history_cursor), a version and the rendition's state; the original file is never written. api-client PhotoEdit; Photo.edit is its PhotoEditSummary api/photos/<photo_id>/edit/ (OpenAPI PhotoEditState) PhotoEditViewSet (api/photos/edit/<id>/), the api/photosedit/ routes and the OpenAPI component PhotoEdit (PhotoEditSerializer, api-client PhotoEditResponse) are older names for changing a photo's fields and flags, not an Edit Edit recipe The settings of an Edit and of each history step: sparse JSON, {"version": 1} changes nothing; parsed by api/editing/recipe.py, whose CONTROLS holds every range; api-client EditRecipe settings (OpenAPI EditRecipe) Rendition The edited picture at full size the server renders from the recipe (api/editing/renditions.py, protected_media/edits/<image_hash>.jpg); Photo edits are non-destructive: the original file is never written. An edit is a small JSON edit recipe stored next to the photo. Two renderers turn a recipe into pixels and have to agree: the preview in the browser, WebGL2 shaders in apps/frontend/src/components/editor/engine; the rendition on the server, numpy in apps/backend/api/editing, which writes the edited file the rest of the app shows (thumbnails, lightbox, downloads, shares, mobile). This page is the contract between the two. A change to a formula here changes both renderers and the golden values in the same pull request. The stage order follows LightCraft's develop pipeline (geometry, scene-linear, tone map, colour, display); the formulas are our own and much simpler. Backend paths are relative to apps/backend, frontend paths to apps/frontend.

A recipe is sparse: a missing key means its default, and the default recipe ({"version": 1}) changes nothing. Unknown keys are rejected. Numbers outside their range are rejected, never clamped silently. Group Key Range Default UI label version 1 1 geometry orientation 0, 90, 180, 270 (clockwise) 0 Rotate flip_h, flip_v boolean false Flip straighten -45 to 45 degrees 0 Straighten crop null or {cx, cy, w, h}, each 0 to 1, w and h above 0 null Crop aspect null, "original", "1:1", "4:5", "5:7", "2:3", "4:3", "16:9", "16:10" and each ratio's inverse ("5:4", ...) null Aspect ratio (UI lock only) wb temp, tint -100 to 100 0 Temperature, Tint light exposure -5 to 5 (stops) 0 Exposure contrast, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks -100 to 100 0 same curve master, red, green, blue 2 to 16 points [x, y], each 0 to 1, x strictly increasing [[0, 0], [1, 1]] Tone curve color vibrance, saturation -100 to 100 0 same treatment "color", "bw" "color" Black & white mixer red, orange, yellow, green, aqua, blue, purple, magenta each {hue, sat, lum}, -100 to 100 0 Color mixer bw_mix the same eight bands -100 to 100 0 B&W mix grading shadows, midtones, highlights, global each {hue: 0 to 360, sat: 0 to 100, lum: -100 to 100} 0 Color grading blending 0 to 100 50 Blending balance -100 to 100 0 Balance effects texture, clarity, dehaze -100 to 100 0 same vignette amount -100 to 100 0 Vignette midpoint, feather 0 to 100 50 Midpoint, Feather roundness -100 to 100 0 Roundness grain amount 0 to 100 0 Grain size 0 to 100 25 Size roughness 0 to 100 50 Roughness seed integer, 0 to 4294967295 0 detail sharpen_amount 0 to 150 0 Sharpening sharpen_radius 0.5 to 3 1 Radius nr_luminance, nr_color 0 to 100 0 Noise reduction, Color noise The simple mode and the advanced mode of the editor write the same recipe; the simple mode only shows fewer controls.

An edit keeps its history: a list of at most 200 steps and a cursor. A step is the recipe after that step plus what the step did: { "action": "set", "control": "light.exposure", "value": 0.35, "at": "2026-11-12T09:30:00Z", "settings": { "version": 1, "light": { "exposure": 0.35 } } } action is one of set (one control, named by control, with its new value when that is a number, boolean or string), crop, preset (value is the preset id), auto, paste, reset and import. The UI builds the step's label from action, control and value, so labels are translated when shown, never stored. Going to a step moves the cursor and loads its recipe without adding a step; steps after the cursor stay listed until a new edit drops them. The edit's current recipe is the recipe of the step under the cursor (the default recipe when the cursor is -1). When a new step would be the 201st, the oldest one is dropped.

The recipe is applied to the photo's source: the upright picture (file orientation already applied) in the sRGB primaries. Kind From Encoding max srgb8 JPEG, PNG, HEIC, WebP, ... display-referred, sRGB transfer, 8 bits 1.0 linear16 RAW files, developed with FlashRaw (LibRaw for what FlashRaw cannot read) scene-linear, 16 bits, value = max * (u / 65535) ** 2 above 1.0: highlight headroom A linear16 source is the RAW developed with the camera's white balance, clipped highlights, a linear transfer, no automatic brightening and the camera's own white level, so 1.0 of its output is where the sensor clips, whatever the picture holds. FlashRaw develops it (linear-rgb16 in the sRGB primaries, the camera's recommended crop, which is the size of the camera's own JPEG, turned upright by the file's orientation), 5 to 9 times faster than LibRaw with the same levels and colours. A file FlashRaw cannot read (Nikon's High Efficiency NEF, for one) is developed by LibRaw through rawpy instead, with adjust_maximum_thr 0 (LibRaw would otherwise take the brightest pixel of a picture without clipped highlights as the white level and brighten it by up to 0.4 stop); its picture is LibRaw's active area, a few pixels larger than the recommended crop. A load at half the file's size or less (the edit source file, for most cameras) is a 2x2 binned development without a demosaic. That is multiplied by a fixed base gain of 1.4 (half a stop, about what a camera's own rendering keeps above diffuse white), so max = 1.4: the range from 1.0 to 1.4 is the headroom Highlights and Exposure recover, and the roll-off of stage 4.5 folds it into the picture at the default recipe. The preview works on a reduced copy of the source (its long edge at most 2560 pixels, 2048 for linear16: the edit source file below); the server renders the full size. Every spatial amount below is relative to the long edge, so both look alike at the same view size.

LUMA = (0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722) luminance weights of linear sRGB Y(rgb) = dot(rgb, LUMA) oetf(x) = 12.92 x if x <= 0.0031308 1.055 x^(1/2.4) - 0.055 otherwise eotf(e) = e / 12.92 if e <= 0.04045 ((e + 0.055) / 1.055)^2.4 otherwise smoothstep(a, b, x) = t t (3 - 2 t), t = clamp((x - a) / (b - a), 0, 1) mix(a, b, t) = a (1 - t) + b t round(x) = floor(x + 0.5) halves go up, as Math.round does L = long edge, in pixels, of the picture being rendered (after the crop) u = L / 2560 the relative pixel OkLab is Björn Ottosson's, from and to linear sRGB, with his published matrices; C = hypot(a, b) and h = atan2(b, a) in degrees, 0 to 360 (h = 0 when C = 0, where atan2 is undefined in GLSL). Every texture or array lookup outside the picture clamps to the edge. Every lookup at a fractional position is bilinear.

The source has W0 x H0 pixels. k = orientation / 90 quarter turns clockwise give the oriented size W x H (H0 x W0 when k is odd). The flips mirror the oriented picture. The crop is a rectangle of w W x h H pixels centred on (cx W, cy H) and turned with the straighten angle a (radians, positive turns the picture clockwise on screen). Without a crop, cx = cy = 0.5 and w = h = s, the largest rectangle of the picture's own aspect that fits inside it at that angle: s = min(W / (W |cos a| + H |sin a|), H / (W |sin a| + H |cos a|)) The full-size output has Wout = max(1, round(w W)) by Hout = max(1, round(h H)) pixels; a preview scales both by the same factor. Output pixel (i, j) reads the source at: dx = ((i + 0.5) / Wout - 0.5) w W dy = ((j + 0.5) / Hout - 0.5) h H x = cx W + dx cos a + dy sin a y = cy H - dx sin a + dy cos a if flip_h: x = W - x if flip_v: y = H - y k = 0: (xs, ys) = (x, y) k = 1: (xs, ys) = (y, H0 - x) k = 2: (xs, ys) = (W0 - x, H0 - y) k = 3: (xs, ys) = (W0 - y, x) (xs, ys) is in source pixels with pixel centres at half integers. The result is converted to linear light (eotf for srgb8, the square law above for linear16) and called G. The preview linearises before it interpolates when it can (an sRGB texture); a difference of interpolating first stays under the tolerance.

Skipped when nr_luminance and nr_color are both 0. It works on a square-root encoding of G: p = sqrt(max(G, 0)) per channel yp = Y(p) cp = p - yp For the 25 taps (i, j), i and j from -2 to 2, with g(i, j) = exp(-(i i + j j) / 4.5): luminance, taps at (i, j) u pixels, al = nr_luminance / 100, sr = 0.004 + 0.06 al w = g(i, j) exp(-(yp_tap - yp)^2 / (2 sr sr)) yp' = sum(w yp_tap) / sum(w) when al > 0, else yp colour, taps at (i, j) 2 u pixels, ac = nr_color / 100 w = g(i, j) exp(-(yp_tap - yp)^2 / (2 * 0.08 * 0.08)) cp' = mix(cp, sum(w cp_tap) / sum(w), ac) D = max(yp' + cp', 0)^2 Without this stage D = G.

Three blurred planes of D drive the local stages. A plane is D averaged down to the plane size (area average), one value computed per plane pixel, then a Gaussian blur with standard deviation sigma plane pixels (separable, kernel radius ceil(3 sigma)). Plane Long edge Lp Value sigma Used by lc min(256, L) log2(max(Y, 0.0001)) 0.02 Lp Highlights, Shadows, Clarity dk min(256, L) clamp(min(r, g, b), 0, 1) 0.02 Lp Dehaze lf min(1024, L) log2(max(Y, 0.0001)) 0.004 Lp Texture The short edge of a plane is max(1, round(Lp * short / long)). A plane is read at an output pixel's normalised position.
Per pixel, from D (linear) to e (display-encoded, 0 to 1). rgb starts as the pixel of D, and ly = log2(max(Y(rgb), 0.0001)) is taken from it before anything else.
a = dehaze / 100, with x = min(rgb, 1) and rest = rgb - x: a > 0: t = max(1 - 0.6 a dk, 0.4) x = max(0, 1 - (1 - x) / t) a < 0: t = 1 - 0.6 |a| (0.4 + 0.6 dk) x = x t + (1 - t) rgb = x + rest

t = temp / 100, g = tint / 100 k = (2^(0.6 t), 2^(-0.4 g), 2^(-0.6 t)) k = k / dot(k, LUMA) gain = 2^exposure rgb = rgb k gain M = max(1, source.max * max(k.r, k.g, k.b) * gain) M is the largest value a channel can have here. k, gain and M are computed once per render.

dblur = clamp(2^lc gain, 0, 1)^(1 / 2.2) dpix = clamp(Y(rgb), 0, 1)^(1 / 2.2) d = clamp(dblur, dpix - 0.05, dpix + 0.05) ws = 1 - smoothstep(0, 0.5, d) wh = smoothstep(0.5, 1, d) hl = highlights / 100 keep = 1 - min(max(r, g, b) / M, 1)^8 if hl < 0, else 1 rgb = rgb 2^(1.5 (shadows / 100) ws + 0.9 hl wh keep) d is the brightness of the pixel's surroundings, held within 0.05 of the pixel's own so that the edge between a dark object and a bright one gets no halo or bright rim (the smoothsteps are steep there, so a wider band shows as a light band along the edge). keep (from r, g, b after 4.2) leaves alone what is already at the clip level: pulling Highlights down darkens bright areas, and a blown highlight stays white instead of turning grey.

dc = soft(ly - lc) dt = soft(ly - lf) soft(x) = x / (1 + 1.5 |x|) dpix = clamp(Y(rgb), 0, 1)^(1 / 2.2) m = 1 - (2 dpix - 1)^2 rgb = rgb 2^(0.9 (clarity / 100) dc m + 1.2 (texture / 100) dt (0.5 + 0.5 m)) soft keeps small differences as they are and limits large ones, so fine structure gains contrast while a strong edge gets no glow.

Per channel c, with the knee K = 0.8: c = clamp(c, 0, M) if M > 1 and c > K: t = (c - K) / (M - K) p = (M - K) / (1 - K) c = K + (1 - K) (1 - (1 - t)^p) c = clamp(c, 0, 1) e = oetf(c) With M = 1 this is a plain clamp, so an unedited srgb8 picture is unchanged.

e = light(e) per channel, a table of 1024 entries (x = i / 1023, linear lookup) built from Whites, Blacks and Contrast: b = blacks / 100, w = whites / 100, c = contrast / 100 x1 = clamp(x + 0.15 b (1 - x)^3 + 0.15 w x^3, 0, 1) q = 2^(0.75 c) x2 = 0.5 (2 x1)^q if x1 < 0.5 1 - 0.5 (2 (1 - x1))^q otherwise

(Lk, A, B) = oklab(eotf(e)), with C and h from A and B. The hue table has 360 entries (h = i degrees, linear lookup, wrapping at 360) of four values (dh, ds, dl, bw). The bands sit at these hues: red 29, orange 55, yellow 105, green 142, aqua 195, blue 262, purple 298, magenta 330 A hue between two neighbouring bands (going round the circle, magenta to red included) weighs them linearly by its distance to each, and: dh = sum(weight mixer.band.hue) / 100 * 30 degrees ds = sum(weight mixer.band.sat) / 100 dl = sum(weight mixer.band.lum) / 100 bw = sum(weight bw_mix.band) / 100 Then, with mc = smoothstep(0, 0.05, C) and ml = smoothstep(0, 0.12, C): treatment "color": h = h + dh mc C = C (1 + ds mc) Lk = Lk (1 + 0.35 dl ml) skin = exp(-(hue_distance(h, 55) / 25)^2) hue_distance in degrees, 0 to 180 C = C (1 + 0.7 (vibrance / 100) (1 - smoothstep(0, 0.25, C)) (1 - 0.8 skin)) C = C (1 + saturation / 100) treatment "bw": Lk = Lk (1 + 0.5 bw ml) C = 0 Color grading tints by lightness. Each wheel is a vector v = (sat / 100) (cos hue, sin hue): p = 0.5 - 0.25 balance / 100 dd = 0.05 + 0.25 blending / 100 ws = 1 - smoothstep(p - 0.25 - dd, p - 0.25 + dd, Lk) wh = smoothstep(p + 0.25 - dd, p + 0.25 + dd, Lk) wm = max(0, 1 - ws - wh) protect = clamp(Lk / 0.08, 0, 1) clamp((1 - Lk) / 0.04, 0, 1) (A, B) = C (cos h, sin h) + 0.10 protect (ws v_shadows + wm v_midtones + wh v_highlights + v_global) Lk = Lk + 0.2 protect (ws lum_shadows + wm lum_midtones + wh lum_highlights + lum_global) / 100 e = oetf(clamp(oklab_to_linear_srgb(Lk, A, B), 0, 1)) The colour stage is skipped when Vibrance, Saturation, the mixer, the B&W mix and the grading are all at their defaults and the treatment is "color".

e = curve(e) per channel, a table of 1024 entries (x = i / 1023, linear lookup) with three channels: the channel's own curve applied after the master curve, curve_c(master(x)), clamped to 0 to 1. A curve passes through its points with a monotone cubic (Fritsch and Carlson): h_k = x_(k+1) - x_k, s_k = (y_(k+1) - y_k) / h_k tangent at an inner point k: 0 if s_(k-1) s_k <= 0 (w1 + w2) / (w1 / s_(k-1) + w2 / s_k) otherwise, w1 = 2 h_k + h_(k-1), w2 = h_k + 2 h_(k-1) tangent at the first point: s_0; at the last point: s_(n-2) between two points: the cubic Hermite segment of those values and tangents left of the first point: y_0; right of the last point: y_(n-1)
On the display-encoded picture E that stage 4 produced, Ye = Y(e).
