"Before" is the recipe with only its geometry group kept, so the framing matches the edited picture.

An edit is one PhotoEdit row per photo (api/models/photo_edit.py): the recipe, the history, the cursor, a version, the state of the rendition and, while the edit changes the geometry, the face boxes on the unedited picture (below). Only the photo's owner reads or writes it; anyone else gets the 404 of an unknown photo. version goes up by one on every save and on every revert, and never goes back: clients put it into media URLs that are cached for a year, so a number names one picture of a photo for good. A revert therefore resets the row instead of deleting it; the row goes only with its photo. Route Does GET /api/photos/<photo_id>/edit/ The photo's edit. A photo that was never edited answers the default recipe with version 0 and updated_at null; no row is made. A reverted photo answers the default recipe with its last version. PUT /api/photos/<photo_id>/edit/ Saves {settings, history, history_cursor} and renders; answers the edit. DELETE /api/photos/<photo_id>/edit/ Reverts the photo to its original: the default recipe, an empty history, the cursor at -1, rendition none, its files removed, the thumbnails and the face boxes of the original back, and version up by one. A later save goes on from that version. 204, also for a photo never edited, which keeps no row. GET /api/photos/<photo_id>/edit/source/ The reduced source the preview works on, as an edit source file (below). { "photo_id": "4f1c2d3e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001", "settings": { "version": 1, "light": { "exposure": 0.35 } }, "history": [], "history_cursor": -1, "version": 3, "rendition": "pending", "updated_at": "2026-11-12T09:30:00Z" } rendition is none (no edit, a revert, or a recipe that changes nothing), pending, ready or failed. The recipes are stored and answered in their sparse normal form (recipe_to_json): a value at its default is left out, whatever the request wrote out. A photo has something to revert when its history is not empty or its settings are not the default recipe; a version above 0 only says that it was edited at some point. A PUT is refused with a 400 whose errors entry names the field at fault: Code Field When invalid_recipe the dotted path, settings.light.exposure, history.3.settings.curve.master the recipe parser refuses a recipe (unknown key, out of range, not a finite number or too large for a float, a curve's points) invalid_history history it is not a list too_many_steps history more than 200 steps too_large history over 2 MB of JSON invalid_step history.<i> or history.<i>.<key> a step that is not an object, has another key, an action outside the list, a control that is not a dotted path of at most 64 characters, a value that is not a finite number, a boolean or a string of at most 64 characters, an at that is not an ISO 8601 timestamp invalid_cursor history_cursor above the last step (-1 with an empty history) settings_mismatch settings settings is not the recipe of the step under the cursor (the default recipe at -1), compared as recipes not_editable non_field_errors the photo is a video not_decodable non_field_errors the file cannot be read as a picture With an empty history settings stands alone. A photo whose file is not on disk is a 404 file_missing on PUT and on the source route. A save does two renders. The first one runs in the request at the size the big thumbnail needs (its long edge at most 2048 pixels, never larger than the source), and the thumbnails are regenerated from it, so the edit shows everywhere as soon as the save returns. The source it renders from is loaded with its long edge at most 4096 pixels, so the first render of a tiny crop comes out smaller and the rendition makes the thumbnails again. The second render runs in a background task at full size and writes the rendition, a JPEG (quality 92, sRGB, no metadata) at protected_media/edits/<image_hash>.jpg. The task marks the row ready with one update conditional on its version, then puts the file in place, in one transaction: a task whose version is no longer the edit's (after a newer save, a revert or the photo's deletion) writes nothing. A failed one leaves failed, and the thumbnails keep the first render. A recipe that changes nothing has no rendition: the thumbnails come from the original again and the history stays. The first render is kept until the rendition is ready, as protected_media/edits/<image_hash>.preview.jpg. Whatever regenerates a photo's thumbnails (a rotation, a regenerate job, a new big thumbnail height, a rescan) makes them from the rendition when it is ready, else from that file (api/editing/thumbnail_source.py), so nothing renders the recipe again only to make a thumbnail; the photo's rotation is in both already. When the first render was smaller than the big thumbnail wants, the thumbnails are made again once the rendition is ready. The perceptual hash stays the original's, which is what a rescan compares the file with. The first render and the thumbnails are replaced inside the save's transaction, each replaced file kept beside it until the transaction commits (DiskChange in api/editing/files.py). When the save fails at any step, they are put back as they were; when the photo was deleted meanwhile, they are removed. The old rendition and the share copies go once the save commits.

/media/photos/<image_hash> of an edited photo, a still whose recipe changes something, never hands its original to anyone but its owner: Requester ?original=1 Gets the owner no the edited picture the owner yes the original file anyone else: a direct share, an album member, a library share with or without originals, a public link either the edited picture; the parameter is ignored, never an error The edited picture is the rendition when it is ready, else the first render (while pending, and after failed), else a rendition of an earlier version still on disk; a lost first render is made again, and an edit none of whose files can be made answers 404, never the original. A library share without originals, a public link without every switch on and an album that keeps originals back get their metadata-free copy made from that same edited picture. A copy is named after the version and the file it was made from (<image_hash>.edit3.jpg, <image_hash>.edit3-preview.jpg), so a copy of another picture of the photo is never served, and every save and revert clears the copies once it commits. A photo whose recipe changes nothing serves its original as before, and so do videos; zip downloads and the downloads of a photo's files are its owner's only and use the original files.

The photo summaries the grids list carry thumbnail_version: twice the edit's version, plus one once its rendition is ready, and 0 for a photo without an edit row. It never goes back, as version rises on every save and revert. The extra step is there because a save's thumbnails come from its request-time render, and when that render is smaller than the thumbnails want (a tight crop) the server makes them again from the rendition once it is ready, under the same version. The web lightbox likewise puts the rendition state into every picture URL of an edited photo (?v=e<version>-<rendition>), and when the photo details it polls go from pending to ready it refreshes the grids so their tiles pick up the new thumbnail_version. The web grid adds ?v= to its tile URLs, a digest of the ThumbHash and thumbnail_version together (withThumbhashVersion in src/components/react-pig/utils/thumbhashDataUrl.ts), and the server lets the browser keep a versioned thumbnail for a year. A subtle edit such as sharpening or grain may leave the ThumbHash as it was; the version still changes, so the tile URL does. A photo without an edit keeps the URL it always had.

Rotating an edited photo (POST /api/photosedit/rotate/) turns its recipe instead of local_orientation, whose frame the crop is expressed in: the orientation, the flips, the crop's centre and size and the aspect lock turn with the picture (turn_geometry and mirror_geometry in api/editing/geometry.py), a set step of geometry.orientation (or geometry.flip_h) is added after the cursor, and the photo is saved and rendered again. A photo without an edit, or whose edit changes nothing, rotates as before. The photo detail (GET /api/photos/<image_hash>/) carries edit, for the photo's owner only: null for a photo without a rendition (no edit, a revert, or one that changes nothing), else {version, rendition, width, height} with the size of the edited picture at full size. Clients put the version and the rendition state into the ?v= of every thumbnail or full-size URL of an edited photo (the web app sends e<version>-<rendition>), so a cached picture of an earlier state is not shown: under one version, the full-size picture changes when rendition turns ready, and so do the thumbnails when the save's render was smaller than they are. Face boxes are stored in pixels of the big thumbnail, which shows the edit. While the edit changes the geometry, PhotoEdit.face_boxes keeps each face's box on the unedited picture, keyed by the face's id (api/editing/faces.py): { "42": { "unedited": [0.25, 0.25, 0.5, 0.5], "shown": [0, 0, 30, 20], "original": [30, 20, 60, 40], "size": [120, 80] } } unedited is [left, top, right, bottom], 0 to 1 across the upright source, and every shown box is derived from it through the current geometry, clamped to the picture: a box left entirely outside the crop keeps its face, one pixel wide at the edge it left by, and comes back whole with the next crop that shows it. shown is the box last written to the face. A face whose box no longer matches it (moved or resized by the user), or that has no entry (found or drawn while the photo is edited), is taken back onto the unedited picture from its box, unclamped, the next time the boxes are placed. original and size are the face's box and the big thumbnail's size before the first geometry edit: a revert, a reset or a save without a geometry change puts that box back exactly and empties the map. Entries of deleted faces are dropped. Face regions read from the file are of the unedited picture too and are placed on the big thumbnail the same way, and the regions written back to the file are the faces' unedited boxes (to_original_box). The positions of recognised text are left out for a photo whose edit changes the geometry (the text stays searchable). When a scan finds the file of an edited photo replaced (rekey_replaced_file in api/directory_watcher/file_handlers.py), the edit follows the verdict: Verdict The edit the same picture (a metadata write) kept as it is a similar picture (saved again) or one that cannot be compared rendered again from the new file: a new version, a new first render and thumbnails, the rendition queued, the old rendition removed; failed, its files removed, when the new file cannot be rendered a new picture reset like a revert, its files under the old hash removed: a crop made for another picture is not applied to this one; the thumbnails are made from the new original Deleting a photo deletes its edit and both files.

documents.t: GET .../edit/source/ answers application/octet-stream with Cache-Control: private, no-cache and an ETag that changes with the file and the photo's rotation (a matching If-None-Match is a 304): bytes 0-3 "LPES" byte 4 format version, 1 byte 5 kind: 0 = srgb8, 1 = linear16 bytes 6-7 0 bytes 8-11 length N of the header, unsigned 32-bit little-endian bytes 12... the header, N bytes of UTF-8 JSON: {"kind", "width", "height", "full_width", "full_height", "max"} then the payload, to the end of the file width and height are the size of the payload picture, full_width and full_height the size of the full source (both upright). The payload of an srgb8 source is a JPEG (quality 95, no chroma subsampling, no metadata, long edge at most 2560). The payload of a linear16 source (long edge at most 2048) is a zlib stream (the server writes it with Huffman coding only, which is twice as fast as LZ77 matching on these planes and gives a smaller stream) of six planes of width * height bytes each, in the order red high bytes, red low bytes, green high, green low, blue high, blue low. A channel's values are u = round(65535 * sqrt(clamp(v, 0, max) / max)) with the low four bits cleared, then replaced along each row by the difference to the pixel on their left (modulo 65536; the first pixel of a row keeps its value) before they are split into bytes.

The light table, the tone curve table, the hue table and the white balance values are computed by plain functions on both sides (api/editing/tables.py, src/components/editor/engine/tables.ts). api/editing/testdata/goldens.json holds their values for a set of recipes; the backend suite fails when the file is stale and the frontend suite fails when its tables differ from it by more than 1e-4. The same file holds per-pixel cases (input colour, recipe, expected output) for stage 4 and for the vignette and the grain, checked by the backend suite and by the editor's browser test. Per-pixel stages agree within 2/255. The spatial stages (noise reduction, planes, sharpening) use the same definitions on different resampling code and are only compared by eye.

api/editing/testdata/goldens.json is written by python -m api.editing.goldens --write (from apps/backend), computed in float64 and rounded to 6 decimals. Its keys: Key Holds format 1 table_indices the 65 table entries sampled, round(k * 1023 / 64) for k from 0 to 64 hue_degrees the hue table entries sampled: every 5th degree, 0 to 355 pixel_inputs per source_max (1.0 and 1.4), the stage 4 inputs: {rgb, lc, lf, dk}, a linear colour and the plane values it is developed with cases stage 4 cases: {name, recipe, light, curve, hue, runs} finish_points the stage 5 inputs: {uv, e}, a normalised position and a display-encoded colour finish_cases vignette and grain cases: {name, recipe, runs} In a stage 4 case, recipe is the sparse recipe, light the light table at table_indices (a list of 65 numbers), curve the tone curve table there (65 [r, g, b]) and hue the hue table at hue_degrees (72 [dh, ds, dl, bw]). A table that is the identity (light, curve) or all zero (hue) for that recipe is null. Each of its runs is {source_max, wb: {k, gain, M}, e}, where e lists, in the order of that source_max's pixel_inputs, the [r, g, b] stage 4 produces. Geometry, noise reduction and sharpening have no golden values, being spatial. In a finish case each run is {width, height, e}: the output size (Wout, Hout, which the vignette's aspect and the grain cells depend on) and, in the order of finish_points, the colour after the vignette and then the grain (Ye of the grain taken after the vignette), each applied only when its amount is not 0.
LibrePhotos offers two main installation methods to suit different deployment scenarios:

Recommended for most users A simplified single-container deployment that serves both the API and frontend from Django. This method supports both internal and external database configurations: With Internal Database (All-in-One): Beginners wanting a simple setup Users with external reverse proxies (Traefik, Caddy, cloud load balancers) Deployments that don't require nginx-specific optimizations With External Database: Cloud deployments with managed databases (RDS, Cloud SQL) Existing PostgreSQL infrastructure Simplified container management Note New in 1.5.0 The unified image runs the machine learning models on an Intel, AMD or NVIDIA GPU like the standard setup does: give its container the same settings as the backend service in Utilizing GPU Acceleration. Up to 1.4.0 it was CPU-only, and GPU acceleration needed the standard setup with the NVIDIA-only reallibrephotos/librephotos-gpu image.

For advanced users and high-traffic deployments The traditional multi-container setup with separate nginx proxy. Choose this if you: Need nginx-specific features and optimizations Run high-traffic deployments Prefer the original architecture

Unraid Installation - For Unraid NAS systems Windows standalone - One folder with librephotos.exe, no Docker or Python Kubernetes - Kustomize manifests in deploy/k8s, with their own install and upgrade steps

This page is the reference for the environment variables LibrePhotos reads and what each one does. The bundled .env file names most of them in lowerCamelCase (the .env key); with the Compose setup you set the .env key, and the variable is the name the backend container receives. Where a variable has no .env key, pass it to the container directly, as the examples below show.

The bundled Compose files run pgautoupgrade/pgautoupgrade:18-alpine, PostgreSQL 18. Releases up to 1.3.0 used the latest tag, which moves to a new PostgreSQL major as soon as one comes out, so any docker compose pull could upgrade your database. The major is now pinned, and moving to the next one is a LibrePhotos release with its own upgrade note. Back up the database directory (${data}/db, or ${data}/dbcursor with docker-compose.unified.yml) before such an upgrade. Breaking Change With Postgres v18+, mounting a volume to /var/lib/postgresql/data can fail in Docker/Kubernetes due to an upstream change that enforces a new data directory (/var/lib/postgresql/MAJOR/docker) and adds a symlink from /var/lib/postgresql/data to /var/lib/postgresql. Action required: Mount your volume to /var/lib/postgresql instead of /var/lib/postgresql/data. pgautoupgrade will detect any existing data there and migrate it to the new structure.

New in 1.5.0 The regular backend image, reallibrephotos/librephotos, runs the machine learning models (face recognition, semantic search, scene tags, captions, OCR) on a GPU from any vendor: Intel, AMD and NVIDIA. It uses the WebGPU plugin of ONNX Runtime, which talks to the GPU through Vulkan. There is no separate GPU image anymore: releases up to 1.4.0 published reallibrephotos/librephotos-gpu (NVIDIA only, CUDA), which is no longer built. If you use it, switch the backend service back to reallibrephotos/librephotos:${tag} and follow the steps below for your GPU. Without a GPU, or without the settings below, the same image runs every model on the CPU, as before. Nothing has to be configured for that. Intel and AMD: pass the GPU's device nodes to the backend container. The image includes Mesa's Vulkan drivers. services: backend: image: reallibrephotos/librephotos:${tag} devices: - /dev/dri:/dev/dri NVIDIA: this needs a Linux host whose NVIDIA driver includes its Vulkan driver. Check on the host first: vulkaninfo --summary lists the GPU, and /usr/share/vulkan/icd.d or /etc/vulkan/icd.d holds an nvidia_icd.json (or nvidia_icd.x86_64.json). Some distributions ship that part separately, for example libnvidia-gl or nvidia-vulkan-icd on Debian and Ubuntu. Then install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, reserve the GPU for the backend, and ask for the graphics capability: with it the toolkit mounts the host's Vulkan driver into the container. It cannot add one the host does not have, and with only compute the models stay on the CPU. services: backend: image: reallibrephotos/librephotos:${tag} environment: - NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=compute,utility,graphics deploy: resources: reservations: devices: - driver: nvidia count: 1 capabilities: [gpu] Check that the driver arrived in the container: docker compose exec backend ls /usr/share/vulkan/icd.d /etc/vulkan/icd.d lists an nvidia_icd file next to Mesa's. Docker Desktop and WSL2 on Windows: the models run on the CPU there. NVIDIA's driver for WSL2 brings CUDA into Linux containers but no Vulkan driver, and Mesa's Vulkan on Direct3D 12 (Dozen) sees the GPU but WebGPU does not accept it. LibrePhotos running on Windows itself, outside Docker, reaches the GPU through Direct3D 12 instead. Check that it works: when a machine learning service has started its first model on the GPU, the backend log says so, once per service. On Linux ONNX Runtime does not report the GPU's name, so the line shows the vendor, the PCI ids and the slot: ML models run on the GPU through WebGPU: NVIDIA 10de:1f82 at 0000:01:00.0 Without a usable GPU, the log says one of these instead, and the models run on the CPU: No GPU found for WebGPU, ML models run on the CPU. Docker: pass /dev/dri to the container for Intel and AMD GPUs, ... WebGPU failed, ML models run on the CPU from now on: ... The results are the same as on the CPU. On a GTX 1660 Ti, the models ran about 1.6 to 5 times faster than on a 6-core Ryzen CPU. New in 1.5.1 The image's Vulkan includes Mesa's software renderer (lavapipe), which draws on the CPU. In 1.5.0, a container that saw the host's GPU without getting its driver ran the models on lavapipe, about 20 times slower than ONNX Runtime's own CPU code, while the log said ML models run on the GPU through WebGPU: with an empty name (#2445). The machine learning services now start with VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_DISABLE=*lvp*, so Vulkan skips lavapipe and the models fall back to the CPU properly. Setting VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_DISABLE yourself (even to an empty value) replaces that default. On 1.5.0, ONNX_PROVIDERS=CPUExecutionProvider avoids it. Note GPUs in Docker on Linux have not been tested on every setup yet (see #2445). If the log says WebGPU failed although you passed a GPU, check the Vulkan driver files above on the host and in the container. Report what you see on the issue. To keep the models off the GPU, set ONNX_PROVIDERS=CPUExecutionProvider. Which device the models run on​ Every machine learning model runs on ONNX Runtime. The models use CUDA when the installed ONNX Runtime is a CUDA build (onnxruntime-gpu, which the images do not ship), then WebGPU when it found a GPU, then the CPU. Variable Default What it does ONNX_PROVIDERS CUDA if available, then WebGPU if it found a GPU, then CPU Comma-separated ONNX Runtime execution providers, most preferred first; the first one decides the device. CPUExecutionProvider keeps the models off the GPU, for example to leave it to another application, and skips the GPU check. Names the installed ONNX Runtime does not offer are skipped. ONNX_INTRA_OP_THREADS ONNX Runtime's default (one per physical core) How many threads one model may use at a time. See Threads per model. CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES 0 when the container has nvidia-smi Which GPUs CUDA may use, as a comma-separated list of indices (1, 0,1). The entrypoint prints nvidia-smi and sets 0 unless you set it; releases up to 1.3.0 always set 0 in the GPU image. None of them is in the bundled .env file; pass them to the backend container directly: services: backend: environment: - ONNX_PROVIDERS=CPUExecutionProvider Before 1.2.0, every model ran on the CPU, even in the GPU image.

The backend container runs two things: uvicorn, which answers API requests, and a pool of background workers, which scan your library — thumbnails, face detection, captioning. Almost all of the CPU and memory LibrePhotos uses goes to the background workers, and by default there is one worker per CPU core. Start with the worker count, not a CPU limit​ The instinct is to cap the container in docker-compose.yml: services: backend: cpus: 0.8 On its own this usually backfires. A cpus: limit throttles the container, but it does not change how many workers LibrePhotos starts — the worker pool is sized from the number of cores the host reports, which a cpus: limit does not change. You end up with just as many workers competing for a fraction of the CPU, and the API gets slow along with them. So set the worker count instead, with workerConcurrency in your .env (the variable it fills in is WORKER_CONCURRENCY): # One background worker instead of one per core workerConcurrency=1 This is the setting that actually gives resources back to the rest of the machine. Scanning takes longer, but the API stays responsive and nothing gets killed. Each worker is recycled once it passes roughly 300 MB of resident memory, so the worker count is also the main lever on the backend's memory footprint. If you also want a hard cap​ Once the worker count is sensible, a container limit is a reasonable backstop: services: backend: cpus: 2.0 mem_limit: 4g cpuset works too, if you would rather pin LibrePhotos to specific cores than give it a fraction of all of them: services: backend: cpuset: "0-2" Under Docker Swarm the equivalent is a deploy.resources block: services: backend: deploy: resources: limits: cpus: "2.0" memory: 4G Note cpu_shares only sets a relative priority between containers and has no visible effect when nothing else is competing for the CPU, which is why it often looks like it does nothing. Threads per model​ Each machine learning service is a separate process, and by default each model in it may use one thread per physical core. With several of them busy during a scan they compete for the same cores. ONNX_INTRA_OP_THREADS caps every model at that many threads (0 or unset keeps the default), which pairs well with a cpus: limit: set it to the number of cores you give the container, or fewer. New in 1.5.0 The face recognition models follow it too; up to 1.4.0 the library that loads them did not pass the setting through. Memory the models keep between photos​ ONNX Runtime keeps a memory arena per model: once a model has needed a buffer, it holds on to it for as long as the model stays loaded. For text recognition (OCR) and captioning, whose input sizes change from photo to photo, that kept the memory of the largest photo they ever saw, several hundred MB each. Since 1.3.0 those two run without the arena, which costs a few percent of their speed; the other models keep it. ONNX_CPU_ARENA=1 gives every model the arena again, ONNX_CPU_ARENA=0 takes it from every model. New in 1.5.0 That includes the face recognition models, which kept their default up to 1.4.0. The services also start with OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 unless you set it: they do their heavy work in ONNX Runtime, and otherwise every one of them reserved buffers for a thread per core. Warning Do not cap the container so hard that the first scan cannot finish. Face detection and captioning load sizeable models; below roughly 2 GB of memory the backend will be killed by the kernel — and that really is an out-of-memory kill. Requests at the same time​ Two settings size the web API, separately from the background workers. WEB_CONCURRENCY is the number of uvicorn worker processes that answer requests. The bundled .env sets it through gunniWorkers (default 2); the backend image defaults to 1 and the single-container image to 4. WEB_THREADS (default 16) is how many requests each worker serves at once, each holding a thread while it runs. With more than one worker, each is restarted after WEB_MAX_REQUESTS requests. Variable .env key Default What it does WEB_CONCURRENCY gunniWorkers 1 (backend image), 4 (single-container image) Number of uvicorn worker processes. Above 1 each worker is recycled after WEB_MAX_REQUESTS requests, so a recycled one never takes the whole API down. WEB_MAX_REQUESTS (none) 50 (backend image), 2000 (single-container image) With more than one worker, the requests a worker answers before it is restarted. The single-container image serves the web app and the photos through Django too, so it restarts them less often. WEB_THREADS (none) 16 Requests one uvicorn worker serves at the same time; further requests wait for a free thread.

Every part of the library scan that costs real CPU, memory or network can be switched off at deploy time with a FEATURE_* environment variable. All of them default to on, so an upgrade changes nothing until you set one. Accepted "on" values are true, 1, yes and on, and "off" values false, 0, no and off (any capitalisation). Anything else counts as off too, and the backend log says so with a warning that names the variable. An empty value (FEATURE_VIDEO=) also counts as off. Every on/off variable on this page is read the same way, DEMO_SITE, NEXTCLOUD_ENABLED and LOG_TO_CONSOLE included; ALLOW_UPLOAD too, except that an empty value leaves uploads on, as it always has. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, NEXTCLOUD_ENABLED=t also switched the Nextcloud integration on. It now counts as off, so write true. Number variables (worker counts, the TRANSCODE_* limits, REFRESH_TOKEN_DAYS and the like) fall back to their default when empty. A value that is not a number stops the backend at startup with a message that names the variable. Variable .env key What turning it off stops FEATURE_VIDEO featureVideo Video files are no longer imported. A scan skips them the same way it skips a file it cannot read, so no Photo is created and no video thumbnail is generated. The motion video inside a "live photo" is not extracted either, so those stay ordinary still images. FEATURE_FACE_DETECTION featureFaceDetection No faces are extracted from photos, neither during a scan nor when you upload one. The face scan is left out of the scan pipeline and Scan faces in the UI reports an error instead of starting a job. The face recognition service is not started, so its model is never loaded. New in 1.4.0 The model is not downloaded either. FEATURE_FACE_DETECTION_IN_VIDEOS featureFaceDetectionInVideos New in 1.5.0 Videos are read for faces on their first frame only, as up to 1.4.0, instead of on up to 8 more frames across the video (see Faces in videos). The face scan of a video then takes one face recognition call instead of up to nine. FEATURE_FACE_DETECTION has to be on as well. FEATURE_FACE_CLUSTER featureFaceCluster Faces are still detected, but never grouped into people to label. Clustering is skipped at the end of a face scan and Train faces reports an error. FEATURE_IMAGE_CAPTIONING featureImageCaptioning No automatic captions are generated, neither during a scan nor from the "Generate caption" button on a photo. Captions you typed yourself are unaffected. The captioning service is not started. New in 1.4.0 The captioning model is not downloaded either. FEATURE_REVERSE_GEOCODING featureReverseGeocoding GPS coordinates are no longer turned into place names, so no lookups run, offline or at an online map provider. Photos keep their coordinates and still show up on the map of an album and of a single photo, but without a place name they do not appear on the Places page, get no Places album, and cannot be searched by place. Searching for a place in the search bar still works. FEATURE_SCENE_CLASSIFICATION featureSceneClassification Photos are no longer tagged by what is in them (beach, kitchen, sunset, ...), so the "Things" albums stay empty for new photos. The tags service keeps running: the same model makes the semantic-search embeddings. FEATURE_VIDEO_PREVIEWS featureVideoPreviews New in 1.4.0 Videos get no animated preview in the photo grid. A scan makes two WebP stills from the video's first frame instead of encoding two short mp4 clips, which is the slowest step of importing a video and takes most of its thumbnail space. Videos still play in full in the photo viewer. Previews made before stay until the video is rescanned. FEATURE_PROCESS_EMBEDDED_MEDIA featureProcessEmbeddedMedia The short video stored inside a "live photo" or motion photo is no longer extracted, so those files stay ordinary stills. FEATURE_VIDEO has to be on as well for extraction to happen. See Feature Toggles for the one way this switch differs from the others. Turning a feature off never deletes anything that was already generated - the existing captions, faces and place names stay in the database and remain visible. Turning it back on picks up where the scan left off. New in 1.4.0 All of these but FEATURE_PROCESS_EMBEDDED_MEDIA also have a switch in the Features card of the site settings that an admin can flip without a restart. A variable set to off is a hard off that the site setting cannot override; see Feature Toggles. With the bundled Compose setup, set the lowerCamelCase keys in your .env: # A machine without much CPU: keep the photos, skip the machine learning featureFaceDetection=false featureFaceCluster=false featureImageCaptioning=false featureSceneClassification=false If you run your own Compose file or Kubernetes manifests, pass the FEATURE_* names to the backend container directly: services: backend: environment: - FEATURE_VIDEO=false Note FEATURE_PROCESS_EMBEDDED_MEDIA is checked only at the moment a file is first imported. Turning it on for a library that has already been scanned extracts nothing for the photos already there — not even with Rescan all photos — so only files added afterwards are affected. The machine learning services follow the switches​ Note New in 1.2.0 On 1.1.0 the switches stop the processing, but the services still start. The backend runs its heavy models in separate sidecar processes, and a watchdog restarts any of them that dies. A switch that is off keeps its service from being started at all, and the watchdog leaves it alone rather than bringing it back a minute later — which is where the memory saving actually comes from, since a loaded model costs its memory whether or not anything asks it a question. Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) A service whose switch is turned off while it runs is stopped at the watchdog's next check, within a minute. A service that still runs but answers no health check for three minutes, longer than any request to it may take, counts as hung and is restarted; one that is only busy answers in time and is left alone. Switch Service that stops being started FEATURE_FACE_DETECTION face_recognition FEATURE_IMAGE_CAPTIONING image_captioning The remaining services — exif, thumbnail, tags and image_similarity — carry the scanning and search that the rest of LibrePhotos is built on, so they have no switch and always run. tags runs OpenCLIP, which makes the tags and the semantic-search embeddings alike, so FEATURE_SCENE_CLASSIFICATION stops the tagging but not the service (since 1.3.0). The other feature flags (FEATURE_VIDEO, FEATURE_VIDEO_PREVIEWS, FEATURE_FACE_DETECTION_IN_VIDEOS, FEATURE_FACE_CLUSTER, FEATURE_REVERSE_GEOCODING, FEATURE_PROCESS_EMBEDDED_MEDIA) gate work that happens inside the backend itself and have no service of their own to stop. ocr has no environment variable either, but it is not always on: it follows the OCR model choice in Site settings, which ships with nothing selected. The service starts once a model is picked, and stops being started if the choice is set back to none — the watchdog re-reads the setting every minute, so neither direction needs a restart. A configuration the backend cannot read counts as a model being selected, so a database that is still starting can never take the service away. New in 1.4.0 image_captioning follows the Captioning model choice the same way: with None selected the service is not started and the model is not downloaded, even while FEATURE_IMAGE_CAPTIONING allows captioning. A skipped service is named once in the backend log at startup, so docker logs backend tells you why something is not running. The Admin area's Services list shows one as Disabled rather than as unhealthy, and offers no Start button for it.

A video is converted as it plays when the viewer's browser says it cannot play it, or when it turns out not to decode (see Videos your browser cannot play). A user who turns on Always transcode videos (Settings → Experimental) has every video converted. A conversion happening live has no known length, so it carries no Content-Length and no Accept-Ranges, and it cannot be sought at all — no duration, no scrub bar, no skipping. The same conversion is therefore written to a file once, and every later play of that video is served from the file instead, as an ordinary seekable mp4. The first play still streams live and starts exactly as quickly as it does today: the copy never starts alongside a live conversion that has only just begun or is struggling to keep ahead of playback, because that conversion would lose a share of the machine to a second ffmpeg. It starts once the live conversion has finished, or, while that conversion is held to TRANSCODE_LIVE_READRATE, once it is a minute ahead of anything the viewer can have reached, which at the default settings is about half a minute in. Otherwise (a host too slow to get that far ahead, the readrate at 0, or an ffmpeg without -readrate) it waits until the live conversion has finished, or the viewer closes the video, whichever comes first. The copy is also niced and limited to half the cores, so playback, thumbnails and a running scan all outrank it. The cache costs somewhere between 10 and 20 MB per minute of video — how much movement there is in the footage decides where in that range it lands — and only for the converted videos somebody actually opens. No setting has to be on for this: since 1.3.0, a library of HEVC phone videos watched in Firefox fills the cache on its own. A library whose videos all play in your users' browsers, with nobody using Always transcode videos, writes nothing. Variable .env key Default What it does TRANSCODE_CACHE_MAX_GB transcodeCacheMaxGb 10 How large the cache may grow, in GB. Roughly an hour of video per GB. Set it to 0 to switch caching off entirely and keep only the live streaming. TRANSCODE_CACHE_MIN_FREE_GB transcodeCacheMinFreeGb 2 How much free space to leave alone on the volume, in GB. The cache never writes into this, and a conversion already running is abandoned if the free space drops into it. TRANSCODE_CACHE_MAX_CONCURRENT transcodeCacheMaxConcurrent 1 How many conversions may be written at once. Each is an ffmpeg process, so raising this trades CPU for having more videos become seekable sooner. TRANSCODE_CACHE_NICE transcodeCacheNice 10 How far the background conversion stands back from everything else, as a nice value. 0 turns the courtesy off. When either ceiling is reached, the least recently played entries are deleted until the new one fits; if even that is not enough, the video simply is not cached and plays live as before. Nothing is ever served before its conversion has finished, so an interrupted one leaves no half-playable file behind. The files live under protected_media/transcoded/, named by image hash, and are deleted along with the photo. Deleting the directory by hand is safe at any time — it costs only the CPU to convert those videos again.

The conversion a viewer is waiting on is bounded too, and for a different reason than the cached copy. Left to itself ffmpeg uses every core and converts as fast as the hardware allows, so one person opening one video can starve the web UI, a running scan and every other user — while playback needs output only a little faster than real time. The extra throughput buys nothing: on a fast host it races through footage the viewer may never reach. Variable .env key Default What it does TRANSCODE_LIVE_CPU_FRACTION transcodeLiveCpuFraction 2 Cap the conversion at 1/N of the machine's cores. 2 is half; 1 lets it use all of them. Never fewer than one core, whatever the number. The cap is close rather than exact — decoding, filtering and encoding are each held to it, but reading and muxing are not. TRANSCODE_LIVE_READRATE transcodeLiveReadrate 2 Hold the conversion to this multiple of real time, so a minute of video takes about half a minute to convert. Set it to 0 to convert as fast as the host can. TRANSCODE_LIVE_BURST_SECONDS transcodeLiveBurstSeconds 30 How much video to convert at full speed before the rate limit applies, so playback still starts instantly and the browser still has a buffer ahead of it. Unlike the cached copy, the live conversion is not niced: somebody is watching it, so it should outrank the background work rather than yield to it. TRANSCODE_LIVE_READRATE and TRANSCODE_LIVE_BURST_SECONDS need a recent ffmpeg — -readrate arrived in ffmpeg 5.0 and -readrate_initial_burst in 6.1. The images have both. A host supplying its own older ffmpeg (or the GPU image of releases up to 1.4.0, whose ffmpeg was 4.4) does not: there these two settings have no effect and only TRANSCODE_LIVE_CPU_FRACTION applies. Nothing has to be configured for that — the option is simply not passed, and the core cap still holds. TRANSCODE_LIVE_CPU_FRACTION is a divisor, so a larger number means fewer cores: 4 is stricter than 2. Raising it, or lowering the readrate, makes a busy server more responsive while a video is playing; going the other way favours the person watching. If a video stutters on a slow machine, set TRANSCODE_LIVE_CPU_FRACTION to 1 first: a stutter means the conversion cannot keep ahead of playback, and it is the core cap that decides how fast it can go — the readrate is a ceiling it never reached. For scale, one core converts 1080p to 720p at about 1.5x real time, and two at about 2x, so a machine with few cores has little margin at 1080p and none to spare for a second viewer.
documents.s: What a live conversion may take

documents.t: Every photo gets three WebP thumbnails: a big one, 1080 px high by default, which the lightbox shows and the duplicate detection, face detection and search read, and two squares of 500 and 250 px, which the timeline and album grids show by the hundreds. The big one is encoded at quality 95. The squares are encoded at 80 since 1.3.0 (95 before): they come out 60–70 % smaller and encode a third faster, so a grid loads fewer bytes and the server sends more of them per second, for a difference that is hard to see at their size. A video gets a still big thumbnail and, instead of the squares, two short silent mp4 previews of its first seconds, 500 and 250 px high, which the grids play. New in 1.4.0 With the animated previews turned off (FEATURE_VIDEO_PREVIEWS above, or Animated previews in the Features card), a video gets two WebP squares of its first frame instead. Variable .env key Default What it does SQUARE_THUMBNAIL_QUALITY squareThumbnailQuality 80 WebP quality (1–100) of the 500 and 250 px square thumbnails. 95 brings back the old size and look. BIG_THUMBNAIL_QUALITY bigThumbnailQuality 95 New in 1.4.0 WebP quality (1–100) of the big thumbnail. BIG_THUMBNAIL_HEIGHT bigThumbnailHeight 1080 New in 1.4.0 Height in pixels (500–4320) of the big thumbnail. A photo smaller than that is never enlarged. VIDEO_PREVIEW_SECONDS videoPreviewSeconds 5 New in 1.4.0 Length in seconds (1–30) of the animated video previews. VIDEO_PREVIEW_CRF videoPreviewCrf 20 New in 1.4.0 x264 quality (CRF, 0–51) of the animated video previews. Lower looks better and takes more space; every 6 roughly doubles or halves the file size. A value outside its range is set to the nearest limit. The thumbnails stay WebP and the previews mp4: every client and the server's media serving rely on those formats, so there is no setting for the format beyond turning the previews off. A larger or higher-quality big thumbnail looks sharper in the lightbox, especially on a 4K screen, but takes more disk space and makes each scan and the jobs that read it (faces, search, captions) slower. A taller big thumbnail also means fewer RAW files can use the preview their camera embedded, and more of them go through the slower RAW conversion. Longer video previews take longer to make and more space, and the grids download them in full. These settings apply to thumbnails rendered from then on: those of newly scanned photos, and of a photo you rotate or whose file changed on disk. Existing thumbnails keep their size and quality until they are rendered again; there is no job that renders every thumbnail again. When a big thumbnail is rendered again at a new height, the face boxes found on the old one are scaled with it. Do not delete thumbnail files by hand to have them rendered again: a face box is stored in pixels of the big thumbnail its face was found on, and it would no longer line up with the face.

New in 1.5.0 The words LibrePhotos can find in a photo for the Things albums come from a list that ships with it. An admin can add more in a text file, one word or short phrase per line; see Teaching LibrePhotos new things. Variable Default What it does OPENCLIP_CUSTOM_TAGS $BASE_DATA/protected_media/data_models/openclip_vitb32/custom_tags.txt Where that file is. Without the variable LibrePhotos reads custom_tags.txt in the OpenCLIP model folder; in the Docker images that is /protected_media/data_models/openclip_vitb32/custom_tags.txt. A missing file adds nothing.

Once an hour, LibrePhotos marks a job failed when it has made no progress for a day, so a job whose worker was killed (out of memory, a restart) does not keep the queue busy forever. The day counts from the job's last progress, not from its start: a first scan of a large library on slow hardware can take several days and is left alone as long as it keeps importing photos. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, every job was marked failed 24 hours after it started. New in 1.5.0 A job that a running worker is still busy with is never marked failed, however long it goes without progress. Some jobs report none during one long step, such as Find similar faces while it groups the faces of a large library. Up to 1.4.0, such a job could be marked failed while it worked, and still showed as failed after it succeeded. Variable .env key Default What it does STUCK_JOB_HOURS stuckJobHours 24 Hours without progress after which a job that no worker is busy with counts as stuck.

New in 1.5.0 Once a day, and right after the first start, the backend asks GitHub which LibrePhotos release is the newest and tells admins when it is newer than the one they run: an Update available card in the Admin area, a dot next to the version in the sidebar, and on the Windows app a tray menu item and one notification. Users who are not admins see nothing. What is sent: one plain GET https://api.github.com/repos/LibrePhotos/librephotos/releases request, without a login, cookie or anything about your server, its users or its photos. GitHub sees your server's IP address, as with any request. The answer is kept in the database, so the pages that show it never contact GitHub. Development builds (dev, a source checkout) have no release to compare and never ask. Admins can turn the check off in Admin area > Site settings > Check for new releases. To turn it off for good, for example on a server without internet access, set the variable below; the switch is then locked off. Variable .env key Default What it does UPDATE_CHECK updateCheck true false sends no request to GitHub at all and locks Check for new releases off. On the Windows app, set it in a small .cmd file that starts LibrePhotos, as Using another port shows for the service ports.

New in 1.6.0 LibrePhotos keeps the errors of its backend and web app, scrubbed, on your server, and sends nothing until an admin picks a server in Admin area > Site settings > Error reporting or sends a report from Error reports. Error reporting explains the choices and lists exactly what a report holds. Variable .env key Default What it does SENTRY_DSN sentryDsn empty The DSN of your own GlitchTip or Sentry project. Set, it makes My own server available, and Send once and Send all go there while it is chosen. ERROR_REPORTING_MAINTAINERS_DSN (none) the maintainers' project Where Share with the LibrePhotos maintainers and Send once go. Set it empty to make sharing with the maintainers unavailable; set it in the backend's environment, not in .env.

New in 1.6.0 The machine learning models run on ONNX Runtime, Microsoft's inference library. Since its version 1.29, its Linux and macOS builds send usage telemetry to Microsoft by default: which models run (names and hashes of the model files), the hardware and execution provider, errors and timings, and a device id that it keeps under ~/.cache/Microsoft/DeveloperTools/. The events describe the models and the machine, not the photos the models look at. LibrePhotos turns this off: the Docker images set ORT_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1, the backend starts its machine learning services with it unless you set it yourself, and the services also switch off the event logging the Windows build of ONNX Runtime does instead. LibrePhotos 1.5.0 and 1.5.1 shipped ONNX Runtime 1.31 without this, so their Docker images sent the telemetry. 1.4.0 and older used ONNX Runtime 1.27, which had none on Linux. The device id lived inside the container and is gone once the container is recreated. Variable Default What it does ORT_DISABLE_TELEMETRY 1 0 lets ONNX Runtime send its telemetry to Microsoft again.

The backend talks to its helper services (thumbnails, metadata, faces, tags, captions, OCR, search) over HTTP inside the container. They have no authentication, so they listen on 127.0.0.1 only and cannot be reached from outside the container. Variable Default What it does SERVICE_HOST 127.0.0.1 Address the helper services listen on. The backend always calls them on 127.0.0.1, so there is rarely a reason to change it; anything else exposes unauthenticated services to whatever can reach that address. Releases before 1.2.0 listen on 0.0.0.0. New in 1.4.0 Each helper service has its own port. In Docker nothing else runs in the container, so they never need to move. On the Windows standalone build and other installs without Docker, another program on the PC may already use one of them; the service then cannot start, the log and the Services list in the Admin area name the program holding the port, and one of these variables moves the service to a free port. Set it for the whole backend (every process reads it), not for one service alone. Variable Default Service SIDECAR_PORT_IMAGE_SIMILARITY 8002 Similar photos and the second step of semantic search SIDECAR_PORT_THUMBNAIL 8003 Thumbnails of RAW files SIDECAR_PORT_FACE_RECOGNITION 8005 Face detection and recognition SIDECAR_PORT_IMAGE_CAPTIONING 8007 Captions SIDECAR_PORT_EXIF 8010 Reading and writing metadata (ExifTool) SIDECAR_PORT_TAGS 8011 Tags and search embeddings (OpenCLIP) SIDECAR_PORT_OCR 8012 Text recognition A value that is not a port number between 1 and 65535 stops the backend with a message naming the variable.

With the Nextcloud integration switched on, every user enters their own Nextcloud server address, and it is the backend that connects to it. So that this cannot be used to make the backend reach things only it can reach, LibrePhotos looks up the address before each connection and before saving it, and refuses it if the host name resolves to any of these: loopback addresses (localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1), which would be the backend's own services link-local addresses (169.254.0.0/16, fe80::/10), which include the metadata endpoint of cloud providers unspecified, multicast and reserved addresses Redirects from the Nextcloud server are checked the same way. Only http:// and https:// addresses are accepted. Addresses on a private network - your LAN (192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x), a Docker network such as http://nextcloud in the same Compose project, a Tailscale address (100.64.0.0/10) or an IPv6 unique local address - are allowed, because that is where most self-hosted Nextcloud instances live. Variable .env key Default What it does NEXTCLOUD_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ADDRESSES nextcloudAllowPrivateAddresses true Set it to false if users on your instance should only be able to connect to Nextcloud servers on the public internet, for example when you host LibrePhotos for people you do not know and do not want them to reach anything on your local network. NEXTCLOUD_CA_BUNDLE nextcloudCaBundle (empty) New in 1.4.0 Path, inside the container, of a PEM file with the certificates to check Nextcloud servers against, for a Nextcloud with a self-signed certificate or one from your own certificate authority. Empty means the public certificate authorities. With a path set, only the certificates in the file are trusted for Nextcloud, and a missing or unreadable file stops browsing and scanning with a message naming this variable. Certificate checking cannot be switched off. See Nextcloud with a self-signed certificate. A Nextcloud on the same machine as LibrePhotos cannot be reached as localhost; use its Docker service name, or host.docker.internal for one running directly on the host.
documents.s: Which Nextcloud servers may be contacted

documents.t: The backend writes its log files into the directory named by BASE_LOGS. librephotos.log is the one to look at first (ownphotos.log in 1.3.0 and older, see Upgrading); it is also downloadable from the Admin area (see Internal files and Library). Variable Default What it does BASE_LOGS /logs/ Directory the log files are written to. It is created on startup if it is missing; if it cannot be created the backend stops with an error naming the path it tried, rather than starting up with no log at all. With the bundled Compose setup you do not need to set this - the path inside the container is fixed at /logs, and the host directory behind it follows data from your .env (${data}/logs:/logs). Set it when you run the backend outside that setup, for example directly on the host. LOG_LEVEL INFO Lowest level that gets written. One of CRITICAL, ERROR, WARNING, INFO, DEBUG. An unrecognised value falls back to INFO and says so in the log. LOG_LEVELS (empty) Per-logger overrides of LOG_LEVEL, as comma-separated logger=LEVEL pairs, for example api.directory_watcher=DEBUG,nextcloud=WARNING. Logger names are Python module paths, so a package name covers every module in it. A malformed entry is skipped and says so in the log. LOG_TO_CONSOLE 1 Also send the log to the container's standard output, where docker logs backend (or kubectl logs) can read it. Set it to 0 to write only the file. Accepted "on" values are the same as for the feature switches above. LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG adds per-photo and per-request detail. That is what you want while reproducing a bug, but on a large library the file grows quickly - put it back afterwards. If you already know which part is misbehaving, LOG_LEVELS=api.directory_watcher=DEBUG (the scanner, in this example) keeps the rest of the log at its usual volume. Keep LOG_TO_CONSOLE on if the log directory does not survive a restart. On Kubernetes /logs is often an emptyDir, and then standard output, kept by a cluster log collector, is the only copy of the log that can outlive the pod. None of these is in the bundled .env file; pass them to the backend container directly: services: backend: environment: - LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG Warning In 1.3.0 and older, secret.key lives in BASE_LOGS, next to the log files. Zipping that whole folder for a bug report hands out your Django secret key, which is what every session and token on your instance is signed with. Attach ownphotos.log by itself instead. Deleting secret.key is not a fix either: it logs every user out. Releases after 1.3.0 keep the key in protected_media instead and move an existing BASE_LOGS/secret.key there on their first start; see Internal files.

Variable Default What it does DEBUG (off) Set to exactly 1 to run the development settings (librephotos.settings.development), with Django's debug mode on, which shows tracebacks to whoever gets an error, and uvicorn with --reload. true does not count. Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) The released images do not include the development tools (Silk under /api/silk); the development compose build adds them. The bundled Compose file sets DEBUG=0. This is for working on LibrePhotos, not for a server other people use.

Variable Default What it does BASE_DATA / The root of the data LibrePhotos keeps: protected_media/ (thumbnails, converted videos and the machine learning models) and, with SQLite, db/. The containers use /; the Windows standalone app points it at its data folder. PHOTOS $BASE_DATA/data The top folder a library may be scanned from: scan directories must be inside it. The Windows standalone app uses your home folder unless you pass --photos.

Variable .env key Default What it does SECRET_KEY shhhhKey (generated) The Django secret key that signs sessions and tokens. Set it and LibrePhotos uses it. Leave it unset and the backend generates one and keeps it in secret.key in protected_media (in the logs directory in 1.3.0 and older; a newer release moves it on its first start, see Internal files). Changing the key signs every user out.

FRONTEND_BASE_URL is the URL your users actually browse to, for example https://photos.example.com (no trailing slash). Leave it unset and LibrePhotos falls back to the origin each request appears to have arrived on. That fallback is wrong behind the bundled proxy, which forwards /api/ to the backend with the Host header rewritten to backend — a name that only resolves inside the Docker network. The rewrite is deliberate (it means Django's host validation passes whatever domain you use), but it does mean the backend cannot work out its own public address on its own. So set this whenever LibrePhotos has to hand a URL to something outside the container: Password-reset emails — the link in the email. Without it the fallback can produce a link pointing at http://backend/..., which no mail recipient can open. The unified and standalone images accept any Host header, so there the request's origin is only used when it is listed in CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS; otherwise no reset email is sent and the backend log asks for FRONTEND_BASE_URL. A link built from a Host header the requester chose would hand the reset token to whatever site they named. Single sign-on — the OAuth redirect_uri sent to your identity provider, which the browser has to follow and the provider has to recognise. SSO refuses to start rather than send a broken one, so this is effectively required for OIDC.
documents.s: Telling LibrePhotos its own public address

documents.t: The mail server itself is set in the app, under Admin area → Site settings → Email. The variable here only supplies a default. The password-reset rate limit is under Sign-in rate limits. Variable Default What it does DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL LibrePhotos <no-reply@localhost> The sender address for mail when the Email settings have no From address. A From address saved there takes precedence.

New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, only the password-reset request was rate limited. Signing in, refreshing a token, setting a new password from a reset link and signing up are rate limited per client. A client that goes over a limit gets 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header until its counter runs out. Sign-in counts per client address and username together, so people who share an address (a household behind one router) only use up each other's attempts at the same account, and someone guessing passwords for one account does not lock the others out. An admin adding users in the user editor is not limited. Wrong passwords in Basic auth requests (curl -u) come out of the same per-address-and-username budget as sign-in; requests with the right password are not counted. Variable Default What it limits AUTH_THROTTLE_RATE 10/minute Sign-in (/api/auth/token/obtain/) and wrong passwords in Basic auth requests, together, per address and username; setting the new password from a reset link; sign-up and first-time setup. TOKEN_REFRESH_THROTTLE_RATE 60/minute /api/auth/token/refresh/, per address. Every open tab and the mobile app refresh their token every few minutes, and a refused refresh signs the web app out, so keep this well above the number of devices behind one address. PASSWORD_RESET_THROTTLE_RATE 5/hour Requesting a password-reset email, per address. PUBLIC_GALLERY_THROTTLE_RATE 300/minute New in 1.5.0 The public gallery's answers, per signed-in user and, for visitors who are not signed in, per address. A visitor scrolling the timeline asks for one page of photos per day on screen. NUM_PROXIES 1 (Compose, Kubernetes); 0 (unified image, Windows standalone) How many reverse proxies in front of the backend append the client address to X-Forwarded-For. See below. A rate is a number, a slash and second, minute, hour or day (only the first letter counts, so 10/m works too). The backend counts per client address, which it takes from the X-Forwarded-For header: the entry the proxy closest to it added, NUM_PROXIES entries from the end. Entries before that were written by the client and are ignored, so a client cannot pick its own address. Set it to match your setup: Bundled Compose setup: 1, the default. The proxy container appends the client address. Your own reverse proxy (Traefik, Caddy, nginx, a load balancer) in front of the bundled proxy: 2, as long as your proxy also appends to X-Forwarded-For (they all do by default). The Kubernetes manifests set 2 for the ingress controller in front of the proxy container. Unified image or Windows standalone reached directly: 0, their default. The address of the connection is used and the header is ignored. Unified image behind your own reverse proxy: 1. With a value that is too low, every client shows up with your proxy's address and shares its counters, so the limits are reached sooner; sign-in still counts each username separately. With a value that is too high, clients can choose the address they are counted under and get around the limits. The counters are kept in the memory of each backend process. With WEB_CONCURRENCY above 1, each process counts on its own, so a client gets up to that many times the rate before every process refuses it, and a restart of the backend starts every counter again.

CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS (csrfTrustedOrigins in .env) lists the addresses the Django admin at /api/django-admin/ accepts logins from. Set it to the URL your users browse to, including the scheme, for example https://photos.example.com. Several origins are separated by commas: csrfTrustedOrigins=https://photos.example.com,https://photos.internal.lan Each entry must match the address in the browser exactly, scheme and port included. The photo app itself authenticates with JWT and is not affected by this setting. Note Releases before 1.2.0 treated the whole value as a single origin, so a comma-separated list only worked with the unified image.
documents.s: Trusted origins for the Django admin

documents.t: New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the auth cookies were never Secure. Variable Default What it does AUTH_COOKIE_SECURE 0 Gives the sign-in cookies (jwt, and access/refresh after an SSO login) the Secure flag, so the browser sends them over HTTPS only. The backend already marks the cookies Secure when a request reaches it over HTTPS. Behind the bundled proxy it never does: the proxy talks plain HTTP to the backend and forwards its own scheme, which is http when your reverse proxy in front of it terminates TLS, and the backend does not trust a forwarded scheme anyway (Django's SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER is not set). So: Reached only over HTTPS (a domain behind Traefik, Caddy, nginx or a tunnel): set AUTH_COOKIE_SECURE=1 on the backend container. Reached over plain HTTP, also only sometimes (http://192.168.1.10 on the LAN): leave it off. Browsers refuse a Secure cookie over plain HTTP; signing in still works, but photos and videos stop loading. The other flags are fixed: see Cookie flags.

How long a sign-in lasts. Every sign-in uses an access token that expires after 5 minutes and is renewed in the background with a refresh token; when the refresh token expires, the user has to sign in again. Variable Default What it does REFRESH_TOKEN_DAYS 7 Days the refresh token of a normal sign-in lasts. In the browser such a sign-in also ends when the browser is closed. REMEMBER_ME_DAYS 30 Days a sign-in with Remember me ticked lasts, closing the browser included. 0 removes the checkbox from the login page. New in 1.5.0 Up to 1.4.0 there was no Remember me: every browser sign-in ended when the browser was closed or after REFRESH_TOKEN_DAYS. Single sign-on always signs in like a normal sign-in. A sign-in does not get longer by being used: after REMEMBER_ME_DAYS the user signs in again. Logging out ends a remembered sign-in on that browser at once.

DB_PASS (dbPass in .env) is the password of the PostgreSQL user in DB_USER. The bundled Compose file, the unified image instructions and the Kubernetes manifests all pass it. If it is missing, the backend still falls back to the old built-in default password so existing installs keep starting, but it now logs a librephotos.W001 warning on every start (in the migrate output). Set DB_PASS explicitly to silence it; the fallback may be removed in a future release.

These describe the PostgreSQL server. The bundled .env sets the first three; DB_PORT is not in it. Variable .env key Default What it does DB_HOST dbHost db Host name of the PostgreSQL server. The bundled Compose file uses the db service. DB_PORT (none) 5432 Port of the PostgreSQL server. DB_NAME dbName db Name of the database. DB_USER dbUser docker The user the backend connects as. Its password is DB_PASS.

The single-container image (see Unified deployment) has three variables of its own. The Compose stack sets DB_BACKEND=postgresql and leaves the others unset. Variable Default What it does SERVE_FRONTEND (off) true makes the image serve the web app from Django on port 8001, with no proxy in front. Its entrypoint then uses the no-proxy settings. DB_BACKEND sqlite sqlite keeps the database in BASE_DATA/db; postgresql connects with the DB_* variables above. The Compose stack always uses PostgreSQL. DB_BACKUP_KEEP 3 New in 1.4.0 With SQLite, how many of the database backups made before a migration stay in BASE_DATA/db/backups; older ones are deleted. Applies to the Windows standalone build too. See Automatic backups.

DEMO_SITE=true runs LibrePhotos as a public demo: password changes submitted through the API are ignored. It is off unless set to true, 1, yes or on. (Before 1.2.0, any value other than exactly False - including false, 0 or an empty value - switched demo mode on.)

By default LibrePhotos is served from the root of a domain (e.g. https://photos.example.com/). If you need to host it under a sub-path instead (e.g. https://example.com/photos/), the frontend has to know that base path. The frontend reads it from the VITE_PUBLIC_URL build-time variable. It sets the base path the app's static assets are loaded from and the prefix its API calls are made against, and defaults to /. (PUBLIC_URL is also read by vite.config.ts, but only for the asset paths — set it on its own and the app's API calls still point at the domain root and fail, so use VITE_PUBLIC_URL.) Because it is applied when the frontend is built, the prebuilt images are served from /. To use a sub-path you need to build the frontend yourself with the variable set, for example: # building the frontend directly VITE_PUBLIC_URL=/photos yarn build Note Do not add a trailing slash: use /photos, not /photos/. The app joins this value directly with /api and /login, so a trailing slash produces doubled paths such as /photos//api. Vite adds the slash it needs for the asset URLs on its own. The bundled proxy — not the frontend container — is the one published to the host (on httpPort, 3000 by default), and its nginx config matches /api, /media and the other backend paths anchored at the root. So an outer reverse proxy has to strip the sub-path before handing requests on to it, for example: location /photos/ { # the trailing slash on proxy_pass strips the /photos/ prefix proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000/; } Alternatively, re-anchor the location blocks in deploy/docker/proxy/nginx.conf under the sub-path yourself. Warning Sub-path hosting is not fully working today. VITE_PUBLIC_URL re-bases the assets and the API calls, but the client-side router (apps/frontend/src/App.tsx) is created without a matching base path, so once the app has loaded its in-browser routes are still matched against root-relative paths and navigation breaks. Fixing this needs a change in the frontend, not just the build variable.

Container names are set directly in docker-compose.yml through the container_name keys (proxy, db, frontend and backend). Edit those values if you want different names, for example when running more than one LibrePhotos stack on the same host: services: backend: container_name: myphotos-backend These are the names you pass to docker exec, docker logs and similar commands. They are separate from the service names — the proxy:, db:, frontend: and backend: keys themselves — which the containers use to reach each other over the Compose network. The bundled proxy resolves frontend and backend by service name, so leave those keys as they are. Note Older guides mention a make rename helper that rewrote these names from your .env file. It was removed together with deploy/Makefile; edit docker-compose.yml directly instead.

Variable Default What it does BACKEND_HOST backend The host name the bundled proxy gives the backend in the Host header. Django accepts it in ALLOWED_HOSTS, and requests carrying it count as coming from inside the deployment. Change it only together with the backend service name, which the proxy resolves. WEBSERVER_UID 101 The user ID the proxy's nginx runs as inside its container. The media diagnostics use it to explain why a file cannot be served. WEBSERVER_GID 101 The group ID, as WEBSERVER_UID. Set both only if you rebuilt the proxy to run as another user. The Kubernetes config sets 65534, the user the Pod runs as.
documents.s: Backend host name and proxy user IDs

documents.t: These are now site settings: setting them here only supplies the default used on the first set-up, after which the value lives in the site settings and any change you make there takes precedence. # Comma delimited list of patterns to ignore (e.g. "@eaDir,#recycle" for synology devices) skipPatterns= # Allow uploading files allowUpload=true # Where place names come from: exiftool (offline, the default), nominatim, # mapbox, maptiler, tomtom or opencage. mapApiProvider=exiftool # API key for the geocoding map provider. Only needed if you switch the provider # to Mapbox, MapTiler, TomTom or OpenCage; ExifTool and Nominatim # (OpenStreetMap) need no key. mapApiKey= The same settings have environment variables, which set the first-run default in the same way: Variable .env key Default What it does on the first set-up SKIP_PATTERNS skipPatterns (empty) The patterns of files and folders to ignore, as in the example above. ALLOW_UPLOAD allowUpload true Whether uploads are allowed. An empty value leaves them allowed. MAPBOX_API_KEY mapApiKey (empty) The key for the geocoding provider, as in the example above. MAP_API_PROVIDER mapApiProvider exiftool The geocoding provider: exiftool (offline, no key needed), nominatim (no key needed), mapbox, maptiler, tomtom or opencage. It applies only until the setting is first stored, which happens with the first place lookup or a save in Site settings, so changing it on an install that has already geocoded photos does nothing: change Map provider in Site settings instead. New in 1.4.0 The default was nominatim up to 1.3.0, and the compose files did not pass it on. MAP_TILE_PROVIDER (none) photoprism The map background behind the photo pins. You can change it afterwards in Site settings, without a restart. GEOCODE_LANGUAGE (none) (empty) New in 1.5.0 The language online map providers name places in: a code such as de or pt-BR, or for Nominatim a list in order of preference such as de,en. Empty asks for the provider's default, as before. Mapbox and ExifTool ignore it. You can change it afterwards in Site settings, as Place name language; see Place names in your language.

New in 1.4.0 DEFAULT_FAVORITE_MIN_RATING no longer exists as a variable. Up to 1.3.0 it set the rating a photo needs to count as a favourite for users created afterwards (default 4). It is now always 4, and a value you set is ignored. Users who already exist keep their own value, which they change under Settings, in Minimum image rating to interpret as favorite (see Settings). If your .env sets it, you can remove the line. A value other than 4 also made the models disagree with the database migrations; that no longer happens.

userName, userPass and adminEmail are not site settings. They are still live environment variables, wired to ADMIN_USERNAME, ADMIN_PASSWORD and ADMIN_EMAIL in docker-compose.yml: # Username for the Administrator login. userName=admin # Password for the administrative user you set above. userPass=admin # Email for the administrative user. adminEmail=admin@example.com Whenever both userName and userPass are set, the entrypoint runs createadmin on every container start. All images do this the same way, including the single-container image: On the first start it creates the superuser. The username is lower-cased, and adminEmail is used for the account. A blank adminEmail creates the account without an address; you can add one in the UI later. On every later start the existing user's password is overwritten with userPass. Leaving userPass set therefore resets the admin password on each restart — a password you changed in the UI will not survive a docker compose restart. This is the same behaviour described under How to change the admin password, when you can't log in. adminEmail is only applied when the account is first created; on later starts createadmin ignores it (and says so in the log when it differs), so the address you set in the UI stays. Releases up to 1.3.0 had the single-container image write adminEmail to the account on every start, clearing the address when adminEmail was blank. To stop the password from being reset, clear userPass (or userName): the entrypoint then skips createadmin. Releases up to 1.3.0 still ran it with only userName set, and it aborted on each start with "Admin password cannot be empty".
We recommend you use docker compose as this matches the demo and development environment the most.
You need an x86 or ARM64 processor, and it is recommended to have 4GBs of RAM. Due to limited memory & processing power, ARM64 will not be as fast.
You will need at least 10 GB of HDD Space for the docker images, thumbnails, database and machine learning models.

Clone the repo: git clone https://github.com/LibrePhotos/librephotos.git Navigate to the deploy/compose folder: cd librephotos/deploy/compose Copy the template variable file (containing options such as the location of your photos): cp librephotos.env .env Info It is important that you rename it to .env. Otherwise docker compose cannot find your variables. Open .env in your favorite text editor and make the required changes. E.g., using nano: nano .env Do not forget to create the directories you specified in the .env file if they do not exist. PostgreSQL v18+ Volume Mount Change If you are using Postgres v18+, you must mount your database volume to /var/lib/postgresql instead of /var/lib/postgresql/data. See the advanced usage guide for details. Start LibrePhotos with docker compose up -d You should have LibrePhotos accessible after a few minutes of boot-up on localhost:3000

Once LibrePhotos is running, you'll be guided through a First Time Setup Wizard that will help you: Create your admin account Configure site settings (uploads, user registration) Set up your photo scan directory For more details, see the first steps guide.

To update LibrePhotos when using Docker Compose, first refresh your checkout so you also pick up changes to docker-compose.yml, then update the running containers. From the librephotos/deploy/compose folder that was created when you installed LibrePhotos, run: git pull # updates docker-compose.yml and the other tracked files docker compose down docker compose pull # only refreshes the container images docker compose up -d While the backend updates the database, the web app says "LibrePhotos is updating", and docker compose ps shows the backend as starting until it serves (healthy). If the update fails, the backend stays up as unhealthy and the web app says why; see "LibrePhotos is updating". New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0 the backend had no healthcheck, and a failed update restarted it in a loop. Coming from 2025w44 or older? Releases after 1.1.0 cannot upgrade a database from before 2026w10 directly. Go through 1.1.0 first, as described in Upgrading from a release older than 2026w10. Coming from 1.2.1 or older? Run the thumbnail cleanup once after the update, so older thumbnails stop carrying the photo's GPS position. See After upgrading from 1.2.1 or older. Note docker compose pull only downloads newer container images. docker-compose.yml is a tracked file in the repository and gains new settings over time. Recent versions, for example, added the lines that pass workerConcurrency and frontendBaseUrl from your .env through to the backend, and changed the database volume path for Postgres v18+. If your docker-compose.yml predates those changes, setting the matching variables in .env has no effect until you git pull. Your .env is not tracked by git, so git pull will not touch your settings. After updating, compare it against the shipped librephotos.env to pick up any newly documented variables. If you edited docker-compose.yml yourself — for instance to pass a GPU to the backend or to set resource limits, as described in the advanced usage guide — git pull may refuse to update or report a conflict. Run git stash before the pull and git stash pop afterwards, then re-apply your changes on top of the updated file.
Single container deployment serves both the LibrePhotos API and frontend from one unified container. Choose between internal database (SQLite) or external PostgreSQL.
Best for: Simple home servers, quick testing, first-time users

Create directories for data mkdir -p /home/yourusername/librephotos/{db,protected_media,logs} Start LibrePhotos sudo docker run -d \ --name librephotos \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 3000:8001 \ -v /home/yourusername/librephotos/db:/db \ -v /home/yourusername/librephotos/protected_media:/protected_media \ -v /home/yourusername/librephotos/logs:/logs \ -v /path/to/your/photos:/data \ -e SERVE_FRONTEND=true \ -e DB_BACKEND=sqlite \ reallibrephotos/librephotos-unified:latest Access: http://localhost:3000 Notes: Secret key: Optional - if not provided, one will be generated and saved to /protected_media/secret.key (/logs/secret.key in 1.3.0 and older; a newer release moves it on its first start). Do not delete this file (see Internal files). To supply your own, pass -e SECRET_KEY=... Database: SQLite file will be created automatically in the /db directory. New in 1.4.0 Before an update migrates it, the container copies it into /db/backups and keeps the newest three (see Automatic backups) Updates: New in 1.4.0 While the container updates the database, the page says "LibrePhotos is updating" and opens LibrePhotos by itself when it is done; a failed update stays on a page that says why instead of restarting the container (see "LibrePhotos is updating") Photos: You can mount your photo directory read-only (-v /path/to/photos:/data:ro), but this disables uploading, deleting photos, and writing metadata back to files — uploads are otherwise written to an uploads/ folder inside /data. Uploads are on by default, so if you use :ro, also pass -e ALLOW_UPLOAD=false (or turn off "Allow Upload" in the setup wizard). See Why is the scan directory not mounted read-only?
Best for: Cloud deployments, existing PostgreSQL, production setups

Existing PostgreSQL: New in 1.5.0 LibrePhotos needs PostgreSQL 15 or newer (Django 6.1 dropped 14). Up to 1.4.0, PostgreSQL 14 worked. Upgrade an older server before you update LibrePhotos; the bundled Compose setup already runs 18. Create the database and a user that owns it. On first start the container runs manage.py migrate as this user, so it must be able to create tables — and since PostgreSQL 15, GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE no longer conveys that. Make the app user the database owner instead: CREATE USER librephotos_user WITH PASSWORD 'your_secure_password'; CREATE DATABASE librephotos OWNER librephotos_user; If the database already exists, run ALTER DATABASE librephotos OWNER TO librephotos_user;.
