For a database carried over from PostgreSQL 14 or earlier, also connect to it (\c librephotos) and run GRANT ALL ON SCHEMA public TO librephotos_user;. New PostgreSQL container: Create a shared network first so the database and LibrePhotos containers can reach each other by name, then start PostgreSQL on it (creating the database through POSTGRES_USER/POSTGRES_DB makes librephotos_user its owner, so no extra grants are needed): sudo docker network create librephotos-net sudo docker run -d \ --name librephotos-db \ --network librephotos-net \ --restart unless-stopped \ -e POSTGRES_DB=librephotos \ -e POSTGRES_USER=librephotos_user \ -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your_secure_password \ -v /home/yourusername/postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql \ postgres:18 PostgreSQL 18 is the major the Compose setup runs. From 18 on, the image keeps its data under /var/lib/postgresql, not /var/lib/postgresql/data. If you started the database with an older version of this page (postgres:17, mounted at /var/lib/postgresql/data), recreate that container with its old tag and mount: the official image does not upgrade an existing data directory, and pointing postgres:18 at it starts an empty database.

sudo docker run -d \ --name librephotos \ --network librephotos-net \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 3000:8001 \ -v /home/yourusername/librephotos/protected_media:/protected_media \ -v /home/yourusername/librephotos/logs:/logs \ -v /path/to/your/photos:/data \ -e SERVE_FRONTEND=true \ -e DB_BACKEND=postgresql \ -e DB_NAME=librephotos \ -e DB_USER=librephotos_user \ -e DB_PASS=your_secure_password \ -e DB_HOST=librephotos-db \ -e DB_PORT=5432 \ reallibrephotos/librephotos-unified:latest Set DB_HOST to match your database: Sibling librephotos-db container: keep --network librephotos-net and use -e DB_HOST=librephotos-db (the container name), as shown above. DB_HOST=localhost will not work — inside the container it points back at LibrePhotos itself, not the database. Existing PostgreSQL server: drop --network librephotos-net and set -e DB_HOST=<hostname or IP of that server>. If it runs on the Docker host itself, add --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway and use -e DB_HOST=host.docker.internal, and make sure PostgreSQL listens on all interfaces with a matching pg_hba.conf entry.

If you put this container behind an HTTPS reverse proxy (Traefik, Caddy, a cloud load balancer), add -e CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://photos.example.com (comma-separated for several origins; each must include the scheme and match the browser-visible address exactly). The unified image starts with an empty trusted-origin list, so without it the Django admin at /api/django-admin/ rejects logins with a CSRF error. The photo app itself is unaffected — it authenticates with JWT and its API endpoints are CSRF-exempt. Also add -e NUM_PROXIES=1, so the sign-in rate limits count each client by the address your proxy passes on instead of counting everyone as the proxy (see Sign-in rate limits).

Once LibrePhotos is running, you'll be guided through a First Time Setup Wizard that will help you: Create your admin account Configure site settings (uploads, user registration) Set up your photo scan directory For more details, see the first steps guide.

You have to download docker-compose. You can add the following to your /boot/config/go file to make sure it's always available: curl -L "https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/download/v2.5.0/docker-compose-$(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" -o /usr/local/bin/docker-compose chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-compose Check if it's working: docker-compose --version You'll need to create a folder under /mnt/user (e.g. librephotos) within there you'll need two files: mkdir /mnt/user/librephotos && cd /mnt/user/librephotos Download this file and save it as .env: wget -O .env https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LibrePhotos/librephotos/dev/deploy/compose/librephotos.env ​Download this file to the same directory, but keep the original name: wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LibrePhotos/librephotos/dev/deploy/compose/docker-compose.yml You'll need to edit the .env file and set the two mandatory variables: scanDirectory, the folder holding your photos (e.g. /mnt/user/pictures), and data, a folder for LibrePhotos' internal state - its database, protected media, logs and model cache (e.g. /mnt/user/appdata/librephotos). Create both folders before you start the stack, and keep note of the default HTTP port, 3000. The map API key is no longer set in this file. After first boot, set it under your avatar -> Admin area -> Site settings. See Old environment variables if you'd rather seed it as a first-boot default. You should have LibrePhotos accessible after a few minutes of boot-up on unraidip:3000 unless you changed this in the .env file. ​Once done, you can fire up the containers by typing: docker-compose up -d This will cause the containers to startup in the background. You can check the status of them by running: docker logs {container name} You can get a name for each of the containers by typing: docker ps | grep librephoto Finally, you can access the UI by going to http://unraidip:3000 Furthermore, you can also monitor progress from the shell prompt by tailing the backend log. It lives at logs/librephotos.log inside the data folder you set in .env (with the example above, that is /mnt/user/appdata/librephotos/logs/librephotos.log; ownphotos.log in 1.3.0 and older, see Upgrading): tail -f /mnt/user/appdata/librephotos/logs/librephotos.log Or, independent of where you mounted it - the backend container is always named backend: docker exec backend tail -f /logs/librephotos.log To shut everything down: docker-compose down If you want to grab any updates, run: docker-compose down docker-compose pull docker-compose up -d Running docker-compose pull on its own only downloads the new images; the containers keep running the old ones until they are recreated, so pull the images and then bring the stack back up. If your install is on 2025w44 or older, go through release 1.1.0 first; see Upgrading from a release older than 2026w10. Coming from 1.2.1 or older, run the thumbnail cleanup once after the update; see After upgrading from 1.2.1 or older.

After a reboot, docker-compose is not installed anymore, since unRAID loads everything from ram. Someone created a Docker Compose Manager app in the Apps catalog for unRAID. This makes sure docker-compose is installed every time you reboot unRAID, and they are currently working on a Web GUI. Thanks to u/Tusc00 and Martijn (Spiek90) for this write-up!
Next, take a look at the first steps after setup.

Every LibrePhotos release brings its own database migrations. The backend applies them by itself each time it starts, so upgrading is normally just pulling the new images and starting them again. The exact commands depend on how you installed LibrePhotos: Standard Docker setup Single container deployment: pull reallibrephotos/librephotos-unified again and recreate the container. unRAID Windows standalone: New in 1.5.0 Download update on the Update available card (or in the tray menu), then Restart to update. By hand, and up to 1.4.0: quit LibrePhotos from the tray, rename the old program folder, unzip the new release next to it and start it. Kubernetes: the image tags in kustomization.yaml are pinned, so check out the new release's tag, whose manifests name its images. Since 1.3.0 the manifests run PostgreSQL 16 instead of 13, so an older install moves its database with a dump and restore first. New in 1.5.0 LibrePhotos needs PostgreSQL 15 or newer. The bundled Compose files (18) and the Kubernetes manifests (16) already run a newer one; if you point LibrePhotos at your own PostgreSQL 14 or older, upgrade that server before you update LibrePhotos, or the backend stops at start with an error naming the version. Back up your database before any upgrade. It is the only way back if a migration fails halfway, and it is cheap: # Standard Docker setup, from the folder with your docker-compose.yml and .env docker compose exec -T db pg_dump -U docker librephotos > librephotos-backup.sql Replace docker and librephotos with the dbUser and dbName from your .env if you changed them. The Windows standalone build and the single container deployment with SQLite make this backup themselves, see below. On Windows, also keep your own copy of the db folder and of protected_media\secret.key on another drive, as Backing up and restoring shows step by step.

New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the web app showed empty pages or the login toast "No connection to backend server, try again in a few minutes." while the backend was not answering. While the backend updates the database or starts up, the web app shows a page that says so instead of the login or your photos. It checks every 5 seconds and goes back to where you were by itself when LibrePhotos answers again; Check now asks at once. LibrePhotos is updating: the database update is running. A few minutes is normal; a large library can take longer. Do not stop the containers or quit the Windows app in the meantime. After 15 minutes the page adds a hint; if nothing changes for an hour, look at command_migrate.log in the logs folder. LibrePhotos is starting: the update is done and the backend is starting its services. LibrePhotos is not answering: the browser gets no answer from the backend at all, for example while its container restarts. If this lasts, check that the backend container (docker compose ps) or the Windows app is running. The update could not finish: the database update stopped with an error, and LibrePhotos did not start. Your photos are unchanged. The reason is in the logs folder, in command_migrate.log (Docker) or console.log (Windows app). This LibrePhotos is too old to update in one step (reason code E001): see Upgrading from a release older than 2026w10. This database belongs to a newer LibrePhotos (reason code E002): see Going back to an older release. On a failure page, For the person who runs this server shows the reason code, and Copy details (on HTTPS and localhost) copies the state, reason code, version and time for a support question.

From the moment the backend container or the Windows app starts until LibrePhotos serves, a small start-up page answers on the backend's port and says what is going on. With the standard Docker setup the web app shows it as described above. The single container and the Windows app also show it as a plain page of its own, so opening LibrePhotos during an update shows LibrePhotos is updating instead of "connection refused". The Windows app opens your browser on it right away. After a failed update the backend no longer exits and restarts in a loop. It stays up and keeps showing the failure page: Too old (E001) or newer database (E002): nothing is tried again, because the fix needs you (see the linked sections). Restart the container, or start the Windows app again, after you fixed it. Any other reason: Docker tries the backup and the update again after 30 seconds, 1, 2 and 5 minutes, then every 5 minutes, so a database that came up late still gets there by itself. The Windows app shows the failure page until you close its message box. The page never shows error messages or file paths, only the reason code; the details are in the logs folder: command_migrate.log, or command_backup_database.log when the backup before the update failed (Docker), and console.log on Windows. With Docker Compose, the backend's healthcheck asks /api/healthz/ready, so docker compose ps shows the backend as starting while it updates, healthy once it serves, and unhealthy after a failed update (the healthcheck gives an update 15 minutes before it counts). /api/healthz answers from the first seconds on, so scripts that wait for LibrePhotos to serve should ask /api/healthz/ready instead.

New in 1.5.0 When a newer release is out, admins see an Update available card at the top of Account menu > Admin area: "LibrePhotos 1.5.0 is available", the release you run, and when the new one was published. The sidebar shows a dot next to the version, with "Update available: 1.5.0" when you point at it. How to update opens the steps for your install: Windows, or the top of this page for Docker and the rest. The Windows app shows Download update instead, then Restart to update, and installs the release itself (Updating from LibrePhotos). Release notes opens the release on GitHub. Read them before you update: some releases ask you to do something once. Skip this release hides the card and the dot until a newer release comes out. Undo in the message that follows, or Show it again under Check for new releases in Site settings, brings it back. The close button hides the card for a week. Only admins see it. The card comes from a daily check that can be turned off; see Checking for new releases. Docker installs that run the dev image, and installs from source, have no release to compare and never show it.

New in 1.5.0 After an update, each user sees a small What's new card once, in the bottom left corner of the first page they open (on a phone, above the menu at the bottom). It lists the highlights of the new version, the same ones as the "What's new for you" part of the release notes. When you skipped a few updates, it shows the highlights of up to three of them. See what's new opens every highlight with a Learn more link to these docs and, where it fits, Open to go to the place in the app. Several versions have a switch at the top. Release notes opens the release post on this site. The close button hides the card. Closing the card or opening See what's new counts as seen, on every browser and device of that user, so the card does not come back until the next update. Account menu > What's new and the version line at the bottom of the sidebar show the highlights again at any time (while a newer release is out, the version line takes admins to the Update available card instead). Admins also see how many tasks the Finish the upgrade card still has. The highlights are part of the app, so nothing is downloaded and nothing about your server is sent. They are in English for now. Someone who joins after an update does not get the card for that version, and installs that run the dev image never show it. Each user can turn the card off under Settings > Interface, and admins can turn it off for everyone under Site settings with Show users what's new after an update.

New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the work an update left was only described in the release notes, and some of it needed a terminal. Some updates leave work to do once: data an older release stored needs reading again or cleaning up. LibrePhotos checks after each start what this server still needs, and shows it to admins on a Finish the upgrade card at the top of Account menu > Admin area. While anything is left, the avatar in the top right corner has an orange dot and the Admin area item in its menu shows how many tasks are left. Nothing is shown to other users, and nothing blocks the app meanwhile. Each task has one row: what it does, why, and what happens to your photos (they are never changed). A running task shows how far it got and links to its job, which also shows in Worker logs and on the avatar's progress ring. Automatic tasks start by themselves after the update. If one fails, its row says why and offers Retry; it is not started again by itself. Optional tasks wait for you: Start runs it, Not now hides it for good. While another job runs, Start waits and says so. When a task is done, its row says so for a day, then goes; the card goes with its last task. A new install never shows the card: the tasks are about data an older release left behind. Task Kind When it shows Update search for the new search model Automatic Photos still have search data from an earlier search model. Search results may be incomplete until it finishes. Remove photo details from old thumbnails Automatic After updating a server that already had photos: thumbnails from 1.2.1 or older carry the photo's location (details). Read shutter speeds again Automatic After updating from 1.3.0 or older with shutter speeds stored wrongly (details). Make still pictures of older videos Automatic New in 1.5.0 After updating a server that already had videos: the photo grid shows a still picture of each video and plays it only while you point at it (Make Video Posters). Move faces tagged on a turned picture Optional New in 1.5.1 After updating a server where a photo has a face without an encoding next to one with: faces imported from tags a quarter turn off the face are moved onto it (Repair Turned Faces). Read colour information of older videos Optional Videos added before LibrePhotos checked their colours when scanning, while ffprobe is available (Probe videos).

New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, nothing was backed up automatically. When a start brings database migrations, the Windows standalone build and the single container deployment with its internal SQLite database copy the database first, before anything else opens it. Nothing is migrated without that copy. A start without migrations writes nothing. The copies go into a backups folder next to the database: Install Backups folder Windows standalone %LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos\db\backups (or db\backups in your --data-dir) Single container with SQLite backups in the folder you mount at /db Each backup is named after the release that made it, which is the release you updated to, and the time in UTC, for example librephotos-<release>-20261013T083000Z.sqlite3. It holds the database as the release you ran before left it, so it is what you need to go back to that release. A .json file with the same name says which migrations were about to run. The newest three are kept; set DB_BACKUP_KEEP to keep more or fewer (see Environment variables). Each one is about as large as the database. A backup needs twice the size of the database in free disk space. If there is less, LibrePhotos does not start and says how much space to free (on Windows in a message box, in Docker in command_backup_database.log in the logs folder). Only the database is copied. Thumbnails, converted videos and the machine learning models can all be made again, and a migration never changes your photos. PostgreSQL databases are not backed up automatically: use pg_dump as shown above.
documents.s: Automatic backups with SQLite and on Windows

documents.t: Quit LibrePhotos (on Windows: Quit LibrePhotos in the tray menu; in Docker: docker stop librephotos). In the db folder, rename librephotos.sqlite3 (for example to librephotos.sqlite3.broken). If librephotos.sqlite3-wal and librephotos.sqlite3-shm are there, rename them the same way. Copy the backup from db/backups into the db folder and name it librephotos.sqlite3. Start the release you ran before the update. On Windows, put its program folder back (Going back to the previous release) or unzip its librephotos-windows-x64.zip from the releases page; for Docker, use that release's image tag. Starting the release named in the backup's file name, or any newer one, on the restored database runs the update again, after making a new backup.

New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, an older release started on a newer database without a word and failed later, when it saved a change. A release cannot run on a database that a newer release has migrated: the newer release changed tables the older one does not know about. LibrePhotos refuses to start in that case and says so (in a message box on Windows, in command_migrate.log in the logs folder with Docker): ?: (librephotos.E002) The database 'default' was last used by a newer LibrePhotos release (it has migration api.0170_..., which this release does not know). Running this older release on it could damage it. HINT: Start the newer release again, or restore the backup made before that upgrade ... Nothing has been changed at that point. Either start the newer release again, or go back with the database as it was before the upgrade: SQLite (Windows standalone, single container with SQLite): restore the automatic backup made before the upgrade. Its file name names the release you upgraded to, and it holds the database as the release before left it. PostgreSQL: restore the pg_dump you made before upgrading into an empty database, then start the older release. Changes made since the upgrade (faces named, albums edited, photos added) are not in the backup. The next scan finds photos that were added since. Releases after 1.3.0 keep the secret key in protected_media/secret.key and move it there from the logs folder on their first start. 1.3.0 and older look for it in the logs folder (logs\secret.key on Windows, /logs/secret.key in Docker): when you go back to one of them, copy the key there first. Without it, that release makes a new key, everyone has to log in again, and the saved email server and Nextcloud passwords have to be entered again.
documents.s: Going back to an older release

documents.t: New in 1.5.0 Some hosts (Coolify, Kubernetes) start the new container before they stop the old one. Once the new release has migrated the database, the old release's background worker takes no more tasks and leaves them to the new one. Its log says: A newer LibrePhotos release migrated the database (api.0193_...), so this cluster takes no more tasks and leaves them to that release This works when the release you upgrade from has it. A worker of 1.4.0 or older can still take the new release's first scheduled tasks and log errors like Function api.updates.check.check_for_updates is not defined. They do no harm: each schedule runs again on its next turn, the update check the next day.
documents.s: While the old container is still running

documents.t: Thumbnails made by 1.2.1 and older still carry the photo's EXIF and XMP: its GPS position, camera serial number and keywords. A public link serves those thumbnails, so anyone holding one can read the location, even with location sharing off. Since 1.3.0, new thumbnails are written without it, but the ones already on disk keep it until you run the cleanup once. New in 1.4.0 It runs by itself after the update, and the Finish the upgrade card shows its progress. Up to 1.3.0, it had to be started by hand. An admin can also start it in the web app: Account menu > Admin area > Admin tools > Remove photo details from old thumbnails, then Start. It runs as a job over the thumbnails of every user. The row shows how far it got and links to the job; its progress also shows in Worker logs and on the avatar's progress ring. The job ends as failed, with the count and the thumbnails it could not clean, if any thumbnail still carries metadata afterwards. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the cleanup was only available as the command below. To run it from a script, or without the web app, use the management command: # Standard Docker setup, from the folder with your docker-compose.yml and .env docker compose exec backend python manage.py strip_thumbnail_metadata # Single container deployment docker exec librephotos python manage.py strip_thumbnail_metadata On the Windows standalone build, open cmd, go to the program folder and run the command with start /wait, as Running a command shows step by step: cd /d "C:\Users\<you>\LibrePhotos-app\librephotos" start /wait librephotos.exe manage strip_thumbnail_metadata rem With another data folder, --data-dir comes before manage: start /wait librephotos.exe --data-dir D:\LibrePhotos manage strip_thumbnail_metadata Both only rewrite thumbnails that still carry metadata, and keep their pixels and colour profile, so running them again is safe. Add --dry-run to the command to only count them. See Management Commands.

New in 1.5.0 The Windows app of 1.3.0 and 1.4.0 was built without a module it needs for the perceptual hash of a photo. Every photo it scanned or received as an upload stopped right after its thumbnail: the scan job counted it as failed, and the photo has no date, place or camera details, and no search text. Docker installs were not affected. After updating to 1.5.0 or newer, each user scans once: Go to Account menu > Library and click Scan. A plain Scan is enough: it reads every photo whose details were never read, whatever its file date. Rescan does it too, but reads every photo again and takes longer. It is done when the job in Account menu > My jobs has finished. Places, faces, things and search follow by themselves after the scan. If you use them, run Detect duplicates (on the Duplicate photos page), Detect photo stacks and Generate event albums again, because they only ran on the photos that had a date and a hash. If you skip it, those photos stay without a date (they show up under Without Timestamp) and without a place.

New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the shutter speed shown in Info was stored wrongly for fast and long exposures: anything faster than about 1/2000 s as 0, 1/1250 to 1/2000 s as 1/1000, and 2.5 s as 5/2. The old value cannot be repaired from the database, so the exposure time of those photos is read again, once. New in 1.4.0 This runs by itself after the update, as the Read shutter speeds again job, and the Finish the upgrade card shows its progress. Only that one value is read from each photo and only the shutter speed is stored; your files are not changed. To run it again from a script, use the management command: # Standard Docker setup, from the folder with your docker-compose.yml and .env docker compose exec backend python manage.py refresh_exposure_time # Single container deployment docker exec librephotos python manage.py refresh_exposure_time On the Windows standalone build, run start /wait librephotos.exe manage refresh_exposure_time in cmd, from the program folder (see Running a command; with another data folder, --data-dir comes before manage). It reads only the exposure time and writes only the shutter speed, so running it again is safe. Add --dry-run to only count the photos. A Rescan from the Library page fixes them too.

New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the backend log in the logs folder (BASE_LOGS, /logs in the container) is called ownphotos.log. Newer releases call it librephotos.log. The first start of a newer release renames ownphotos.log and its older parts (ownphotos.log.1, ownphotos.log.2, ...) to the new name, so the history is kept, and logs a warning saying so. The lines in it look the same as before. Anything that reads the file by name has to be pointed at the new one: Promtail, Fluent Bit or Vector configs, fail2ban filters (logpath), tail -f aliases and scripts. The Server logs download in the Admin area follows by itself. If the old file cannot be renamed (on Windows, another program such as an editor or a log viewer has it open), it is left as it is, the backend logs a warning and writes to a new librephotos.log. The same happens to an old file found next to an existing librephotos.log: it is left alone, and the log says so once. Delete ownphotos.log once you no longer need it. The .__ownphotos.lock file next to it is no longer used either and can be deleted.
documents.s: The log file is now librephotos.log

documents.t: Releases after 1.1.0 combine the first 100 database migrations into a single one. That keeps new installs and the test suite fast, but it means these releases can no longer bring a database from an older release up to date on their own. Your current release What to do 2026w10, 2026w14, 2026w25, 1.0.0 to 1.0.3, 1.1.0, or anything newer Upgrade directly, as usual. 2025w44 or older Upgrade in two steps, as described below. Installs on 2026w10 or later can upgrade directly. Older installs must first upgrade to any release from 2026w10 up to 1.1.0 (1.1.0 is the last release with the individual migrations), start it once so its migrations run, and then upgrade to the latest release. If you skip the intermediate step, nothing is changed: the backend stops before migrating and its log (command_migrate.log in your logs folder) says which release to go through first: ?: (librephotos.E001) The database 'default' was created by a LibrePhotos release older than 2026w10: ... HINT: Upgrade in two steps. First run any release from 2026w10 up to 1.1.0 ...
documents.s: Upgrading from a release older than 2026w10

documents.t: Back up the database as shown above. In your .env, pin the intermediate release by setting tag=1.1.0. Then pull and start it: docker compose pull docker compose up -d docker compose logs -f backend Wait until the backend has finished migrating and LibrePhotos opens in your browser as usual. Migrating a large library can take a while; do not stop the containers in the meantime. Set tag back to latest (or the release you want to run), then pull and start again: docker compose pull docker compose up -d For the single container deployment the steps are the same: run reallibrephotos/librephotos-unified:1.1.0 once with your existing data, wait for it to finish starting, then switch back to reallibrephotos/librephotos-unified:latest.

If you run 1.2.0 or newer, you can always upgrade directly. Otherwise, before upgrading, ask the backend you are running now: docker compose exec backend python manage.py showmigrations api | grep -E '0100_|squashed_0100' If this prints [X] (or [-]) in front of 0100_metadataedit_metadatafile_photometadata_stackreview_and_more or of 0001_squashed_0100, your database is recent enough to upgrade directly. Releases since 1.2.0 print the second one. If it prints [ ] in front of 0100_metadataedit_..., or nothing at all, use the two-step upgrade.
documents.s: Not sure which release you are on?

documents.t: Download librephotos-windows-x64.zip from the latest release (64-bit Windows). Every release since 1.2.0 carries it under Assets on the releases page. New in 1.4.0 The same zip is also there as librephotos-<version>-windows-x64.zip, so a downloaded file says which release it is, next to SHA256SUMS to check your download. A new release becomes the latest one only once its Windows zip is attached, a few hours after it is published; until then this link gives the previous release.

A single folder, librephotos\, holding librephotos.exe and everything it needs: the API server, the web frontend, the job workers, every machine learning sidecar, ExifTool and ffmpeg. The backend is compiled with Nuitka, so no Python, Docker or database server has to be installed. The database is SQLite, the same setup as the single container deployment with its internal database. It is meant for one person's library on their own PC. For a shared server, or for PostgreSQL, use one of the Docker deployments. LibrePhotos keeps two things apart: The program folder: the librephotos folder from the zip, with librephotos.exe. An update replaces it. The data folder, %LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos: the database (users, albums, people, settings), thumbnails, the machine learning models and the logs. An update keeps it, and every copy of the program uses the same one. Your photos stay in your own folders. LibrePhotos reads them there and never moves them into either folder.

Download librephotos-windows-x64.zip (see above). It is about 450 MB. To be sure it arrived complete, check it. Open your Downloads folder, right-click librephotos-windows-x64.zip and choose Extract All.... In the box under Files will be extracted to this folder, replace the suggested path with a folder in your user folder, for example C:\Users\<you>\LibrePhotos-app (with your Windows user name instead of <you>), and click Extract. Choosing a folder says why. Windows creates the folder and puts a librephotos folder in it. Open C:\Users\<you>\LibrePhotos-app\librephotos and double-click librephotos.exe. Windows may show Windows protected your PC, because the program is not signed: click More info, then Run anyway. No window opens: LibrePhotos runs in the background with an icon in the notification area (the tray, bottom right), and your browser opens http://localhost:8000/. While the first start sets up the database, the page says "LibrePhotos is updating" and turns into LibrePhotos by itself. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0 the browser only opened after the first migrations. Windows 11 may put a new icon behind the ^ arrow (Show hidden icons) next to the clock; drag it from there onto the taskbar to keep it in view. Create the admin account on the first-time setup screen, then set the scan directory of your user (Admin area → Users) to the folder with your photos and start a scan. The models for face recognition, tagging, captions and semantic search are downloaded on the first scan, into the data folder; that needs an internet connection once. To start LibrePhotos from the desktop next time, right-click librephotos.exe and choose Show more options → Send to → Desktop (create shortcut) (on Windows 10: Send to directly). Right-click the tray icon for Open LibrePhotos (also a plain click), Check for updates (see Knowing when there is an update), Open data folder, Open logs and Quit LibrePhotos. Quitting stops everything: the workers and the machine learning processes are children of librephotos.exe and go down with it, also when it is ended from Task Manager. If it cannot start, a message box usually says why: for example that another program already uses port 8000 (see Using another port). New in 1.4.0 The icon appears right after the double-click. While LibrePhotos starts, the first, greyed line of its menu and its tooltip say what it is doing: Starting..., Updating the database (3 of 7) after an update with database changes, Starting services..., and finally Running at http://127.0.0.1:8000/. The first start after such an update also shows a notification, because updating the database can take a few minutes. Quit LibrePhotos works during the start too. Only one LibrePhotos runs per data folder. Starting it again while it runs just opens the browser on the running one. New in 1.4.0 A start while the first one is still starting shows the notification "LibrePhotos is already starting", waits for it and then opens the browser; nothing else happens. Once the first one shows its start-up page, a second start opens the browser on that page at once. Up to 1.3.0 a second start during the first one's database update started a second copy, which could show an error and stop the first copy's background services. Started from a terminal instead, it prints its log there and Ctrl-C stops it; --no-tray leaves the icon out. Without a terminal that output goes to console.log in the logs folder. New in 1.4.0 The log of the start before is kept as console.previous.log next to it, so a failed start can still be explained after you tried again. For commands, see Running a command.

New in 1.4.0 Every release lists the SHA-256 checksums of its zips in a file called SHA256SUMS, under Assets next to the zip. If the checksum of your download is the same, the file arrived complete and is the one the release build made. It does not say who made the build: the program is not signed yet. Download SHA256SUMS from the same release as the zip, into the same folder (usually Downloads). Open that folder in File Explorer, click the address bar, type powershell and press Enter. Paste these lines into the blue window and press Enter: $zip = "librephotos-windows-x64.zip" $line = Select-String -Path SHA256SUMS -SimpleMatch -Pattern " $zip" | Select-Object -First 1 (Get-FileHash $zip -Algorithm SHA256).Hash -eq $line.Line.Split(" ")[0] For the zip with the version in its name, put that name in the first line instead. True means the download is fine. False means the file is incomplete or not the release's: delete it and download it again. You can also compare by eye: Get-FileHash librephotos-windows-x64.zip prints the Hash, and SHA256SUMS (open it with Notepad) has the same value in small letters in front of the file name.

Put the program folder in your own user folder, for example C:\Users\<you>\LibrePhotos-app. Windows lets you change files there without administrator rights, so an update is just unzipping, and LibrePhotos can create the extra process names it needs next to librephotos.exe (see What the processes are). Avoid these places: C:\Program Files: unzipping there, and every update after it, needs administrator rights, and every process shows up as librephotos.exe. The Desktop, Documents, or another folder OneDrive backs up: the program files then sync to the cloud. The folder Extract All... suggests, Downloads\librephotos-windows-x64: it works, but it is easily deleted when you tidy up Downloads, and you then end up with the program in Downloads\librephotos-windows-x64\librephotos\. Whichever folder you choose, the library is the same: the data folder does not depend on where the program is.

LibrePhotos runs as a handful of processes, each under its own name in Task Manager's Details tab, tasklist and Resource Monitor, so you can see which part is busy: Process What it does librephotos.exe The one you started: web server and API. Closing it stops all the others. librephotos-jobs.exe Runs the background job queue (scans, thumbnails, machine learning jobs). librephotos-worker.exe The job queue's workers and helpers; two workers by default. librephotos-thumbnails.exe Thumbnails for RAW photos. librephotos-metadata.exe Reads and writes EXIF/XMP metadata (ExifTool). librephotos-faces.exe Face detection and recognition. librephotos-similarity.exe The similar-photos index. librephotos-tags.exe Automatic tags, and the image and text embeddings for semantic search. librephotos-captions.exe Image captions. librephotos-ocr.exe Text recognition, once an OCR model is selected. The extra names are hard links to librephotos.exe that are created next to it on the first start; they take no additional disk space. If the folder is read-only they cannot be created, and every process simply shows up as librephotos.exe. The machine learning processes only listen on 127.0.0.1.

What Where Database db in the data folder, %LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos\db (--data-dir to move the whole data folder) Database backups made before an update New in 1.4.0 %LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos\db\backups (see Upgrading) Secret key %LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos\protected_media\secret.key (1.3.0 and older: logs\secret.key, see below) Thumbnails, profile pictures, machine learning models %LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos\protected_media Logs %LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos\logs (tray: Open logs) Photos Stay where they are; scan directories may be anywhere under your home directory (--photos to allow another top directory, e.g. --photos D:\) To open the data folder, choose Open data folder in the tray menu, or type %LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos into the address bar of File Explorer and press Enter.

librephotos.exe --help librephotos.exe run --port 8080 --no-browser librephotos.exe --data-dir D:\LibrePhotos --photos D:\Pictures librephotos.exe --data-dir D:\LibrePhotos run --port 8080 librephotos.exe manage createadmin -u admin admin@example.com librephotos.exe manage <any manage.py command> --data-dir and --photos belong to librephotos.exe itself, so they come before run or manage: librephotos.exe run --data-dir D:\LibrePhotos is refused, and after manage they are handed to the command, which does not know them. Two background workers run the scan, thumbnail and machine learning jobs. That suits a single-user PC; set WORKER_CONCURRENCY before starting librephotos.exe to use more (each worker is a full copy of the backend, a few hundred MB of RAM). The environment variables of the Docker images work too, set in the console before starting librephotos.exe; the data directory options above only fill in BASE_DATA, BASE_LOGS and PHOTOS when they are not set. A default SECRET_KEY is generated and kept in protected_media\secret.key in the data directory (releases after 1.3.0; 1.3.0 and older kept it in the logs directory, and a newer release moves it on its first start).

Some release notes ask you to run a command once after an update. librephotos.exe is a Windows program without a window of its own, so cmd and PowerShell do not wait for it; start /wait makes cmd wait and keeps the output in order: Start the new release once, as usual, so that it updates the database. It may keep running while the command runs. Press Windows key + R, type cmd and press Enter. Go to the program folder (the quotes matter if the path has spaces): cd /d "C:\Users\<you>\LibrePhotos-app\librephotos" Run the command, for example the thumbnail cleanup from Upgrading: start /wait librephotos.exe manage strip_thumbnail_metadata With another data folder, put --data-dir before manage: start /wait librephotos.exe --data-dir D:\LibrePhotos manage strip_thumbnail_metadata Piping works as well: librephotos.exe manage strip_thumbnail_metadata | more.

LibrePhotos shows its pages on port 8000. If another program already uses that port (a development server, another self-hosted tool), LibrePhotos does not start, and a message box names that program and its process ID. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, LibrePhotos started its background processes, showed the tray icon for a moment and quit without a message. Either close the other program, or start LibrePhotos on another port: Right-click librephotos.exe and choose Show more options → Create shortcut (on Windows 10: Create shortcut directly). Right-click the new shortcut, choose Properties, and add run --port 8080 to the end of Target, after the closing quote: "C:\Users\<you>\LibrePhotos-app\librephotos\librephotos.exe" run --port 8080 Start LibrePhotos with that shortcut from now on. The browser and the tray icon's Open LibrePhotos then use port 8080. Any free port above 1024 works. Windows keeps some port ranges for Hyper-V, WSL or Docker; if the message box says LibrePhotos cannot use the port, pick another one (netsh interface ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp lists the reserved ranges). The background services use ports 8002 to 8012 on 127.0.0.1. If another program holds one of them, LibrePhotos does not start either, and the message box lists each blocked port with the program holding it, for example Port 8010 (exif): python.exe, process ID 4321. Close that program, or move the service with its SIDECAR_PORT_<NAME> variable (the name in brackets, see Environment variables). Environment variables do not fit in a shortcut, so start LibrePhotos from a small .cmd file next to it instead, for example LibrePhotos.cmd: @echo off set SIDECAR_PORT_EXIF=18010 start "" "%~dp0librephotos.exe" New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, LibrePhotos started anyway, and the service failed for every photo of the next scan with the reason only in console.log.

An update replaces the program folder and keeps the data folder: your photos, albums, people, users and settings are all still there afterwards. LibrePhotos can do it itself (Updating from LibrePhotos); by hand works for every release.

New in 1.5.0 When a newer release is out (see Knowing when there is an update), LibrePhotos downloads it and restarts into it. The first release that can do this is 1.5.0: to get from 1.4.0 or older to 1.5.0, update by hand once. Back up the database if you want a copy on another drive. LibrePhotos makes a copy in db\backups itself before it updates the database. In the browser, open Admin area and click Download update on the Update available card. Or right-click the LibrePhotos icon in the tray and choose Download LibrePhotos 1.5.0. LibrePhotos downloads the release from GitHub (about 450 MB) while it keeps running. The card shows how far it got, and the tray menu says Downloading 1.5.0 (42 %). An interrupted download continues where it stopped when you try again. When the card says the update is downloaded and checked (and a notification says "LibrePhotos 1.5.0 is ready"), click Restart to update on the card, or choose Restart to update to 1.5.0 in the tray menu. If a job such as a scan is running, LibrePhotos asks first: the restart stops the job, and you can start it again afterwards. LibrePhotos quits, puts the new release in place and starts it. After a minute or two (longer when the release updates the database) the browser page reloads by itself on the new release. What happens on your disk, next to the program folder (for example in C:\Users\<you>\LibrePhotos-app): The download goes into librephotos-1.5.0.partial and is unpacked into librephotos-1.5.0. Nothing else changes until you restart; quitting LibrePhotos meanwhile is fine, and the next start knows the update is ready. On Restart to update, the old librephotos folder is renamed to librephotos-old and librephotos-1.5.0 to librephotos. Shortcuts to librephotos\librephotos.exe keep working. The new release starts with the same options as the old one (--data-dir, --port, ...). librephotos-old stays: it is the way back to the previous release. The librephotos-old of the update before is deleted, but only once the new release has started and answers, and only if it holds nothing but that release: anything you put into it yourself keeps it there. A log of each update is in update.log in the logs folder (tray: Open logs). If the new release does not start, nothing is deleted and a message box says where the old release is; Going back has the steps. LibrePhotos only downloads from the LibrePhotos release page on github.com, over HTTPS, and checks the zip against the SHA256SUMS file of the same release, like Checking your download does by hand: a damaged download is deleted and not installed, and a release without SHA256SUMS cannot be installed this way. That proves the download is the file the release has; it does not prove who made the release. The release files are not signed yet: once the project has chosen how to sign them, LibrePhotos will also check a signature of SHA256SUMS before installing. LibrePhotos updates by hand only, and the card links these steps instead, when it cannot replace its own folder: the program folder is somewhere it cannot write next to, such as C:\Program Files (see Choosing a folder); the data folder (--data-dir) is inside the program folder, which an update replaces; a photo folder is inside the program folder: the topmost photos folder (--photos), a user's scan directory or upload folder, or a library folder. Keep your photos outside the program folder.

The steps assume the program is in C:\Users\<you>\LibrePhotos-app\librephotos; use your own folder if it is somewhere else. Back up the database. New in 1.4.0 The new release also makes a copy of the database itself before it changes it (see below), but a copy on another drive is the safe way back. Quit LibrePhotos: right-click its icon in the tray (behind the ^ arrow if you do not see it) and choose Quit LibrePhotos. Wait until the icon disappears, which takes a few seconds. Download the new librephotos-windows-x64.zip from the releases page, and read that release's notes: some ask you to do something once after the update. In File Explorer, open C:\Users\<you>\LibrePhotos-app, right-click the librephotos folder, choose Rename and call it librephotos-old. If Windows says the folder is in use, LibrePhotos is still running: wait a moment and try again, or end librephotos.exe in Task Manager. Do not unzip the new release over the old folder instead. Files that are still in use cannot be replaced, and files the new release no longer has stay behind, so the folder can end up with a mix of both releases. The old folder is also your way back. Right-click the new zip, choose Extract All..., and extract it into C:\Users\<you>\LibrePhotos-app again. You now have a new librephotos folder next to librephotos-old. Shortcuts to librephotos\librephotos.exe keep working. Double-click librephotos.exe in the new librephotos folder, once. If the release brings database changes, the first start updates the database, and the browser shows "LibrePhotos is updating" meanwhile (what the page says). That can take a few minutes with a large library: wait, and do not start it again meanwhile. Check that LibrePhotos works: log in and open a few photos and albums. Then delete the librephotos-old folder. Keep it for a while if you might want to go back. New in 1.4.0 What the first start after an update does (up to 1.3.0 it only updated the database, and nothing showed until the browser opened): It copies the database into db\backups in the data folder before it changes anything. The copy is named after the new release and the time, and holds the database as the old release left it. The three newest copies are kept. If there is not enough free disk space for the copy, LibrePhotos does not start, and a message box says how much space to free. See Automatic backups. The tray icon says Updating the database (3 of 7) while it works, and a notification says that the database is being updated. After an update from 1.3.0 or older, it moves the secret key from logs\secret.key to protected_media\secret.key. If the new release does not start, the message box says why, and console.log in the logs folder (tray: Open logs) has the details. You can always go back to the old release.

New in 1.5.0 LibrePhotos asks GitHub once a day whether a newer release is out (see Checking for new releases for what that sends). When one is, and its librephotos-windows-x64.zip can be downloaded: a Windows notification says "LibrePhotos 1.5.0 is available" once for that release; the tray menu has Download LibrePhotos 1.5.0, which updates from LibrePhotos (where LibrePhotos cannot update itself: Update to 1.5.0 available..., which opens these steps); admins see an Update available card at the top of the Admin area, with Download update (or How to update the Windows app), Release notes and Skip this release. Check for updates in the tray menu asks at once and answers with a notification, also when LibrePhotos is up to date. A release skipped on the Admin page is not announced again; the next one is. To turn the check off, switch off Check for new releases in Admin area > Site Settings.
documents.s: Knowing when there is an update

documents.t: New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, LibrePhotos on Windows took the time on your PC's clock for UTC when it recorded when a photo was added and when it checked whether a file had changed since the last scan. West of Greenwich (UTC minus some hours, as in the Americas) a normal scan could therefore skip a file you edited within those hours after a scan, and the places and faces of photos added shortly after an earlier run were not looked up. Run a full rescan once after the upgrade: on the Library page, in the Scan library section, click the arrow next to Scan and choose Rescan (or Rescan All Photos in the Ctrl+K command palette). East of Greenwich nothing was missed. Either way, the times in Recently added stay shifted by your UTC offset for photos added before the upgrade.

The most complete backup is a copy of the whole data folder, %LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos. It can be many GB, mostly thumbnails and machine learning models, which LibrePhotos makes again by a rescan or downloads again. If that is too much, back up at least these two, which nothing can make again: What Why The db folder The database: users, albums, people and face names, favourites, ratings, captions, settings. protected_media\secret.key (1.3.0 and older: logs\secret.key) Encrypts the saved email server password and Nextcloud app passwords, and signs every login. Without it, everyone has to log in again and those passwords have to be entered again. Two small folders in protected_media are worth copying too: faces (the face pictures shown under People) and avatars (profile pictures).

Right-click the LibrePhotos icon in the tray and choose Open data folder. (Without the icon: type %LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos into the address bar of File Explorer and press Enter.) Right-click the icon again and choose Quit LibrePhotos. Wait until it disappears: a copy of the database made while LibrePhotos runs can be incomplete. Copy the db folder, with everything in it, to a safe place, for example an external drive: right-click db, choose Copy, open the target folder and press Ctrl+V. If there are files named librephotos.sqlite3-wal or librephotos.sqlite3-shm in it, they belong to the database and have to be copied too. Open protected_media and copy secret.key to the same safe place, and the faces and avatars folders if you want them. With 1.3.0 or older, secret.key is in logs instead. Start LibrePhotos again. For the complete backup, copy the whole LibrePhotos folder in step 3 instead, and skip step 4. New in 1.4.0 The automatic copies in db\backups are made on the same drive as the database, so they help after a failed update, but not when the drive fails. See Automatic backups.

Quit LibrePhotos (tray: Quit LibrePhotos). Open the data folder (%LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos) and rename the db folder to db-broken. Copy the db folder from your backup into the data folder. Copy secret.key from your backup into protected_media, replacing the one there, and the faces and avatars folders if you backed them up. When you go back to 1.3.0 or older, copy secret.key into logs instead, as logs\secret.key: those releases look for it there. Start the release you made the backup with (or a newer one, which updates the database again). Releases after 1.3.0 refuse to start on a database a newer release has updated, see Going back to an older release. When everything works, delete db-broken. To restore a complete backup, quit LibrePhotos, rename the LibrePhotos data folder to LibrePhotos-broken, and copy your backup in its place. To restore one of the automatic copies from db\backups instead, see Restoring a backup on the Upgrading page.

The previous release is in librephotos-old next to the program folder, whether you updated from LibrePhotos or by hand. Quit LibrePhotos. In C:\Users\<you>\LibrePhotos-app, rename the new librephotos folder to librephotos-new, and librephotos-old back to librephotos. If the new release updated the database, put the database from before the update back: your own backup, or the newest automatic copy in db\backups, the one named after the new release (Restoring a backup). An older release cannot run on the database a newer one has updated: releases after 1.3.0 refuse to start and say so, 1.3.0 and older start but fail later. When you go back to 1.3.0 or older and the new release moved the secret key, copy protected_media\secret.key to logs\secret.key. Start librephotos.exe in the librephotos folder. Changes made with the newer release (faces named, albums edited) are not in the old database. The next scan finds photos added since.
documents.s: Going back to the previous release

documents.t: The zip installs nothing outside its folder: no Start menu entry, no service and no registry settings. To remove LibrePhotos: Quit LibrePhotos (tray: Quit LibrePhotos). Delete the program folder, for example C:\Users\<you>\LibrePhotos-app (with librephotos and any librephotos-old in it), and the shortcuts you made to it. Only if you do not want to keep your library: delete the data folder, %LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos (or the folder you gave with --data-dir). It holds the database, thumbnails, models and logs and can be many GB. Back it up first if you might want your albums, people and settings back: if you keep it, a later install picks up the library where you left it. Your photos in your own folders are not touched by any of this.

cd apps\backend py -3.14 -m venv .venv .\.venv\Scripts\pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements.standalone.txt .\.venv\Scripts\python scripts\build_standalone.py --zip This builds the frontend (Node 24 and Yarn on PATH; --skip-frontend reuses apps/frontend/dist), collects the static files and compiles the backend; Nuitka needs Visual Studio's C++ build tools and downloads the rest itself. Expect the first build to take well over an hour, later ones are much faster thanks to Nuitka's cache. The result lands in apps\backend\build\standalone\librephotos\. With --zip, the zip and SHA256SUMS are next to that folder. To check a build the way the release workflow does, run the zip on a fresh data folder: the script starts it on free ports, creates an admin, checks every background service that needs no model, scans three sample photos, then ends librephotos.exe and fails if any of its processes is left. .\.venv\Scripts\python scripts\smoke_standalone.py build\standalone\librephotos-windows-x64.zip

Sample photos from Unsplash and others, see the credits. Unlike commercial service that store your photos in the cloud and scan/index them to train their machine learning models and collect ad targeting data on you, LibrePhotos keeps all your photos and metadata on your local machine. Your data is never sent to or stored on a 3rd party server. Get the same power as those commercial services without giving up your personal data and privacy.
Install LibrePhotos — pick a deployment method and get the server running. First steps — what to do right after your first login. Development setup — build LibrePhotos locally and contribute.

Support for all types of photos, including raw photos Support for videos Live Photos and RAW+JPEG file variant support Timeline view Scans pictures on the file system Multiuser support Generate albums based on events like "Thursday in Berlin" Face recognition / Face classification Reverse geocoding Object / Scene detection Semantic image search Search by metadata (person, file type, lens, camera, path) Duplicate detection with perceptual hashing Public album sharing via link with fine-grained privacy controls Photo details sidebar showing location, people, albums, and similar photos Slideshow mode and fullscreen lightbox Memories: the photos you took on this day in earlier years Spotlight search with keyboard navigation

Image Conversion: libvips RAW Conversion: LibRaw via rawpy Video Conversion: FFmpeg EXIF Support: ExifTool Face detection: InsightFace (SCRFD detector + ArcFace embeddings) Face classification/clustering: hdbscan clustering and a scikit-learn multilayer perceptron, both ported to numpy Image captioning: LFM2.5-VL, a small vision-language model that also takes the recognised people and the place into account Tags, semantic search and similar photos: OpenCLIP ViT-B/32 trained by LAION on DataComp-XL (model card, MIT licence), one model for all three, with embeddings searched exactly (inner product, numpy) ML runtime: every model above runs on ONNX Runtime; there is no PyTorch or llama.cpp in the image Reverse geocoding: ExifTool's Geolocation database with place names from GeoNames (default, offline), Nominatim and other providers (Mapbox, MapTiler, OpenCage, TomTom)

Welcome to the LibrePhotos user guide. These pages walk you through everyday use of your photo library, from your first login through organizing, sharing, and administering your collection. If you have not installed LibrePhotos yet, start with the Installation section first. New here? Begin with First steps.

First steps — what to do right after your first login. Viewing photos — photo views, the lightbox, and the photo details sidebar. Upload — adding photos through the web interface. Search — finding photos with spotlight, semantic, and text search.

Albums — creating and managing photo albums. Places — how geolocation and the places map work. Face recognition — training and using the face dashboard. Image captioning — automatic captions for your photos. Stacks & file variants — how RAW+JPEG pairs, Live Photos, and bursts are grouped. Sharing — sharing photos and albums with other users or via public links.

Library management — scanning, Nextcloud integration, and server management. Auto scan all folders — scanning every folder automatically. Missing photos — understanding and clearing missing photos. Duplicate detection — finding and managing duplicate photos. Trash — how the trash works. Statistics & data visualization — interactive visualizations of your library.
Exif data — which EXIF fields LibrePhotos reads, writes, and filters on. Internal files — a tour of the folders and files LibrePhotos keeps on disk.

Settings — where the settings live and what they control. Manage multiple users — adding and managing additional user accounts. Feature toggles — turning individual features on and off. Job system — what the background worker jobs and logs mean. Offline usage — running LibrePhotos without an internet connection. API authentication — authenticating against the API with JWT or Basic auth.
Mobile apps — the companion mobile apps for LibrePhotos.
Feature comparison — how LibrePhotos compares with other photo managers. FAQ — answers to common questions and problems.
LibrePhotos supports several types of albums to help you organize your photo library.
Albums you create manually to organize photos however you like. You can add any photos to these albums. To keep many of them in order, group them into collections.

Automatically generated albums based on face recognition. Each recognized person gets their own album. The People page shows each person as a round picture of their cover face, the same face the Albums page shows; their name and number of faces sit under it. Choosing Set as cover… on a person's page also makes that person's face in the photo their cover face. A person whose face has no picture yet shows the whole cover photo instead, and a person without faces shows a placeholder. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the People page showed the whole cover photo for everyone. A person's page has a ⋮ button (Person actions) at the right of its header: Rename renames the person. A name another person already has offers Merge into that person instead (see below). Add birth date… (Birth date… once there is one) sets, changes or removes the person's birth date (see below). Groups… puts the person in your groups of people (see below). Merge into… merges this person into another one you pick from your people, then shows that person's page. Review faces opens the face dashboard on the Labeled tab, showing only this person's faces. Remove the person's chip in its toolbar to see everyone's faces again. Delete person removes the person from People and takes you back there. The photos stay in your library; the faces labelled with that person go back to the unknown faces, where you can label them again. A photo that shows up under the wrong person can be taken off them from the person's page: select it (or several), open the selection's ⋮ menu and choose Remove from this person under Album actions. After you confirm, the person's faces on those photos go back to the unknown faces of the face dashboard, and the photos leave the person's page; they stay in your library and in any albums. This works on photos you selected one by one, not after Select all. If you write face tags to your files, the files are updated too. Birth date and age​ New in 1.5.0 A person can have a birth date. Set it with Add birth date… in the person's ⋮ menu, or click the line under their name once there is one; the dialog also has Remove birth date. A date in the future is refused, and the dialog warns when some of the person's photos are older than the date, because those are often a wrong date or a wrong face. With a birth date, the person's page shows "Born date · N years old" under their name, and their age on each day beside the day's date ("Age 6", "4 months", "Newborn"). Photos without a date, or from before the birth, show no age. A person without a birth date looks as before. Only you see a birth date: it is not part of shared albums, public links or what other users see of a photo. Face training also uses it: it never suggests a person for a face on a photo taken before their birth date. Groups of people​ Groups gather people, for example "Family", "Work" or "Climbing club", so you can look at one circle at a time. A person can be in several groups, and only you see your groups. To put a person in groups, open the ⋮ on their tile on the People page (or on their page) and choose Groups…. Tick the groups they belong to; every tick is saved at once. Type a name under the list and click Add to make a new group with this person in it. To show only one group, use the group button in the People header (it says All people until you pick one). On a phone it is in the header's ⋮, under Groups. The list shows each group with how many people are in it. The page keeps the choice in its address, so Back from a person returns to the same group. Manage groups… at the bottom of that list renames and deletes groups and adds new ones. Deleting a group keeps its people. When you merge two people, the person you merge into joins every group the merged person was in. The face dashboard has the same choice under Groups in its Filter, to label one group at a time. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, people could not be grouped. Merging two people​ The same person can end up under two names: a typo, a nickname, or two face groups you labelled separately. Two people cannot share a name, so giving a person a name that someone else already has means they are the same person: the rename dialog (on the People page, the person's page or the face dashboard) shows Merge into followed by that name instead of Rename. On a person's page, Merge into… in the ⋮ menu does the same with a person you pick from a list. Before anything changes you confirm the merge. Then: all faces of the merged person move to the person you merge into, including the faces LibrePhotos only suggests for them, so the photos show up on that person's page and in a search for their name; the merged person disappears from People; the person you merge into keeps their name and cover photo. A merge cannot be undone. If you write face tags to your files, the files of the moved photos are updated in the background. The face classifier picks up the merged labels the next time you run Train faces. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, two people could not be merged, a person's page had no menu, a photo could only be taken off a person in the face dashboard, and a deleted or unknown person's page said "Loading" for good instead of "Person not found".

Albums that group your photos into events based on when they were taken. Grouping is purely chronological: a photo joins the current event if it was taken less than 1 day and 12 hours after the previous photo already in that event, so a continuous trip stays a single event however long it runs. An event needs at least two photos — a single photo on its own produces no album. Location and recognized people are not used for the grouping itself; they only feed the album's generated title (for example "Weekend in Paris") and its position on the map. Note Unlike People, Places and Things albums, event albums are not created during a scan. To create them, open Account menu > Library, find the Event albums section and click Generate next to Generate event albums (or run the Generate event albums command from the search spotlight), and re-run it after importing new photos. Regenerate event titles only refreshes the titles of existing albums, which is useful once you have named faces or after reverse geocoding has filled in place names. It also cleans up titles made by 1.2.1 and older, which could read "with Unknown - Other" or contain a double space. See Job System for the underlying jobs. Event titles follow the language you picked for the web app: "Wednesday Afternoon with Anna in Berlin" reads "Mittwochnachmittag mit Anna in Berlin" in German, once that language has the translation. Place and person names stay as they are. An event made before this change keeps its English title until the next Generate event albums run or a Regenerate event titles; the mobile app and search still use the English title. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, event titles were always English. An event's cover on the Events page is its first photo until you pick another one with Event actions (⋮) → Set as cover… on the event's page (see Setting an Album Cover). Running Generate event albums again keeps your pick: events are updated in place and only gain photos, and when new photos join two events into one, the merged event keeps the older event's cover, or the other one's if the older had none. Delete all event albums (Admin area, Admin tools) removes the picks along with the events. A cover you hide or move to the trash later is replaced by the first photo again.

The Folders page lists the folders of your scan directory. Each tile shows the newest photo in the folder or below it (by the date it was taken), with a small folder badge in its corner so that folders do not look like albums. Hidden photos, photos in the trash and other users' photos are never a folder's cover. The All subfolders list on a folder's page shows the same photo next to each folder. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, every folder showed the same folder icon.

Automatically generated albums based on the GPS location data in your photos. The Places card under Collections on the Albums page shows a small map zoomed to fit your places, or the whole world while you have none; click it to open the Places page. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the card always showed the whole world.

Albums for your own tags — the labels you type yourself, as opposed to the things OpenCLIP detects. Every tag gets an album, and the Tags card under Collections on the Albums page opens the list of them, each with a photo count. Tags also come in from your files: keywords stored in a photo's XMP Subject or IPTC Keywords (including .xmp sidecars, so tags applied in Lightroom or digiKam are picked up) become tags during a scan. See Tagging photos below for how to apply them, and Search for finding photos by tag.

Automatically generated albums based on detected objects and scenes in your photos. Things Albums are filtered by the currently active Tagging Model (configurable in Site settings), so only things from the selected model are shown. Switching models does not delete your existing things, but it also does not detect things with the newly selected model — until things exist for that model, the Things section will look empty. New in 1.5.0 To find the things in your photos again, open Account menu > Library and, under the Things heading, click the arrow next to Find and choose Find things again for all photos. It asks first, because on a large library it runs for hours. Every photo is labelled again with the current list of things, and the Things albums follow; your own tags, keywords and captions stay as they are. Find alone covers only the photos that have no things yet, which a scan also does by itself. Each user runs it for their own photos. Albums created from #hashtags you typed into photo captions are always shown, regardless of the active model. New in 1.6.0 A photo gets fewer things, and far fewer wrong ones: up to five, each only when the model is sure enough for its kind of thing. People and kinds of picture (screenshot, chat, meme, chart, drawing) count at a few percent, while activities, sports and occasions need near certainty, because the model mostly guesses those. Up to 1.5.x a photo got up to ten things from a longer list, and most of them were wrong or said little, such as "teenager", "meditating", "bachelor party" or "receipt" on a chat screenshot. Photos keep their old things until you run Find things again for all photos. New in 1.5.0 Things show in the language you picked under Settings > Profile > Language, in the Things albums, the photo's info panel and the statistics word cloud, as far as that language has been translated; a thing without a translation shows in English. Hover over a translated thing in the info panel or the word cloud to see its English word. Search still finds things by their English word only: searching Strand finds nothing, beach does. Clicking a thing searches for its English word for you. Your own words (below) and hashtag albums show as you wrote them. Teaching LibrePhotos new things​ New in 1.5.0 LibrePhotos finds things by comparing each photo with a list of about 500 words that ships with it (beach, dog, birthday cake, screenshot, ...). It needs no training to learn a new one: adding the word to the list is enough. An admin can add their own words, such as "tortoise", "sourdough" or "climbing wall": Create a text file named custom_tags.txt in the OpenCLIP model folder: protected_media/data_models/openclip_vitb32/ in your data volume (/protected_media/data_models/openclip_vitb32/custom_tags.txt inside the Docker containers). To keep it somewhere else, point OPENCLIP_CUSTOM_TAGS at it (see Environment variables). Write one word or short phrase per line. Empty lines and lines starting with # are skipped, and so is a word the list already has (in any capitalisation). Restart the backend, or wait until nobody has scanned or searched for a couple of minutes: the tags service reads the file each time it loads its model, and it unloads the model when it sits idle. The backend log then says how many of your words were added. Things to know: Only photos labelled from then on get your words. To label the photos you already have with them, run Find things again for all photos (see above). Every photo gets the words that fit it best out of the whole list. A specific word ("tortoise") works well; a very generic one ("thing", "photo", "outdoors") competes with the built-in words and can push them out of photos where they fit better. New in 1.6.0 A photo gets at most two of your words, and only those the model is fairly sure of. A photo gets at most five things in all, and fewer when the model is unsure, so a word that never shows up may just be hard to see: describe it instead. Write word = description, for example sourdough = a loaf of sourdough bread with a dark crust. The album is still called by the word before =. Several descriptions separated by | are averaged: tortoise = a tortoise | a tortoise shell on grass. Up to 1.5.x, every line was a plain word, and a photo got up to ten things, many of them wrong. The file stays when you update LibrePhotos, as it lives in your data volume next to the downloaded model.

My albums, Events, Things, Places, People, Tags and Folders have a Sort button at the right of their header; on a phone it is an icon (on People, it is in the header's ⋮). It names the current order, for example Sort: Name. Click it and pick: under Sort by, what to sort on; under Order, which way round: A to Z or Z to A for names, Most first or Fewest first for numbers, Newest first or Oldest first for dates; Reset to default, to go back to the page's usual order. It only shows while you use another order, and so does the button's coloured background. Page Usual order Other orders My albums Name, A to Z Number of photos; Date taken Events Date taken, newest first Name; Number of photos Things, Tags, Folders Name, A to Z Number of photos Places Size of place, largest first (countries first, then the places with the most photos) Name; Number of photos People Name, A to Z Number of faces Date taken on My albums is when the album's oldest photo was taken, not when you made the album; photos in the trash or hidden do not count, and albums without a dated photo come last. People are sorted by their number of faces, the count under each name on the People page. Names sort the way people read them: "Album 2" comes before "Album 10", and upper and lower case do not matter. Each page remembers its order in your browser, so going Back from an album returns to the same list at the same place. The order only changes what you see in the web app; the mobile app keeps its own. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the album lists could not be sorted.
You can customize the cover image for People Albums, User Albums and Events. There are two ways to do this:

Navigate to the album you want to customize (a person, a user album or an event) Click the three-dot menu (⋮) at the right of the album's header (Album actions, Person actions on a person's page, Event actions on an event's page) Click "Set as cover…" A modal will open showing all photos in the album Click on the photo you want to use as the cover The cover is set immediately On an event, the picker marks the cover in use and starts with Automatic, which goes back to the event's first photo. Tip The cover picker loads photos in batches of 50 for better performance. Click "Load more photos" to see additional photos if your album is large.

If you already know which photo you want to use: Navigate to the album Select exactly one photo — click Select at the right of the header and then the photo, or hover over it and click the checkbox that appears in its top-left corner (outside select mode, a plain click on a photo opens it in the lightbox instead of selecting it) Click the three-dot menu (⋮) in the selection bar Click "Set album cover" The selected photo becomes the cover immediately Note "Set as cover…" and "Set album cover" only appear on a People Album, a User Album or an Event. They won't be visible on other pages like the main timeline, Things or Places. Folder covers are always the newest photo. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, an event's cover could not be changed. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the cover picker was "Set album cover" in the selection toolbar's ⋮ with nothing selected.

New in 1.4.0 On My albums, click New album (the + on a phone), give it a title that none of your albums has, and click Create album. The new album opens right away. It is empty, and shows a drop zone: drop photos and videos on it, or click Upload photos, to upload them into the album. You can also fill it from your library as below. If My albums is showing one collection (see Grouping albums into collections), the new album goes into that collection, and the dialog says so. Made from All or Not in a collection, it is in no collection and shows under Not in a collection. Empty albums stay on My albums with a No cover tile, also when you remove the last photo from an album. (Up to 1.3.0, an album without photos was hidden there.)

Select one or more photos from any view: click Select at the right of the page header (an icon on a phone) and click the photos, or tick a photo's checkbox. The selection bar appears under the header while you select; its ✕ or the Escape key ends selecting and clears the selection. On a phone the bar only has the + and ⋮ buttons (favorite, share, download and move to trash are in the ⋮), and menus open as a sheet from the bottom of the screen Click the + button (Add to album or tags) in the selection bar Click "Album" Either: Enter a name for a new album and click "Create" Or click on an existing album to add the photos to it

On the Albums page, every User Album card has a three-dot menu (⋮) in its top-right corner. From it you can: Rename — enter a new title and confirm. Titles must be unique; the dialog blocks a name that another one of your albums already uses. Sharing — open the album sharing dialog (see the Sharing guide). Collections… — put the album into collections (see Grouping albums into collections). Delete — a confirmation dialog appears before the album is removed. The album's own page has the same actions: the ⋮ button (Album actions) at the right of its header offers Upload to this album… (see Uploading into an album), Rename, Sharing, Collections…, Lock album or Unlock album (see Locking user albums) and Delete album. A new title shows on the page right away, and after Delete album you land on My albums. The menu is only there for your own albums; on an album someone shared with you it has Leave album instead (see Leaving an album shared with you). New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, an album could only be renamed, locked or deleted from its card. Caution Deleting an album is permanent and cannot be undone, but it only removes the album itself. The photos it contained stay in your library.
