A collection is a label for albums, such as "Travel", "Family" or "2000s". An album can be in any number of collections, so a family trip from 2004 can be in "Travel", "Family" and "2000s" at once. Collections only group albums: an album stays an album, and deleting a collection never deletes its albums or photos.

Once you have a collection, My albums shows a row of chips under its header: All, one chip per collection with the number of albums in it, and Not in a collection. Click a chip to show only those albums; the header then says how many albums are in it. The chosen collection stays in the page address, so going Back from an album returns to the same filtered list.

Open the album card's ⋮ menu on My albums, or the ⋮ (Album actions) at the right of the album's own header. Choose Collections…. Tick the collections the album belongs in, and untick the ones it does not. Each tick is saved right away. To make a new collection, type its name in New collection and click Add: it is created and the album is put in it. Click Done.

Open the ⋮ at the end of the chip row and choose Manage collections… (while you have no collection yet, click New collection on My albums instead). The dialog lists your collections with their album counts: the pencil button renames a collection; the bin button deletes it, after you confirm. Its albums stay in My albums; New collection at the bottom adds one. Collection names are unique per user, ignoring upper and lower case: you cannot have both "Travel" and "travel". Note Collections are private. When you share an album, the people you share it with see the album but not your collections, and they cannot put your album into collections of their own. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, albums could not be grouped.

User Albums can be shared with other users on your LibrePhotos instance, or publicly via a link. For full details on all sharing features, see the Sharing guide. Navigate to the User Album you want to share Click the three-dot menu (⋮) at the right of the album's header and choose Sharing (or, while selecting photos, in the selection bar's ⋮, Sharing under "Album actions") Search for and select the users you want to share with

You can share albums publicly with anyone via a unique link, without requiring them to have an account on your LibrePhotos instance: Navigate to the User Album you want to share publicly Click the three-dot menu (⋮) at the right of the album's header and choose "Sharing" In the dialog, toggle "Public sharing" on — a unique URL slug is generated automatically that you can share with anyone Click "Show settings" to customize the slug (3–64 characters), set an expiration (7, 30 or 90 days, or never), and control what information visitors can see: Location data Camera information Timestamps Captions Recognized faces Turning "Public sharing" off asks first, because it revokes the link for good: the old address never works again, and turning sharing back on creates a new one. Anyone you gave the old link to needs the new one. Once an album is public, it appears under Sharing → Links, where you can copy the link, open it, or reopen the sharing dialog to change its settings. Albums that are not yet public are not listed there. Default privacy settings for new public links can be configured in Settings → Public sharing defaults. Public albums are accessible at /public/s/{slug} and include a lightbox viewer with the same navigation experience as the main app.
Tags are yours to type: a place name, a project, "to print", whatever you sort by. A photo can carry any number of them.

Anywhere you can select photos — the timeline, a search result, a person, place, thing or user album, or a folder — you can tag the whole selection at once: Select the photos and videos you want to tag. Press t, or open the + menu (Add to album or tags) in the selection bar and click Tags. Type the tags, separating several with a comma. Suggestions narrow as you type — tags that begin with what you typed come first, so a letter or two is usually enough — and anything new is created for you. Click Add tags (or press Enter on an empty box). Every tag in the box is applied to every photo in the selection. Tagging is additive — it never removes a tag a photo already has. Select all works too: with the whole view selected, the tags apply to everything the current view holds, whatever its filters (including the Photos / Videos selector), minus any photo you unchecked. That is one request for the whole library rather than one per photo, so it stays quick on a large one. Note t is used instead of Ctrl+T because browsers reserve Ctrl+T for opening a new tab and a web page cannot intercept it.

Open a photo and use the Tags section of the sidebar — the pencil button opens the same comma-separated editor, and here it both adds and removes: whatever you leave in the box is what the photo ends up with. Click a tag badge to jump to that tag's album. A tag that came from the file's keywords carries a small file icon there; see Tags.

On the Albums page, click the Tags card under Collections. The three-dot menu on any tag offers: Rename — the tag keeps its photos. Merge — pick another tag to fold into this one; its photos move over and it is deleted. Delete — removes the tag. Your photos are untouched. New in 1.4.0 With Write edits to files on, tags are written to the files as keywords, so a rename, merge or delete also changes the keyword in the files of every photo carrying the tag, in the background. Tagging a selection or one photo writes the same way. Note Tags are per user: two accounts can each have a tag called holiday without seeing each other's. A tag outlives its photos. Trashing, hiding or deleting the last photo that carried a tag leaves the tag in place: it stays in the Tags list with a placeholder tile so you can still rename or delete it, and its own page tells you it is empty. That is deliberate — you may well want to create a tag before anything carries it, and deleting photos should never silently delete tags. Caution A tag you add in LibrePhotos is not written back into the image file yet. A tag that came from a file's keywords stays in that file, but new tags live only in LibrePhotos' database.

To remove photos from a User Album: Navigate to the User Album Select the photos you want to remove Click the three-dot menu (⋮) Under Album actions, click "Remove photos" Caution This only removes the photos from the album. The original photos remain in your library.

New in 1.3.0 In the user album list, open an album’s three-dot menu and choose Lock album; on the album's own page, the same item is in the ⋮ at the right of its header. A lock icon marks locked albums in the list, and a grey Locked badge follows the title on the album's page. Choose Unlock album from the same menus to allow changes again. Locking prevents adding photos to the album or removing photos from it. Locked albums are disabled in the add-to-album picker, and Remove photos is disabled in a locked album’s selection menu, saying that the album is locked and has to be unlocked first. The lock protects which photos are in the album, not the photos themselves: you can still favorite, hide, share, tag or delete them, rename the album, change its cover, and manage album sharing. The API enforces the album membership lock. This does not protect the underlying photos from changes made elsewhere in your library or prevent deleting the album itself.

LibrePhotos secures most API endpoints and requires authentication by default. If you see 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden responses when calling API endpoints, you likely need to authenticate using one of the supported methods below.

JWT (recommended): Obtain a short-lived access token via /api/auth/token/obtain/ and present it as a Bearer token. The obtain and refresh endpoints also set an HttpOnly jwt cookie that the browser can reuse (see Cookie flags). Basic authentication: For simple scripts or local testing, you can use HTTP Basic auth. Do not use Basic auth across untrusted networks. Session authentication is not enabled for API endpoints. The frontend uses JWT behind the scenes, not Django sessions.

Request an access token using your LibrePhotos username and password: curl -X POST "http://<backend>/api/auth/token/obtain/" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"username":"myuser","password":"mypassword"}' You will receive a JSON response with access and refresh tokens. The response also sets a jwt cookie with the access token for browser use. Example response: { "refresh": "<refresh_token>", "access": "<access_token>" } Refresh the access token when it expires using: curl -X POST "http://<backend>/api/auth/token/refresh/" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"refresh":"<refresh_token>"}' Access tokens are short-lived and expire after 5 minutes; refresh tokens are valid for 7 days by default. Refreshing returns a new access token only, so keep reusing the same refresh token until it expires. A long-running script should refresh at least every 5 minutes, or simply retry once against /api/auth/token/refresh/ whenever a call returns 401. The access-token lifetime is fixed; the refresh-token lifetime can be changed with the REFRESH_TOKEN_DAYS environment variable on the backend container. New in 1.5.0 Add "remember_me": true to the obtain request for a refresh token that lasts REMEMBER_ME_DAYS (30 by default) instead, as the Remember me checkbox on the login page does. Its tokens carry a remember_until claim with the refresh token's expiry, the obtain and refresh responses give the jwt cookie a matching Max-Age, and the web app does the same for its access and refresh cookies. With REMEMBER_ME_DAYS=0 the flag is ignored. See Sign-in sessions.

To invalidate a refresh token — on logout, or to revoke one you think has leaked — blacklist it: curl -X POST "http://<backend>/api/auth/token/blacklist/" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"refresh":"<refresh_token>"}' No Authorization header is needed; the refresh token itself is the credential. On success you get HTTP 200 with an empty JSON body. Blacklisting stops the refresh token from minting new access tokens, but any access token it has already issued stays valid until it expires (5 minutes by default), so revocation is not instantaneous. This is the same endpoint the web frontend calls when you log out. The response also clears the jwt, access and refresh cookies, whatever the blacklist answers: a refresh token that is already blacklisted (401), expired, or missing from the body (400) still signs the browser out. The web app calls the endpoint on every logout, because the jwt cookie is HttpOnly and only the server can delete it. Clearing the cookie does not revoke the access token in it: a copy taken before logout keeps working until it expires. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the endpoint only blacklisted the token and the web deleted the cookies itself.

Include the token in the Authorization header: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer ' \ "http:///api/photos/" In a browser, the jwt cookie set by the obtain and refresh endpoints is sent automatically, which is how and
documents.s: Call APIs using the JWT access token

documents.t: These endpoints accept an Authorization: Bearer <access_token> header like every other endpoint, and fall back to the jwt cookie when there is no bearer header. When both are sent, the header wins: Media files — GET /media/photos/<image_hash> (originals), plus the thumbnail, square-thumbnail, face-crop, avatar and embedded-media paths (/media/thumbnails_big/..., /media/square_thumbnails/..., /media/faces/..., /media/avatars/..., /media/embedded_media/...) and generated archives at /media/zip/<name>. Basic auth (curl -u user:pass) works here too. Chunked uploads — POST /api/upload/ and POST /api/upload/complete/. Media belonging to an active public or shared album, and photos made public, are served without any credential. An expired or otherwise unusable cookie counts as no credential there: public media is still served, and anything else answers 403 with an X-Media-Error: authentication header, telling you to sign in again. An invalid bearer header answers 401, as on every other endpoint. Note Releases before 1.2.0 read only the cookie on the media endpoints and ignore the header there. The cookie works on every version. From a script, capture the cookie when you obtain the token and replay it: curl -c cookies.txt -X POST "http://<backend>/api/auth/token/obtain/" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"username":"myuser","password":"mypassword"}' curl -b cookies.txt "http://<backend>/media/photos/<image_hash>" -o photo.jpg or send it explicitly with -H "Cookie: jwt=<access_token>". The cookie carries the short-lived access token, so refresh it the same way you refresh the header token.
documents.s: Endpoints that also accept the jwt cookie

documents.t: The backend sets these cookies: Cookie Set by Flags jwt /api/auth/token/obtain/, /api/auth/token/refresh/, the SSO login HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Path=/, Secure (see below) access, refresh the SSO login only (the web app sets them itself after a password login) SameSite=Lax, Path=/, Secure (see below); not HttpOnly, because the web app reads them to send them as bearer tokens The cookies are session cookies, which the browser drops when it closes, except after a sign-in with remember_me: then they get a Max-Age that ends with the refresh token. HttpOnly keeps the jwt cookie away from scripts on the page; only the server reads it. SameSite=Lax still sends the cookies on top-level navigations and on and

curl -u myuser:mypassword "http://<backend>/api/photos/" Basic auth works on the standard DRF endpoints and on the media endpoints, but not on the chunked uploads. Every Basic auth request is a password check, so wrong passwords count against the same limit as sign-in (AUTH_THROTTLE_RATE, per address and username; see Sign-in rate limits). Once it is used up, requests with that username from that address answer 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header, even with the right password, until the window moves on. Requests with the right password are not counted, so a script can send its credentials on every request. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, wrong Basic auth passwords were not rate limited.

These routes are only registered when the backend runs with DEBUG=1 (development builds). The standard docker-compose deployment runs with DEBUG=0, where they all return 404: API help: http://<backend>/api/help — structured JSON with authentication instructions and example curl commands. Schema: http://<backend>/api/schema Swagger UI: http://<backend>/api/swagger Redoc: http://<backend>/api/redoc For the same reason, the extra auth hint that development builds append to a 401/403 error body is not present on a production install, so a production 401 will not point you at /api/help. Without a development build, read the OpenAPI schema from the repository: apps/backend/openapi.json is generated from the code and kept current by CI (on the dev branch; every release since 1.4.0 has it too). Load it into any OpenAPI viewer, such as the Swagger Editor.

Every API error (a status of 400 or above) has the same JSON body: { "errors": [{ "field": "new_password", "message": "This password is too short.", "code": "weak_password" }] } field names the request field at fault, or is non_field_errors or detail when the error is about the request as a whole. message is meant for people and may change between releases. Do not compare it in code. code is meant for programs. Most errors carry DRF's generic codes (invalid, not_found, permission_denied, not_authenticated, parse_error, throttled); the ones a client is expected to act on have their own: Code Status Endpoint Meaning invalid_cursor 400 /api/sync/* The cursor cannot be decoded. cursor_expired 410 /api/sync/* The cursor is older than the deletion log; pull again without one. weak_password 400 /api/auth/password/reset/confirm/ The password validators refused the new password; the link is still good. invalid_reset_link 400 /api/auth/password/reset/confirm/ The link was used already, expired or was mangled. model_downloading 503 /api/photosedit/generateim2txt/ The captioning model is being downloaded; retry after the Retry-After seconds. email_send_failed 502 /api/email-config/test/ The mail server refused the test email; message is its own answer. job_start_failed 500 job endpoints (/api/scanphotos/, /api/trainfaces/, ...) The background job could not be queued. job_already_running 409 job endpoints (/api/scanphotos/, /api/trainfaces/, ...) A job of this kind is already queued or running for you, or, for a job over the whole server, for anyone; or a scan of yours is refused while a move or rename of your photos runs, and the other way round. The entry also carries that job's job_id; follow it instead of starting another. queue_busy 409 job endpoints A job over the whole server that someone else started, and you cannot open, is running. The entry carries no job_id: start yours again when it has finished. Development builds append an extra entry with field auth (code authentication_help) to a 401 or 403; read the first entry. Media file requests (/media/...) are the exception: they answer without a body, as described above. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, a second start of a job that was still queued queued it again instead of answering job_already_running, and duplicate and stack detection (/api/duplicates/detect, /api/stacks/detect/) answered without a job_id. Many endpoints answered errors as {"error": "..."} or {"status": false, "message": "..."}, entries had no code, and three failures (face training that could not be queued, the captioning model download and a refused test email) answered with a 200.

Ensure you are including Authorization: Bearer <access_token> or using Basic auth. Verify the access token is current; refresh if needed. A 403 from /media/... carrying an X-Media-Error: authentication header means the request had no usable credential: send a current bearer token or jwt cookie (see Endpoints that also accept the jwt cookie). A 404 there means you are signed in but may not see that photo. If testing cross-origin from a separate frontend, ensure CORS and credentials are configured properly and that cookies are allowed if relying on the jwt cookie.
LibrePhotos can scan every library by itself, so new photos show up without anyone clicking Scan. Admins set the schedule in the app (below); a cron job on the host still works too.

New in 1.4.0 Open Account menu > Admin area > Site settings and pick a schedule under Scan libraries automatically: Off (the default): nothing is scanned unless a user clicks Scan on the Library page. Every hour: at the start of every hour. Every day, at the time you enter. Custom: on the days you pick, at the time you enter. With no day picked, nothing is saved and the schedule you had stays. The setting is saved as you change it, like the other site settings. Nothing needs a restart.

Each run starts, for every user with a scan directory, the same scan the Scan button on the Library page starts: an incremental scan of their scan directory, followed by the usual face detection, things and places. While the Nextcloud integration is on, a user's Nextcloud folder is scanned too, right after their scan directory. The scans show up in the job list like any other Scan photos job, started by the user whose library they scan. A run never stacks a scan on top of another one. A user whose scan is still queued or running, from the previous run or from a click on Scan, is skipped this time and picked up by the next run. This is what keeps a long first scan of a big library from being started again every hour. A user whose scan directory does not exist, or whose Nextcloud address is not allowed, is counted as failed for that run, and no job is started for them.

The time you enter is in the server's time zone, which the row names. The Docker images run on UTC, so Every day at 03:00 is 03:00 UTC: 05:00 in Berlin in summer, 23:00 the evening before in New York. The status line shows the next run in your own time zone, so you can check what you set. A Custom run that had to wait in a busy queue past midnight still counts as a run for the day it was due.

Under the setting, one line says what the last run did and when the next one is, for example: Last run Oct 14, 2026, 3:00 AM: 3 libraries scanned. Next run Oct 15, 2026, 3:00 AM. Still scanning: anna. The scans of that run are queued or running. Skipped bob: a scan was still running. Could not scan carla; see Worker logs. Her library could not be scanned, or her scan failed. The job in Worker logs says why, for example that the scan directory looks unmounted (see Missing Photos).

An incremental scan only reads files that are new or changed since a scan last read them. A file LibrePhotos wrote metadata into itself does not count as changed (see How a rescan treats your edits). On a library where nothing changed, a run walks the folders, compares each file's modification time with the one it recorded, and finishes. Only a scan that went through the whole library is what the next scan compares against. A scan that was cancelled, failed, or covered only some files (an upload, a single folder) is not, so the next scheduled scan also picks up what that one never got to. A scan that stops making progress, for example because a worker died, is marked failed after a while (STUCK_JOB_HOURS, 24 hours by default) and no longer counts as running, so the schedule picks that library up again. A long scan that is still making progress is left alone.
documents.s: Why a scan every hour is cheap

documents.t: New in 1.4.0 A scheduled scan walks every folder. When something outside LibrePhotos already knows which files are new, such as a sync tool, a camera upload script or a folder watcher, it can name them instead, and they show up within seconds of the call: curl -u myuser:mypassword -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"paths": ["/data/2026/10/IMG_2041.jpg", "/data/2026/10/IMG_2041.CR3"]}' \ "http://localhost:3000/api/scan-files/" POST /api/scan-files/ takes up to 1,000 paths, as LibrePhotos sees them (inside the container that is the scan directory set for your user, such as /data/..., not the folder on the host). It authenticates like every other endpoint, with your user's password over Basic auth or a JWT access token (see API authentication); a script that runs for days is simpler with Basic auth, because an access token expires after 5 minutes. Use HTTPS, or call it from the same machine. The call starts a Scan photos job for those files and answers at once: {"status": true, "job_id": "…", "job_ids": ["…"], "file_count": 2, "removed_count": 0, "ignored_paths": []} A file is read when it is new or changed, as on a Scan. Its things, places and faces follow as after any scan. New in 1.5.0 A path can also be a folder. Its files, and those of its subfolders, are scanned, so a folder copied or moved into the library in one go is picked up with one path. Hidden folders and folders that match the skip patterns in Site settings are left out, as on a Scan. A folder counts as one path in file_count. A subfolder that cannot be read is listed in the job's errors and does not stop the scan. Only existing files and folders inside your scan directory or upload folder are scanned. Paths that do not exist and anything outside your library are listed in ignored_paths. When no path of either list is left, the answer is a 400 with the code no_files_to_scan. While a scan of yours runs, the answer is a 409 (job_already_running) with that job's job_id. Nothing is queued or changed then: send the paths again later. The next scheduled scan picks the files up too. Such a scan never counts as the scan of the whole library that the next Scan compares against, so it cannot make a later scan miss a file.

New in 1.5.0 Files that were deleted or moved out of the library go into a second list, removed_paths (up to 1,000 as well). Their photos are flagged missing right away, as the next scan of the whole library would do (see Missing Photos), instead of showing a broken file until then. A call may name only removed paths; it then starts no scan, and job_id is null. curl -u myuser:mypassword -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"paths": ["/data/2026/sorted/IMG_2041.jpg"], "removed_paths": ["/data/2026/10/IMG_2041.jpg"]}' \ "http://localhost:3000/api/scan-files/" A removed path must be inside your library and must not exist any more. It names the file of one of your photos at that path or, when there is none, every file of your photos below it, so a folder deleted or moved away is one path. removed_count in the answer says how many files were flagged missing. Paths that still exist, lie outside your library or name no file of yours are listed in ignored_paths. A file whose exact copy is still in your library is not flagged missing: the copy takes it over, as on a scan. A file moved inside the library is its old path in removed_paths and its new path in paths, as above. The photo keeps its albums, faces and edits: the scan finds the same file at its new place and gives it back to the photo. The checks of the scan's missing-file check apply. When your scan directory looks unmounted, or more photos than the missing photos limit in Site settings allows would lose all their files, the answer is a 409 with the code library_unavailable, its message says why, and nothing is changed. Send the paths again once the library is back. paths and removed_paths are separate lists on purpose: a typo in paths is ignored, never read as "this file is gone".

This script watches the library on the host with inotifywait (package inotify-tools, plus curl and jq). It collects what changed and sends it once nothing has changed for 30 seconds, so a burst of uploads is one call. New and changed files and folders go into paths, deleted and moved-away ones into removed_paths. A batch is kept when the answer is a 409 and sent again with the next one. #!/usr/bin/env bash # The library on the host, and the same folder as LibrePhotos sees it. HOST_ROOT=/srv/photos LP_ROOT=/data URL=http://localhost:3000/api/scan-files/ # LP_USER and LP_PASSWORD come from the environment. paths=() removed=() to_json() { printf '%s\n' "$@" | jq -R . | jq -sc 'map(select(. != ""))'; } send() { [ $(( ${#paths[@]} + ${#removed[@]} )) -eq 0 ] && return body=$(jq -nc --argjson p "$(to_json "${paths[@]}")" \ --argjson r "$(to_json "${removed[@]}")" '{paths: $p, removed_paths: $r}') status=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -u "$LP_USER:$LP_PASSWORD" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "$body" "$URL") # 409: a scan is running, or the library looks unmounted. Keep the batch. if [ "$status" != 409 ]; then paths=(); removed=(); fi } inotifywait -m -r -q -e close_write -e moved_to -e create -e delete -e moved_from \ --format $'%e\t%w%f' "$HOST_ROOT" | # Ends when inotifywait does; a read that times out (status above 128) means 30 quiet seconds. while IFS=$'\t' read -r -t 30 events path || [ $? -gt 128 ]; do if [ -z "$path" ]; then send; continue; fi path="$LP_ROOT${path#"$HOST_ROOT"}" case "$events" in DELETE*|MOVED_FROM*) removed+=("$path") ;; # A new file is sent once it is written (CLOSE_WRITE), a new folder at once. CREATE,ISDIR|CLOSE_WRITE*|MOVED_TO*) paths+=("$path") ;; esac [ $(( ${#paths[@]} + ${#removed[@]} )) -ge 1000 ] && send done To keep a quiet library from being called every 30 seconds, the script only sends when it has something. Run it as a service​ Save the script as /usr/local/bin/librephotos-watcher and make it executable (chmod +x). Put your credentials into /etc/librephotos-watcher.env, readable by root only (chmod 600): LP_USER=myuser LP_PASSWORD=mypassword Then let systemd start the script at boot, and again whenever it stops, with /etc/systemd/system/librephotos-watcher.service: [Unit] Description=Tell LibrePhotos about changed photos After=network-online.target Wants=network-online.target [Service] ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/librephotos-watcher EnvironmentFile=/etc/librephotos-watcher.env Restart=always RestartSec=10 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Start it with sudo systemctl enable --now librephotos-watcher, and read what it reports with journalctl -u librephotos-watcher. Limits​ New in 1.5.0 A folder watcher only hears about the changes its own machine sees. Keep the schedule on as well, for example Every day, to catch what the watcher misses. Network shares. inotify only reports changes made through the kernel of the machine it runs on. Run the watcher on the machine that writes the files, such as the NAS or file server, not on a machine that mounts the share. On an NFS or SMB mount, files that another machine adds, changes or deletes produce no events at all; rely on the schedule there. Large libraries. inotifywait -r sets one watch per folder, and the kernel limits how many watches a user may set (fs.inotify.max_user_watches, only 8,192 on older kernels). For a big library, raise the limit: echo fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288 | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-inotify.conf sudo sysctl --system When the limit is too low, inotifywait reports upper limit on inotify watches reached when it starts (in the service's journal), and the folders past the limit are not watched. Setting up the watches of a big library also takes a while; changes made during that time are not reported. Containers. Run the watcher on the host, not in a container with the library bind-mounted into it. With Docker Desktop on macOS or Windows, and for a library on a Windows drive under WSL (/mnt/c/...), changes made on the host often produce no events inside the container. Downtime. Nothing is reported while the watcher is not running, for example during a reboot.

You can also start a scan from the host, for example when you want a different schedule per user or already manage your jobs with cron: sudo docker exec --user root backend python3 manage.py scan backend is the default container name set by container_name: in docker-compose.yml; substitute your own if you changed it (see Changing the container names). The plain scan command is incremental too. Use scan -f to force a full re-process of every file, or scan -s /path/a.jpg /path/b.jpg to scan specific files. New in 1.5.0 scan -s also takes folders and scans the files in them. See Management Commands for the full list. Nextcloud users manage.py scan only scans the local scan directory. To scan a connected Nextcloud library from the command line, run manage.py scan -n, and cron it separately. A cron entry that calls this command regularly: # Every day at 3 AM 0 3 * * * sudo docker exec --user root backend python3 manage.py scan >/dev/null 2>&1 Unlike the schedule in Site settings, the command scans every library in turn while you wait and does not check whether a scan is already running, so keep the interval longer than a scan takes. Use one or the other, not both.
documents.s: With a cron job on the host

documents.t: LibrePhotos can detect duplicate photos in your library using both exact file matching and visual similarity analysis. This helps you reclaim storage space and keep your library clean.
Photos that are byte-for-byte identical. These are detected by comparing file hashes (MD5). This catches files that have been copied to multiple locations or imported more than once.

Photos that look the same but may differ in resolution, quality, compression, or minor edits. These are detected using perceptual hashing — a technique that creates a fingerprint of what an image looks like, rather than its raw bytes. Two images with similar perceptual hashes are visually similar even if the files are technically different.

LibrePhotos computes a 64-bit perceptual hash (pHash) for each image using a DCT-based (Discrete Cosine Transform) algorithm. This hash captures the visual structure of the image and is robust against: Resizing Minor compression differences Small color adjustments Format conversions (e.g. JPEG → PNG) Two images are considered visually similar when their Hamming distance (the number of differing bits) is below a threshold. Visual duplicates need a perceptual hash first The perceptual hash is computed while a photo is scanned, from its large thumbnail, and visual duplicate detection only looks at photos that already have one. Photos indexed before this feature was added have no hash, and an ordinary scan skips files it has already indexed — so Detect duplicates can report no visual duplicates on an older library. To fill in the missing hashes, run a Rescan once from the Library page — open the dropdown next to Scan and choose Rescan; this re-processes every photo. Exact-copy detection uses the file's MD5 hash and isn't affected.

For large collections, LibrePhotos uses a memory-efficient two-pass algorithm: Pass 1 — Photos are processed in batches (default 10,000). Within each batch, a BK-tree data structure enables fast Hamming distance lookups to find duplicates. Pass 2 — Cross-batch comparison ensures duplicates that span different batches are also found. This approach keeps memory usage manageable even with hundreds of thousands of photos.

Open Organizing → Duplicate photos: in the dropdown of the Photos page title, choose Duplicates under Organizing. While duplicates wait for review, a N duplicates to review card at the bottom of the sidebar opens the same page. Open the Detection options dropdown and choose what to look for. Do this before you start detection — the detect button runs immediately with whatever options are currently set: Exact file copies (identical content) — find byte-identical files Visual duplicates (similar images) — find visually similar photos Visual sensitivity — Strict (fewer matches, higher confidence), Normal, or Loose (more matches, may include false positives). This only appears while Visual duplicates is enabled. Clear pending duplicates — remove existing pending groups before detection runs Click "Detect duplicates". Detection starts straight away using the options you selected. The Detection options aren't remembered between runs, so set them each time you detect. The default Visual sensitivity and Clear pending duplicates values come from Settings → Duplicate detection and can be changed there; the Exact file copies and Visual duplicates checkboxes always start enabled. Detection runs as a background job. You can monitor progress in the Job System.

Once detection is complete, duplicates appear as groups on the Organizing → Duplicate photos page: Each group shows preview thumbnails of the duplicate photos Badges indicate the type (exact copy or visual duplicate) and review status Potential savings shows how much storage you'd free by keeping only one copy Filtering Results​ Use the filters at the top to narrow down results: Status: Pending review, Resolved, Dismissed, or All Type: Exact Copies or Visual Duplicates Note Dismissing a group unlinks its photos, which drops it below the two-photo minimum the list requires. As a result the Dismissed filter currently returns no groups, even though the Dismissed (N) tab still counts them. Resolving a Duplicate Group​ Click on a duplicate group to open the review modal: Each photo is shown with its resolution, file size, camera, date, and file path The highest-resolution photo is automatically pre-selected as the one to keep The pre-selected photo's button reads "Keep this"; every other photo shows a "Select" button. To keep a different photo, click its "Select" button — that photo's button then changes to "Keep this" Click "Keep selected & trash others" — the other photos are moved to trash The group status changes to Resolved Other Actions​ "Not duplicates" — Dismiss the group if the photos aren't actually duplicates. The group's status changes to Dismissed and it is listed under the Dismissed filter with its photos. Detection does not offer these photos again; a group that gains a new photo (a further copy found later) goes back to Pending. Dismissing a resolved group first takes the photos its resolution trashed out of the trash. Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) Up to 1.6.0, dismissing unlinked the photos, so a dismissed group was listed nowhere and the next detection offered the same photos again. "Revert & restore photos" — For resolved groups only: undo the resolution, restore the photos that resolving moved to the trash, and set the group back to Pending. A photo of the group that you trashed yourself, before or after resolving, stays in the trash. Dismissed groups can't be reverted. Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) Up to 1.6.0, reverting restored every photo of the group that was in the trash. Delete group — Remove the duplicate group record entirely.
You can select multiple duplicate groups using the checkboxes and delete them in bulk.

Start with exact copies — These are guaranteed duplicates and safe to clean up Review visual duplicates carefully — Similar-looking photos from a burst sequence or different angles may not be true duplicates Use strict sensitivity first — Strict gives you high-confidence matches to review. A later run can still form new groups from photos that weren't matched, but visual detection skips any photo already in a visual-duplicate group, so a looser re-run won't add members to groups the strict run already created. To re-evaluate those photos, first clear their groups — enable Clear pending duplicates when you re-run (this deletes pending groups only; resolved groups are kept and their photos stay excluded), or delete the individual groups The batch size parameter can be tuned in the detection API for systems with limited memory (smaller batches use less RAM but take longer)

Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) LibrePhotos has a photo editor. Crop and straighten a photo, pick a filter, or work on light and colour with the controls you know from desktop photo editors. The editor has two modes: Simple, with a few plain sliders, and Advanced, with every control.

Editing never changes your photo file. An edit is a list of settings that LibrePhotos stores with the photo. When you save, the server makes an edited copy of the picture from your original and those settings, and the app shows that copy everywhere: in the grids, in the photo viewer, in downloads and to the people you share the photo with. Because the original stays as it is, you can open the editor again at any time to change an edit, step back through its history, or remove it with Revert to original.... The edited copies are stored in the /edits folder of LibrePhotos' own files, next to the thumbnails, not in your photo folders.

Your own photos. Photos someone shares with you, and photos on a public link, have no edit button. Still pictures: JPEG, PNG, HEIC, WebP and the other image formats LibrePhotos shows, and RAW files (see RAW files). Not videos. The editor runs in your browser and needs WebGL 2, which every current browser has. In a browser without it, the edit button stays visible but does nothing, and its tooltip says This browser can't run the editor: it needs WebGL 2. Turning on hardware acceleration in the browser's settings often helps.

Open a photo in the photo viewer and click the edit button in the toolbar, next to Share link (tooltip Edit (E)), or press e. On a phone the button is in the bar at the bottom of the screen. On a photo's own page, the Edit button under the title opens the editor too. When you close the editor, the focus goes back to the edit button. On a photo you already edited, the button is highlighted and its tooltip says Edit (E). This photo is edited. The grids show no badge for edited photos: they show the edited picture. The editor fills the window. The bar at the top holds the back arrow (Close (Escape)), the file name, the Simple | Advanced switch, undo and redo, the compare buttons, Reset all edits, the ⋮ (More actions) and Save. The controls are on the right, or under the photo on a phone, where the mode switch sits above them and the controls can be hidden to see more of the photo. The editor remembers the mode you used last in this browser. Both modes change the same edit, so you can switch at any time without losing anything. To look closer, scroll or pinch to zoom, drag to move around, and double-click to switch between the whole photo and 100 %. The corner of the photo shows the zoom, with Fit and 100%.

Simple mode has three tabs: Tab What you find there Adjust Auto, then Brightness, Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Saturation, Warmth, Tint, Sharpness and Vignette. Reset adjustments sets them all back. Filters A small preview of the photo with each look: Original, Vivid, Warm, Cool, Fade, Matte, Punch, Golden, Cinematic, Mono, Mono contrast, Sepia and Film. Strength makes the chosen look weaker or stronger. Crop & rotate The crop frame, Aspect ratio, Straighten, and Rotate and flip. Reset crop and rotation takes them back. Auto sets the light of the photo from its histogram, as a starting point you can change. It reads the photo as you framed it, so it is not available while the crop tool is open. Brightness covers about two stops each way; a brighter or darker setting made in the advanced mode's Exposure shows as it is, and the slider moves on from there. Picking a filter replaces the filter you picked before instead of adding to it, and Original takes it off again. A filter never changes the crop. In Crop & rotate, drag the frame, or one of its edges or corners, over the photo. With the frame selected, the arrow keys move it, and Shift + an arrow key moves it further. Aspect ratio locks the frame to Free (no lock), Original (the photo's own shape), 1:1, 5:4, 7:5, 3:2, 4:3, 16:9 or 16:10; Swap orientation turns a ratio between landscape and portrait. Straighten turns the photo by up to 45° either way to level a horizon, and the crop shrinks so no empty corner shows. The buttons next to Rotate and flip are Rotate left, Rotate right, Flip horizontally and Flip vertically. Leave the tab (or press Escape) to see the cropped photo again. Every slider shows its value in a field you can type into. Double-click a slider or its name to set it back to where it started.

Advanced mode shows the histogram at the top and the controls in sections you can fold open and closed. A section you changed has a reset button (Reset and the section's name) that sets just that section back. Section What it is for Histogram How the brightness of the edited photo is spread, in red, green, blue and overall. A marker in the left or right top corner lights up when shadows or highlights are clipped to pure black or pure white. Presets The same looks as the Filters tab, as a list, with Strength. Light Auto, Exposure, Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Whites and Blacks: the brightness of the whole photo and of its bright and dark parts. Tone curve A curve for all channels together (All) or for Red, Green or Blue alone. Click the curve to add a point and drag it; double-click a point or drag it off the curve to remove it. Color Color or Black & white at the top, then the white balance (Temperature, Tint) and Vibrance and Saturation. Vibrance strengthens weak colours more than strong ones and spares skin tones. Color mixer One colour band at a time (red, orange, yellow, green, aqua, blue, purple, magenta), with its Hue, Saturation and Luminance. A dot on a band says it holds a change. Shown for colour photos. B&W mix How light or dark each colour band turns in grey. Shown instead of the colour mixer when you chose Black & white. Color grading Four colour wheels, Shadows, Midtones, Highlights and Global, each with its Luminance, to tint the dark, middle and bright parts of the photo. Blending sets how far the three ranges overlap and Balance moves the split between them. Effects Texture and Clarity bring out fine detail and mid-size contrast, Dehaze cuts through haze (or adds it). Vignette darkens or lightens the corners, shaped by Midpoint, Feather and Roundness. Grain adds film grain, with Grain size and Roughness. Detail Sharpening with its Radius, and Noise reduction and Color noise for photos taken in low light. Crop & rotate The same crop tool as in simple mode. Opening the section shows the whole photo with the crop frame. History Every step of the edit (see below).

Copy settings and Paste settings in the ⋮ (More actions) of the editor, or Ctrl + Shift + c and Ctrl + Shift + v, carry the look of one photo over to another: everything except the crop, the rotation, the straighten angle and the flips, which belong to the photo they were made for. Open the next photo in the editor and paste. The copied settings are kept in this browser only.
documents.s: Copying an edit to other photos

documents.t: Every change is a step: moving a slider, picking a filter, a crop, Auto, a paste or a reset. Undo and redo in the top bar, or Ctrl + z and Ctrl + Shift + z, go back and forward one step. The History section of advanced mode lists every step, newest at the top and Original at the bottom; click one to go back to it. The steps after it stay listed, dimmed, until you make a new change. The history is saved with the edit, up to the last 200 steps. When you open the editor again, on this or any other device, the history is still there and you can go back to any step.

Hold to compare: hold down the compare button in the top bar (tooltip Hold to see the photo before its adjustments, with its crop and rotation ()), or the \ key, to see the photo without its adjustments. It keeps the crop and rotation, so you compare the same framing. Before and after side by side: the button next to it, or y, splits the photo into Before on the left and After on the right. Drag the divider, or move it with the arrow keys. The split view is not available while you crop.

Nothing changes on the photo until you click Save. While the server saves, the editor says Saving the edit… and takes no input, so what is saved is what you see. When the server has answered, the editor closes, says Edit saved, and you are back in the photo viewer: The thumbnails and the photo viewer show the edit right away. The server makes the edited picture at full size in the background, which can take a few seconds for a large photo or a RAW file. Until it is ready, zooming in shows the display-size version, with the label The edited photo is still being prepared at full size. If the save fails, the editor says why and stays open with your changes, so you can try again. If you close the editor (or press Escape, go back or follow a link) with changes that are not saved, it asks Save your changes?: Discard drops them, Keep editing stays in the editor and Save saves them. Reset all edits in the top bar (in the ⋮ on a phone) sets every control back in one step. Like any step, you can undo it, and it is only kept when you save.

Revert to original... in the editor's ⋮ removes the edit for good: its settings, its history and the edited copies. LibrePhotos asks first (Revert to the original?); while it reverts the editor says Reverting to the original…, then the photo shows its original again everywhere. The option is shown once a photo has a saved edit. Rotating an edited photo with the rotate items in the photo viewer turns its edit, crop included, and adds the turn to its history.

On a photo you edited, the photo viewer's ⋮ (More actions) and the Download button of the photo's page have two downloads: Download edited: the edited picture at full size, as a JPEG named after the original with -edited added. It is available once the server has made it. Download original: your untouched original file. Download from a selection in a grid gives you the original files. Everyone else only ever gets the edited picture: users you share the photo or an album with, members of an album, people you share your library with, and visitors of a public link. That holds even when you allow them to download original files, and while the full-size picture is still being made, when they get the smaller version. The edited picture carries no metadata from the original file, such as the GPS position.

Note A RAW file is developed by the server from the RAW data, with a neutral starting look. While the editor opens, it shows the photo as the viewer did; the editable picture follows within a second or two. It can look different from the JPEG your camera makes, which has the camera maker's own colours and contrast. There are no lens corrections and no camera profiles yet. RAW data holds more detail in the highlights than a JPEG, so Highlights and Exposure can bring back bright areas that look white at first. When a photo has a RAW and a JPEG of the same shot (a RAW+JPEG pair), the editor works on the JPEG, the photo's main file. A RAW file on its own is edited from its RAW data.

Face boxes follow a crop, a turn or a flip: they stay on the faces, and a face cropped out keeps its name and comes back when you widen the crop again. Reverting puts the boxes back where they were. On a photo whose crop or rotation you changed, Select text in photo is not offered, but the text found in the photo stays searchable.

When a scan finds that the file of an edited photo was replaced on disk: Only its metadata changed (for example a date written into the file): the edit stays as it is. The same picture, saved again (for example after a small touch-up in another program): the edit is applied to the new file. A different picture: the edit is removed, because a crop made for one picture does not fit another.

No local adjustments: no brushes, masks, healing or red-eye removal. Every control works on the whole photo. Videos cannot be edited. The mobile app shows edited photos, but has no editor yet. While you edit, the preview is a smaller version of the photo (up to 2560 pixels on the long side). The saved photo is made at full size, so very fine detail, such as the effect of sharpening or noise reduction, can look slightly different. The editor needs WebGL 2 in the browser (see Which photos you can edit).

Key Action e Open the editor (in the photo viewer) Ctrl + z (⌘ + z on macOS) Undo Ctrl + Shift + z or Ctrl + y Redo \ (hold) Show the photo without its adjustments y Before and after side by side Ctrl + Shift + c Copy settings Ctrl + Shift + v Paste settings Arrow keys Move the crop frame or the split view's divider; Shift moves further Escape Leave the crop tool, or close the editor The keys do nothing while you type in a value field. For how the editor works inside, see the developer page Photo editing pipeline.

New in 1.6.0 When something breaks, LibrePhotos saves a report of the error on your server. Nothing leaves the server until an admin decides so: errors are kept, scrubbed, so you can still share them later, or never. Both the backend (the web server and the background workers) and the web app save their errors here. The web app hands its errors to your server, never to a reporting server directly.

Admin area > Error reporting decides where new reports go: Off: keep reports on this server (the default). Reports are saved and nothing is sent. My own server: your own GlitchTip or Sentry project. Set its DSN in SENTRY_DSN and restart; until then this choice is greyed out. Share with the LibrePhotos maintainers: the maintainers' GlitchTip project. It helps us find and fix bugs we would otherwise only hear about in an issue. A new server asks during its first-time setup, in the Errors step; Off: keep reports on this server is the first button. A server set up before error reporting existed asks its admins once instead, in a Help fix bugs in LibrePhotos? dialog with the same choices and Not now. Whichever admin answers first answers for the server: the question does not come back, on any device, and the choice can be changed any time under Admin area > Error reporting. Turning sharing on while reports are saved asks a second question first: Send the saved reports too? It lists the saved reports. Only new reports leaves them on your server; Send them too sends them as well.

Error reports (linked from the setting, at /admin/error-reports) lists the saved reports, newest first: the error, whether it came from the server or the web app, when it last happened, how often, the release, and whether it was sent. Each report has: Send once: send just this report, without turning sharing on. It goes to the server chosen under Error reporting, or to the maintainers while it is off. Download: save the report as a JSON file, exactly what would be sent. Email: open your mail app with a message to the maintainers (bugs@reports.niaz.omg.lol) that names the error. Mail links cannot attach files, so attach the file Download saved. This works for a server without internet access too. The address is received by the maintainers' own report mail bridge, which runs on a server in Germany: it passes valid report files on to the maintainers' error tracker and drops everything else in the mail, including your address, the subject and the text. A mail without a valid report file is kept for 30 days with your address, the subject, the text and the attachments so the maintainers can read it, and is then deleted. Delete: remove it from your server. Send all sends every report not sent yet; Delete all removes them all. Reports already sent stay on the server they went to. At most 30 reports are kept, none older than 30 days. The same error again within a day counts as another occurrence of the same report.

A report is a Sentry event rebuilt from an allowlist, so a field LibrePhotos does not know never gets through. It holds: the event's id, time, level (error), platform, logger name, the LibrePhotos release and the environment (production); the error's type and message, and its stack: file, function, line and column, and up to five lines of code around each line; for a logged error, the log message with its values filled in; the name and version of the error reporting SDK, the Python runtime, the operating system and the browser, and for a web app error the browser's User-Agent; for a server error, the HTTP method and the URL pattern (like /api/photos/{pk}/), never the address itself; whether it came from the server or the web app. Before a report is saved, every text in it is scrubbed. These are replaced by placeholders such as <library>, <name> or <email>: paths below a library folder, the data folder and the media folder, other absolute paths, and home folders; the file names of photos, videos, RAW and sidecar files; usernames, first and last names and email addresses of users, and the names of people, albums, events and tags; email addresses, IP addresses, URLs and this server's host names. A report never holds: your photos, the request (its address, query, body, cookies and headers, login tokens included), the signed-in user, breadcrumbs, local variables, extra data, tags, the installed packages, other threads or the server's name. Paths of LibrePhotos' own code are kept, made relative (api/photos/files.py, site-packages/django/...), so a stack stays readable. The web app's script files are kept as paths only (/assets/index-abc123.js). Sending a report is one HTTPS request from your server to the chosen server, with nothing else about your server. That server sees your server's IP address, as with any connection.

SENTRY_DSN takes the DSN of a GlitchTip or Sentry project. Your server gets the same scrubbed reports the maintainers would. ERROR_REPORTING_MAINTAINERS_DSN holds the maintainers' project; set it empty to make sharing with the maintainers unavailable on your server.

LibrePhotos reads a photo's metadata with ExifTool when it scans the photo: from the file itself and from the XMP sidecars next to it. What you change in LibrePhotos (a date, a caption, tags, a location, a rating, a rotation, the people on a photo) is stored in LibrePhotos' database. With Settings → Metadata options → Write edits to files set to Save to sidecar or Save to media file, some of these edits are also written back, so other apps see them. The tag names on this page are ExifTool's. A family 0 group such as XMP: matches every XMP namespace, a family 1 group such as XMP-dc: one of them. To see what a file holds, run exiftool -G1 -a -s photo.jpg. Some names differ from the EXIF standard: ExifTool calls ISO EXIF:ISO (not ISOSpeedRatings), the 35 mm focal length EXIF:FocalLengthIn35mmFormat (not FocalLengthIn35mmFilm) and the EXIF DateTime tag EXIF:ModifyDate. Info New in 1.4.0 Much of this page is new. Up to 1.3.0: the setting was called Synchronize metadata to disk. It wrote ratings, dates, face regions and rotations, but never captions, locations or tags, and rotations never reached a sidecar. In a HEIC, AVIF or RAW original it wrote a wrong orientation, often the opposite turn; a scan wrote a rating it found in a file back to disk, which in sidecar mode created an .xmp holding just that rating (harmless, unless the rating is later changed in the original by another app); a write always went to IMG.xmp, even next to an existing IMG.jpg.xmp, and a failed write looked like a success; face regions of rotated photos were written in the wrong place, adding person names replaced the photo's keywords, and deleting a face left its region in the file; a sidecar's date, position and camera (its exif:, tiff: and exifEX: properties) and the sidecar of a photo's RAW or video file were not read, nor were the IPTC and EXIF captions, the title, creator and copyright, the PersonInImage and HierarchicalSubject keywords, the camera and lens maker, the serial number and the other exposure fields, the altitude, and the date and camera of MKV, WebM and phone videos; shutter speeds faster than about 1/2000 s were stored as 0, and photos and videos turned a quarter by their orientation were stored at their unturned size (the update fixes the size); a photo with a sidecar was stored with the file size of the sidecar, shown in Info. After the update, a Rescan from the Library page reads the new fields of the photos already in your library. python manage.py save_metadata --types face_tags rewrites the face regions of photos written by an older version, and python manage.py refresh_exposure_time reads just their shutter speeds again.

Where a field lists several tags, the first one the photo has is used. In LibrePhotos Tags, best first Notes Date and time XMP:DateCreated, EXIF:DateTimeOriginal, EXIF:ModifyDate, QuickTime:CreationDate, QuickTime:CreateDate, Matroska:DateTimeOriginal, Composite:GPSDateTime, then the file name Decided by your date rules, in the order of your list; this is the default order. A date you set by hand wins over every rule. QuickTime:CreationDate is the local time a phone recorded a video at; QuickTime:CreateDate (MP4, MOV), Matroska:DateTimeOriginal (MKV, WebM) and Composite:GPSDateTime are UTC and are converted with the time zone of the photo's position, or else your default time zone. XMP:DateCreated is where LibrePhotos writes dates. Accounts created before 1.1.0 do not have its rule unless they add it with Add rule or Reset to defaults. New in 1.4.0 Between the tags and the file name, a Google Takeout JSON next to the file gives the date. Time zone of the date EXIF:OffsetTimeOriginal, EXIF:OffsetTime New in 1.5.0 The UTC offset the camera or phone wrote for the capture time (-07:00), stored in the photo's metadata as it is written; blank values some cameras write are skipped. The date rules use it too: Info shows the offset of the photo's date after the time, for example "23:30 (UTC-07:00)", and a date tag written in UTC (2025:06:02 06:30:00Z) is turned into local time with it (see date rules). Location Composite:GPSLatitude, Composite:GPSLongitude ExifTool builds them from the EXIF GPS block, the embedded XMP or a video's GPSCoordinates. The place name (city, country) is looked up from the position. New in 1.4.0 A file without a position takes the one in its Google Takeout JSON, if it has one. Altitude Composite:GPSAltitude In metres, negative below sea level, stored in the photo's metadata. Rating, favorite Rating Without a group ExifTool answers with XMP-xmp:Rating or the EXIF Rating. A photo rated at least Minimum image rating to interpret as favorite is a favorite. Tags XMP:Subject, IPTC:Keywords, XMP:PersonInImage, XMP:HierarchicalSubject All four are merged, and each keyword becomes a tag with a small file icon. New in 1.5.0 A sidecar with a keyword list replaces the photo file's keywords (XMP sidecars). Of a hierarchical keyword (Lightroom, digiKam, darktable) the last level counts: Places|USA|San Francisco adds San Francisco. The XMP-iptcExt:PersonInImage names become tags, not people: people come from face regions. Caption XMP:Description, XMP:Description-*, IPTC:Caption-Abstract, EXIF:ImageDescription The description's default-language entry first, else any language entry, then the IPTC caption (older Photoshop and Lightroom, Picasa, newsroom tools), then the EXIF one. Text cameras put there, such as OLYMPUS DIGITAL CAMERA or SONY DSC, and a description that only repeats the camera model are skipped. New in 1.4.0 Without any of them, the description of a Google Takeout JSON next to the file. Title XMP:Title, XMP:Headline, IPTC:ObjectName Stored in the photo's metadata (/api/photos/{id}/metadata/). Creator XMP:Creator, IPTC:By-line, EXIF:Artist The first name when there are several. Stored in the photo's metadata. Copyright XMP:Rights, IPTC:CopyrightNotice, EXIF:Copyright Stored in the photo's metadata. New in 1.5.0 Shown in the Rights section of the photo's details, see Copyright and licenses. License XMP-cc:License, XMP-xmpRights:WebStatement, XMP-xmpRights:Marked New in 1.5.0 One of a fixed list (All rights reserved, the Creative Commons 4.0 licenses, CC0, Public Domain Mark): from XMP-cc:License, else a WebStatement that is a Creative Commons deed; Marked true without either is All rights reserved. See Copyright and licenses. Faces and people XMP:RegionInfo MWG face regions (XMP-mwg-rs:RegionInfo) with normalized areas. A region with a name becomes a face of the person of that name. LibrePhotos' own face detection runs as well; a detected face that overlaps a region is the same face. Orientation EXIF:Orientation; for HEIC and AVIF QuickTime:Rotation and QuickTime:Mirroring An orientation of 5 to 8 turns the photo a quarter, so its width and height are swapped. A HEIC or AVIF photo is shown under its irot and imir properties, which ExifTool reports as QuickTime:Rotation and QuickTime:Mirroring, whatever its EXIF orientation says. Face regions are placed with the same orientation. Width, height ImageWidth, ImageHeight; for videos also Composite:Rotation The size the photo is shown at, used for its aspect ratio. A video recorded upright on a phone is stored landscape with a rotation of 90 or 270 degrees; its width and height are swapped. 360° photo sphere XMP:ProjectionType, XMP:UsePanoramaViewer New in 1.5.0 Google's Photo Sphere XMP (XMP-GPano), embedded or in a sidecar: equirectangular makes the photo a photo sphere, unless UsePanoramaViewer is false. Without it, a photo exactly twice as wide as tall and at least 6000 pixels wide counts as one. Videos are never marked. Video length QuickTime:Duration, Matroska:Duration MKV and WebM files carry no QuickTime:Duration. Camera EXIF:Make, EXIF:Model; for videos QuickTime:Make, QuickTime:Model Info shows the maker in front of the model ("Fujifilm X-T5"), unless the model already starts with it ("NIKON D850", not "NIKON CORPORATION NIKON D850"). Corporate words at the end of a maker's name are left out there ("OLYMPUS IMAGING CORP." shows as "OLYMPUS"). Lens EXIF:LensMake, EXIF:LensModel Shown like the camera. Exposure EXIF:FNumber, EXIF:ExposureTime, EXIF:ISO, EXIF:FocalLength, EXIF:FocalLengthIn35mmFormat Shown in Info. The shutter speed is shown the way ExifTool prints it: 1/4000 up to a quarter second, then seconds (0.3 s, 2.5 s, 30 s). More exposure details EXIF:ExposureCompensation, EXIF:Flash, EXIF:MeteringMode, EXIF:WhiteBalance, EXIF:SubjectDistance, EXIF:DigitalZoomRatio Stored in the photo's metadata; metering mode and white balance under the names ExifTool prints (Multi-segment, Auto, ...). Subject distance and digital zoom are shown under Show more in Info; 0, which EXIF uses for "unknown" and "not used", is left empty. Camera serial number EXIF:SerialNumber Stored in the photo's metadata, not shown in Info. Colour space, bit depth EXIF:ColorSpace, File:BitsPerSample Stored in the photo's metadata. The bit depth is read from JPEG files only. File size File:FileSize Shown in Info. Read from the photo file, never from a sidecar. Bursts EXIF:SubSecTimeOriginal, EXIF:ImageNumber; MakerNotes:BurstMode, MakerNotes:ContinuousDrive, MakerNotes:SequenceNumber Used by stack detection to find burst sequences. The MakerNotes tags are only read while the matching burst detection rule is on in your settings.

A sidecar is an .xmp file next to the photo. LibrePhotos reads both naming conventions, in lower or upper case. For a photo IMG_2.jpg, from the highest priority down: IMG_2.xmp, then IMG_2.XMP (Lightroom, LibrePhotos up to 1.3.0); IMG_2.jpg.xmp, then IMG_2.jpg.XMP (digiKam, darktable, Immich, LibrePhotos from the next release); the sidecars named after the photo's other files, such as IMG_2.CR2.xmp for the RAW file of a RAW+JPEG pair, or the video of a Live Photo; other .xmp files the scan grouped with the photo; the photo file itself. Each tag is taken from the highest one that has it, so one field can come from the sidecar and the next from the photo. Keywords are the exception: New in 1.5.0 when a sidecar has a keyword list (XMP:Subject, XMP:PersonInImage or XMP:HierarchicalSubject), it is the photo's whole keyword list, and the photo file's own keywords, its IPTC:Keywords included, are not read. A keyword you removed in digiKam or Lightroom, which write sidecars, then no longer comes back from the original. Up to 1.4.0 the photo's IPTC:Keywords, which a sidecar cannot hold, were still added. On a file system that ignores case (Windows, macOS), IMG_2.xmp and IMG_2.XMP are the same file and it is read once. Apps that leave the original untouched (geotaggers, digiKam, darktable, Lightroom) store the EXIF properties of a photo in the sidecar under XMP names. LibrePhotos reads these there: Field Read from the sidecar as EXIF:DateTimeOriginal exif:DateTimeOriginal Composite:GPSLatitude, Composite:GPSLongitude exif:GPSLatitude, exif:GPSLongitude Composite:GPSDateTime exif:GPSTimeStamp EXIF:Make, EXIF:Model tiff:Make, tiff:Model EXIF:LensMake, EXIF:LensModel exifEX:LensMake, exifEX:LensModel EXIF:FNumber, EXIF:ExposureTime, EXIF:ISO, EXIF:FocalLength, EXIF:FocalLengthIn35mmFormat exif:FNumber, exif:ExposureTime, exif:ISOSpeedRatings, exif:FocalLength, exif:FocalLengthIn35mmFilm EXIF:ExposureCompensation, EXIF:MeteringMode, EXIF:WhiteBalance, EXIF:SubjectDistance, EXIF:DigitalZoomRatio exif:ExposureBiasValue, exif:MeteringMode, exif:WhiteBalance, exif:SubjectDistance, exif:DigitalZoomRatio The right column is how the properties are named inside the .xmp file; ExifTool shows them as XMP:DateTimeOriginal, XMP:GPSDateTime, XMP:ISO and so on. The XMP fields (rating, keywords, description, title, creator, copyright, XMP:DateCreated, face regions) are read from a sidecar under their own names. A sidecar's modify date and orientation are never read: they describe the last edit, not the photo, and a sidecar orientation must not turn LibrePhotos' thumbnails. Its flash, colour space and serial number are not read either. Nor are the tags that describe a file rather than the photo: the file size and bit depth (File: tags), and the width and height. Those always come from the photo file, even when a RAW editor's sidecar holds the size of the RAW (tiff:ImageWidth, tiff:ImageLength).

With Write edits to files set to Save to sidecar, an edit goes to the sidecar of the photo file that already exists, so a digiKam or darktable sidecar is updated in place and keeps its other tags. When both IMG_2.xmp and IMG_2.jpg.xmp exist, the edit goes to IMG_2.xmp, the one that is read first (the backend log warns about it). When there is none, LibrePhotos creates IMG_2.jpg.xmp, which other apps also read and which cannot be mistaken for the sidecar of a RAW file next to the JPEG (IMG_2.CR2). The sidecar of a photo's RAW file (IMG_2.CR2.xmp) is read but not written: the edit goes to the sidecar of the photo's main file, the JPEG. A photo that up to 1.3.0 got an IMG_2.xmp next to an existing IMG_2.jpg.xmp keeps both: LibrePhotos reads and writes IMG_2.xmp, and the other app keeps its own file.

New in 1.4.0 A zip download of photos also holds the XMP sidecars next to their files, so the edits saved to a sidecar travel with the photo and another app reads them from the download. That includes a sidecar LibrePhotos created after the last scan and the sidecars of a photo's RAW file. When two photos have the same file name, the second goes in as IMG_2_1.jpg and its sidecar as IMG_2_1.jpg.xmp, so each sidecar keeps the name of its file. Up to 1.3.0, a download held only the sidecars a scan had found, and none that write-back had just created.

New in 1.4.0 To see every tag a photo's file carries, not just the fields above, open All metadata: in the lightbox's info panel it is the link in the file row (next to the size), on the photo page the button at the end of the File card. Only the photo's owner sees it. The dialog asks ExifTool for every tag of the media file and of each XMP sidecar the scan reads (see Which sidecars are read), one tab per file: the media file, then the sidecars, highest priority first. Tags are grouped as ExifTool groups them (IFD0, ExifIFD, GPS, the camera's maker notes, XMP-dc, QuickTime, ...), sorted by name within a group, and their values read as in ExifTool's own output (1/250, Horizontal (normal)); embedded images and other binary data show as (Binary data N bytes). The maker notes start collapsed, since they can be hundreds of tags. Filter tags and values narrows the list to the tags whose group, name or value contain the text, and says how many match. Copy as JSON copies the open tab's tags in the shape of exiftool -json -G1, ready to paste into an issue or a forum post. The tags are read from the files when the dialog opens and are never stored; the file system details (the server's folder, file permissions) are left out, and the file is named by its path below your library folder. If the file is no longer on disk, the dialog says so: rescan its folder or put the file back. This is the quickest way to find out why a date rule picked a tag, why a sidecar value was or was not used, or which tag a camera writes a setting to. For API clients: the photo detail response no longer carries the exif_json field, which was always empty. The tags come from GET /api/photos/{photo_id}/metadata/raw/ instead.

With Off, the default, LibrePhotos never writes to your files. A scan never writes either: it only reads. With Save to sidecar or Save to media file, these edits are written after they are saved in LibrePhotos. An edit of many photos at once (a rating, Change date and time…, a location for a selection, renaming a tag) is written by a background job, so the files can lag the library by a moment. Edit Save to sidecar Save to media file Rating and favorite, also from the mobile app XMP-xmp:Rating XMP-xmp:Rating, and the EXIF Rating if the file has one Date and time XMP-photoshop:DateCreated XMP-photoshop:DateCreated; the camera's EXIF dates stay as they are Rotation XMP-tiff:Orientation, for every image format EXIF:Orientation, into JPEG, PNG, TIFF and WebP files only Caption you type XMP-dc:Description XMP-dc:Description and EXIF:ImageDescription, and IPTC:Caption-Abstract if the file already has IPTC data Location XMP-exif:GPSLatitude, XMP-exif:GPSLongitude In an image GPS:GPSLatitude, GPS:GPSLatitudeRef, GPS:GPSLongitude, GPS:GPSLongitudeRef; in an MP4 or MOV Keys:GPSCoordinates Tags XMP-dc:Subject XMP-dc:Subject, and IPTC:Keywords if the file already has IPTC data Faces and their names, only with Write face tags to image files XMP-mwg-rs:RegionInfo, names added to XMP-dc:Subject the same, in the file Copyright, creator, license New in 1.5.0 XMP-dc:Rights, XMP-dc:Creator, XMP-cc:License, XMP-xmpRights:WebStatement, XMP-xmpRights:UsageTerms, XMP-xmpRights:Marked the same, and EXIF:Copyright, EXIF:Artist, and IPTC:CopyrightNotice, IPTC:By-line if the file already has IPTC data; see Copyright and licenses Title not written not written Never written: the place name (city, country), which is looked up from the position again; a generated caption; albums, hidden and archived photos; and every other tag on this page. The Write edits to files options in the settings list the same edits, and the date editor, the caption and tags editors and the Pick location dialog say in a line under the editor whether the edit reaches the file, with a link to the setting. Photos imported from Nextcloud are never written to: LibrePhotos works on a local copy, which the next scan replaces when the file changes on the server, and nothing is uploaded back. Their edits stay in LibrePhotos.

Save to sidecar works for every format, since the photo itself is never opened for writing. Save to media file needs a format ExifTool can write: JPEG, PNG, TIFF, WebP, HEIC, AVIF, JPEG XL, GIF, MP4, MOV and most RAW formats (CR2, CR3, NEF, ARW, DNG, ORF, RAF, RW2, ...). BMP, MKV, WebM, AVI and a few RAW formats cannot be written, and an edit of such a file stays in LibrePhotos (see Writes that fail). A rotation reaches only JPEG, PNG, TIFF and WebP files, whose viewers apply an EXIF orientation. HEIC, AVIF, RAW, GIF and the other formats are not rewritten for a rotation and keep it in LibrePhotos: libheif shows a HEIC or AVIF under its irot and imir properties, and a RAW decoder ignores the tag, so a written tag would only replace the camera's own value.

A date is written as the local time LibrePhotos shows, without a UTC offset. Removing a date you set by hand (Remove timestamp in the date editor) removes XMP-photoshop:DateCreated again; in a media file that also removes one another app had written there. A rotation in a sidecar is the orientation that shows the original the way LibrePhotos shows it now; for a HEIC or AVIF it starts from the file's irot and imir, not from its EXIF orientation, which can disagree. Apps that take the orientation from a sidecar, such as digiKam, show the photo turned the same way. In a media file the rotation is folded into the file's own orientation, and LibrePhotos' own rotation goes back to none, so it is not applied twice. See Rotating Photos. A caption keeps its line breaks. Clearing the caption removes the description, and removing a location removes the position tags. Setting a location in an image file also removes the file's old altitude (GPS:GPSAltitude, GPS:GPSAltitudeRef), which belonged to the old position, and an embedded XMP-exif:GPSLatitude/GPSLongitude that would disagree with the new one. In an MP4 or MOV the older copies UserData:GPSCoordinates and ItemList:GPSCoordinates go.

Tags are written as keywords, one change at a time: adding a tag adds that keyword (once, never twice), removing it removes that keyword, and the file's other keywords stay. Renaming, merging or deleting a tag on the Albums page changes the keyword in the files of every photo that carries the tag, in one background job. XMP:PersonInImage and XMP:HierarchicalSubject are never written. A tag that came from one of them is not written as a keyword unless you add it yourself, and removing such a tag leaves the name or the keyword path in the file. The names of people that the face write-back added stay, even when you remove a tag of the same name. A new sidecar starts from the photo's own keywords (XMP:Subject and IPTC:Keywords), so it does not hide them. In sidecar mode a removal only reaches the sidecar: a description, position or keyword stored in the photo file itself stays there, and an app that reads the file (or a new import into LibrePhotos) sees it again. Removing the last keyword leaves the sidecar without a keyword list, so the photo file's keywords show again. Inside LibrePhotos the removal stays.

Writing faces needs both Write face tags to image files (Settings → Face options, off by default) and a sidecar or media file chosen under Write edits to files. Then labelling, adding, deleting or restoring a face writes the photo's regions again, as MWG regions in XMP-mwg-rs:RegionInfo with AppliedToDimensions and normalized areas. The areas are in the coordinates of the stored image, as the standard asks, so on a rotated photo (most phone portraits, and photos you turned in LibrePhotos) other apps show them on the faces. Only faces of people you named get a name; the other faces are written as regions without one. The names are added to the keywords (XMP-dc:Subject) for Lightroom and digiKam, which show people as keywords. The photo's other keywords stay, and the name of a person no longer on the photo leaves the keywords, unless the photo has a tag of that name. Deleting the last face removes XMP-mwg-rs:RegionInfo from the photo file; in sidecar mode the sidecar gets an empty RegionInfo instead, so the regions another app wrote into the original stay hidden. A photo that has no faces in LibrePhotos at all (not scanned for faces yet) keeps the regions of its file. XMP-MP:RegionInfoMP (Windows Photo Gallery) and XMP-digiKam:TagsList are never changed.

New in 1.4.0 Write edits to files writes an edit when you make it. The edits you made before turning it on are only in LibrePhotos; Write now under the setting (Settings → Metadata Options, see Settings) writes them as a Write Metadata to Files job, with the same writes a live edit makes. Only a value that says something is written: Kind (types) Photos it writes ratings Rated 1 to 5 stars; a rating of 0 is not written. dates A date you set by hand. rotations Turned in LibrePhotos. captions A caption you wrote; a generated caption is never written. locations A position you set; a position read from the file is already there. keywords With tags: each tag is added to the keywords. face_tags With faces that are not deleted, named or not. Only with Write face tags to image files on. A photo with none of them is not touched, so an unrated library does not get a sidecar per photo. The job writes in batches of 200 photos, each through one ExifTool process; it shows its progress in the job list, can be cancelled there, and ends with how many photos it wrote (written), left alone (skipped: a local copy of a Nextcloud photo, or the setting changed while it ran) and could not write (errors, the first 100 listed with the file and ExifTool's reason). A write it makes is LibrePhotos' own, so the next scan does not read those photos again for it (see How a rescan treats your edits). GET /api/savemetadata/ says what it would write now (the target and a count per kind), and POST /api/savemetadata/ starts the job: {"types": [...]} picks kinds, and leaving it out writes everything your settings write. It answers 202 with the job_id, 400 while Write edits to files is Off or for a kind it does not know, and 409 while the job runs. Up to 1.3.0 it wrote the ratings of every photo, 0 included, inside the request. python manage.py save_metadata makes the same writes for every user whose Write edits to files is on (photos of users who have it Off are skipped), with the kinds each user's settings write. --types limits the kinds, --user limits it to one user, --sidecar or --media-file overrides the setting for that one user, and --dry-run only counts.
