documents.s: Writing the edits of a whole library

documents.t: A Rescan reads every file again, and a scan reads a file again when it or its sidecar changed. New in 1.4.0 A write LibrePhotos makes itself is not such a change. A scan remembers the modification time of every file it reads and of its sidecars, and a write that ExifTool reports as done updates what was remembered, so rating or re-dating a thousand photos does not make the next scan read them all again. In media file mode the write still moves the file's modification time, so backup and sync tools see that the file changed. A change another app makes is still picked up: a file it edited, a sidecar it added or one that was deleted, before or after LibrePhotos' write. A photo indexed by an earlier version gets its times remembered on the first scan that reads it or finds it unchanged; until then, a write makes the next scan read the photo once more, as before. What a scan does to a value you edited in LibrePhotos: Field On a rescan Date and time A date you set by hand wins over every date rule and is kept. Remove timestamp in the date editor hands the photo back to the rules. Location A position you set is kept. A position that came from the file follows the file: it moves when the file's position changes and is cleared when the file has none any more. Caption Kept. A description in the file becomes the caption only when it is new or changed since it was last imported, and only while your caption is empty or still the one imported before. A caption you cleared stays cleared. Title, creator, copyright Kept once you edited them through the metadata API, until you restore the photo from its file. Tags Only a keyword the file did not have at the last scan becomes a tag, such as one another app added; a tag you removed stays removed, even where the file still carries the keyword. A first scan makes a tag of every keyword. New in 1.5.0 This holds with Write edits to files Off too; up to 1.4.0 every keyword of the file became a tag again there. The keywords of the metadata API (PATCH /api/photos/{id}/metadata/) set the photo's tags the same way: a keyword removed there stays removed. Rating New in 1.5.0 Taken from the file only when the file's or sidecar's Rating changed since the last scan, also to 0; a rating or favorite you set in LibrePhotos stays while the file says the same. A file without a Rating changes nothing. On the first rescan after updating, a photo whose rating you changed in LibrePhotos keeps it. Up to 1.4.0, with Off, the file's rating replaced yours on every rescan. Rotation Kept. A sidecar's orientation is never read. Faces The faces LibrePhotos has stay. A face region in the file that overlaps one of them is not added again. POST /api/photos/{id}/metadata/revert-all/ restores a photo from its file: it reads the file and its sidecars again and sets every field (date, location, rating, caption, tags, title, copyright, creator) to what they say, or empties it where they say nothing. Nothing is written. In sidecar mode the sidecar holds the edits LibrePhotos wrote, so those come back as they are there.
documents.s: How a rescan treats your edits

documents.t: Turning Write edits to files back to Off stops further writes; it does not change back what was written. Your edits stay in LibrePhotos either way. Sidecar mode never changes the photo files. To take LibrePhotos' writes back, delete the sidecars it created: IMG_2.jpg.xmp, or IMG_2.xmp for writes up to 1.3.0. A sidecar that another app made and LibrePhotos updated also holds that app's data, so do not delete those blindly; remove single tags with ExifTool instead, for example exiftool -XMP-tiff:Orientation= IMG_2.jpg.xmp. Media file mode changes your originals in place. ExifTool runs with -overwrite_original, so no IMG_2.jpg_original backup is kept; the image data itself is not re-encoded. Keep a backup before you turn it on. To see what LibrePhotos changed in a file, compare exiftool -G1 -a -s IMG_2.jpg of the file and of its backup; LibrePhotos only touches the tags in the table under What LibrePhotos writes.

A write ExifTool cannot make, for example into a read-only library, a damaged file or a format that cannot hold the tag, never undoes your edit: the rating, date, caption, location, tags, face label or rotation stays in LibrePhotos. The backend log names the photo and ExifTool's reason. Labelling a face, drawing one and rotating a photo also return the reason as write_error in the API response, and the Write metadata to files job and manage.py save_metadata list the photos they could not write. In the web app, a face label, a drawn face or a rotation that did not reach the file shows an orange Not written to the file notice next to the usual confirmation: "Saved in LibrePhotos, but not written to the file", followed by the reason. It stays until you close it. Changing a date, a rating, a caption, tags or a location writes the file after the edit is saved, so a failure there is only in the backend log.

The face dashboard is the Faces page, where you label, confirm and clean up faces. New in 1.6.0 Open it in any of these ways: On Albums › People, click the link in the line under the title. It reads N faces to review while suggestions wait for you, and Review faces otherwise, and opens the Inferred tab (narrowed to the group you are looking at, if any). On a person's page, open the ⋮ (Person actions) and choose Review faces. The dashboard opens on the Labeled tab with only that person's faces, and a chip with their name in the toolbar; remove the chip to see everyone's faces. Pin it to the sidebar: click Customize sidebar under the sidebar's pages and tick Faces. The pinned row shows how many faces wait for review. Press Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on macOS) and type "Review faces". On a phone, People is under the Albums tab at the bottom of the screen. Up to 1.5.x, the dashboard was opened with Manage faces in the People page's menu.

To label a face, select it and click the tag button in the toolbar (Add to an existing face ID or create a new face ID), or choose Label as… in the face's ⋮ menu. A pop-up titled Label faces will show up where you can either search for an already existing person or add a new person. We want to add a new person, so type the name into the Person name field under New person and click Add person (the button stays disabled until you enter a name that does not already exist). Now the face is associated with the person. Above the list of people, Recently tagged shows the last ten people you labelled faces as, each as a small face with the name under it. Click one to label the faces as that person without searching for the name. The section hides while you type a name. While you type, the people whose names match are listed with the most faces first, then by name; with nothing typed, the list is in name order. New in 1.5.0 Up to 1.4.0, matches stayed in name order.

New in 1.5.0 Burst frames, exposure brackets and duplicates are separate photos, so the same face is found once in every frame. When you label one of them, LibrePhotos also labels that face in the other photos of the same burst or bracket stack or duplicate group: the message then says, for example, "Also labeled 4 matching faces in the same burst or duplicate group", and its Undo takes all of them back. Only a face that is clearly the same one is labelled along: one that has no name yet, at nearly the same place in the picture, and that looks nearly identical to the face you labelled. The other people in those frames, faces you already named or deleted, and a face you said is not that person (Not name) are left alone. A manual stack, and a duplicate group you dismissed as not duplicates, do not count. Sending a face to "Unknown - Other" only changes that face.
documents.s: The same face in a burst or duplicate group

documents.t: By default, labelling a face only updates the LibrePhotos database — your image files are not touched. If you enable Settings → Face options → Write face tags to image files, then every time you label a face LibrePhotos also writes the face's region and the person's name into the photo as XMP MWG-RS region tags. This makes your face data portable to other photo managers such as Lightroom, digiKam and XnView. The switch only takes effect together with Settings → Metadata → Write edits to files, which decides where the tags go: Save to sidecar: the regions go into the photo's .xmp sidecar file; the original image is left unchanged. Save to media file: the regions are written into the original image file itself. Off (the default): nothing is written, and the switch is greyed out until you pick one of the other two. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, face tags were written into the original image file while synchronization was Off. If you had the switch on with synchronization Off, your originals may already carry face regions and person names; LibrePhotos does not remove them.
documents.s: Writing face tags to your files

documents.t: To change a face to a new person, select it and click the tag button in the toolbar, or choose Label as… in its ⋮ menu. Search for the person you want it to change to and click on them. Now the face is associated with the new person.
documents.s: Change the label of a face

documents.t: You do not have to go through the face dashboard. Open a photo and look at the People section of the sidebar: it shows every face found in that photo as a small tile with the name under it, including the faces nothing has named yet. Hovering a tile draws a box around that face on the photo, so you can tell which face a tile belongs to. A face the clustering and classification have not matched to anyone is shown as Who is this?. Click the tile (or Name this face in its ⋮) to open the same Label faces dialog the dashboard uses, and pick or create a person. Clicking a named face searches for that person. The ⋮ in the corner of each tile (shown when you point at the tile, always on a touch screen) holds the face's actions: Confirm as name for a name the classification guessed, Label as… to pick another person, Not name to reject the guess, and Delete face to remove a detection that is not a face at all. Delete face asks first, as it does on the face dashboard (see Delete faces). A row labelled Unknown 001 (or a similar number) is a face that clustering grouped together with others like it, without anybody naming the group. That label is the group's name, not a person's, so there is nothing to confirm and no Confirm as item; name such a face with Label as….
documents.s: Name a face from the photo itself

documents.t: The detector does not find every face. Someone turned away from the camera, a child, a face behind a hat or sunglasses, a face too small or too blurred — none of those get a face record, so there is nothing to label and the person never appears on the photo. Open the photo, then click the person-plus button (Add a face the scan missed) at the top of the People section of the sidebar. The photo dims and the pointer becomes a crosshair: drag a box around the face, and the Label faces dialog opens so you can pick an existing person or type a new name. Press Escape, or use the Cancel button in the sidebar, to leave without adding anything. New in 1.5.0 The box only has to be rough. While the People section says "Looking for the face in your box…", the face recognition service looks at that part of the photo on its own, enlarged, where it finds faces that are too small or too turned to be found in the whole photo. The face it finds is saved with its own, exact box, and with an encoding like any detected face, so it is grouped with that person's other faces; the message then says "The face was found in your box". Only a face whose middle is inside your box is taken. If there is no face in the box, the section says No face found in the box and offers Keep my box (the face is saved with your box and the name you chose, as before) or Draw again. When the face recognition service is off or not answering, your box is saved as you drew it. Up to 1.4.0, the box you drew was saved as it was. A few things worth knowing: The face you add counts as your own labelling. It is stored exactly like a face you named on the dashboard, and classification trains on it, so adding a few faces the detector missed also helps it recognise that person elsewhere. It never starts a cluster of its own. It is encoded straight away by the face recognition service. If that service is unavailable, the face is still saved with its name — the next Train faces run gives it an embedding. You cannot draw a second face on top of one that already exists. If the box you drag lands on a face that is already recorded, LibrePhotos says so and asks you to label that face instead. A face you deleted does not block you, though: drawing a box there is you overruling the deletion. Zoom and pan are fine, rotation is not. You can zoom in to draw a box around a small face. While the photo is turned, the button is disabled — the box could not be lined up with the photo reliably — so turn it back upright first. The photo needs a thumbnail. Boxes are measured against the photo's big thumbnail, so a photo that has not been fully processed yet cannot take a face. If Settings → Face options → Write face tags to image files is enabled, a face you add by hand is written into the photo (or its sidecar) as an XMP region just like any other, so the work is portable to other photo managers.
documents.s: Add a face the scan missed

documents.t: If you click Train faces in the face dashboard's toolbar (an icon on a phone), or the Train button on the Library page (Account menu > Library, under Faces & People), the system will try to cluster unknown faces and will try to either match them to already known faces or create a new unknown person. New in 1.5.0 After uploads you do not have to: once at least 20 new faces (and 2% of all your faces) came in, LibrePhotos clusters and trains by itself, half an hour after your last upload, at most once an hour and not within 15 minutes of you labelling a face (see Find similar faces). Your names and labels stay as they are. New in 1.5.0 Clustering only replaces its own groups ("Unknown 001" and the like). A person you named stays, even with no faces left: one you created by hand, or one whose faces you all moved to someone else, keeps its name and birth date. To get rid of such a person, delete them from their page. Up to 1.4.0, every clustering deleted the named people that had no faces, those of every user. The dashboard has four tabs: Inferred (the matches training produced), Unknown (faces that were not matched, or that you rejected, grouped under "Unknown - Other"), Labeled (faces you have already named) and Deleted (faces you deleted, so you can restore them). To see the recommendations, go to the Inferred tab. There you can see, for each face, the confidence of the match. By default the dashboard only shows matches it is at least 70% confident about. To lower this threshold and surface weaker recommendations, open Filter in the toolbar and change Confidence (it applies to both the Inferred and Unknown tabs). The same panel switches between Clusters and Classifications under Show. New in 1.5.0 A person with a birth date is never suggested for a face on a photo taken more than a day before it: training suggests the next most likely person instead, or nobody. Photos without a date are not filtered, and you can still label any face by hand. Train again after setting a birth date to update the suggestions. Each tab shows how many faces it holds. Hover over a tab to see how many people (and, on the Inferred tab, groups) those faces belong to. The numbers follow the Sort and Filter settings, so they always match the faces on screen. New in 1.5.0 The dashboard leaves out the faces of photos the photo lists leave out: photos in the trash, hidden photos and missing photos. They are not counted in the tabs either, and training does not use them. Restoring a photo from the trash brings its faces back. Up to 1.4.0, the dashboard still listed them, so the copies you moved to the trash from a duplicate group still had faces to label. To confirm a whole inferred group at once, click the green check-person icon next to the person's name; it appears on the Inferred tab next to persons that already have a name. To confirm individual faces, select them and click the tag button in the toolbar to add them to the person. To reject faces, select them and click the person-off button in the toolbar (Move the faces back to 'Unknown - Other'). While faces are selected, the toolbar starts with how many are selected; click it to clear the selection.

New in 1.4.0 Each group starts with a row that shows the person's face, their name and how many faces they have. The face is the cover from the People page; a cluster such as "Unknown 001" uses its first face. Click the arrow next to the face to collapse the person: they shrink to a single tile with their face, name and face count, and collapsed people sit side by side. Collapse all groups in the toolbar's ⋯ (More actions) collapses every group at once, which turns the tab into a grid of people. A collapsed person loads none of their faces apart from the cover, so a large library opens faster this way. Click a tile to open that person's faces again. The dashboard remembers which people you collapsed, per tab. The Sort button in the toolbar (an icon on a phone) sets two orders. Under Sort by, Confidence or Date sorts the faces inside each group. Under Order people, A–Z sorts the people by name and Most faces puts the people with the most faces first. "Unknown - Other" always comes last. The letter scrubber on the right is only shown in A–Z order. New in 1.5.0 The third order, Similar faces together, puts groups whose faces look alike next to each other. It starts with the group with the most faces and then always takes the group that looks most like the last one, so the clusters of one person ("Unknown 014", "Unknown 087") usually end up in a row on the Inferred tab, often right after that person's name if they are already named. Label them in one pass, or select several groups' faces at once. Groups without a cluster (for example faces that only training suggested) come after the others, by name. A library with more than 3,000 groups keeps name order in this view. New in 1.4.0 To label one circle of people at a time, open Filter and pick a group under Groups (it says All people until you pick one): the Labeled and Inferred tabs then only show the people in that group, and the tab counts follow. Manage groups… under it renames, deletes and adds groups. The Unknown tab has no people, so the field is hidden there.

You can also review faces one at a time, without selecting them first. Point at a face (or move to it with the Tab key) and two buttons appear on it; on a phone or tablet they are always shown: The round green check-person button in the bottom-right corner confirms the face as the person of its group, in one click. It is only there on the Inferred tab, and only in the groups of people that have a name: a cluster such as "Unknown 001" names nobody, so there is nothing to confirm. The ⋮ button in the top-left corner opens the face's menu (a right click on the face opens it too, and so does a long press on Android): Not name sends a wrongly matched face back to "Unknown - Other". In a cluster it reads Move to Unknown - Other. Label as… opens the Label faces dialog for just this face, to give it the right person straight away. Show photo opens the photo the face is in. Delete face removes the face after you confirm, as described in Delete faces. On the Deleted tab the menu only offers Restore face and Show photo. "Not name" is remembered​ New in 1.5.0 When you send a face back with Not name (or the person-off button in the toolbar, or Remove from this person on a person's photos), LibrePhotos remembers that the face is not that person. Train faces never suggests them for that face again; it may suggest someone else, or leave the face in "Unknown - Other". The message after Not name says so, for example "Anna won't be suggested for this face again". To take it back, click Undo in that message, or label the face as that person yourself. When you merge Anna into another person, the face is not suggested as the merged person either. Up to 1.4.0, the next training often suggested the same person again. A face you acted on fades out and leaves the group once the list has refreshed. While you have faces selected, the menu only offers Show photo: the toolbar buttons act on the selection. New in 1.4.0 A face whose thumbnail is missing (faces from old versions, or a thumbnail that could not be saved) shows a grey person icon instead of the face. It is a face like any other: you can select it, label it, open its photo with Show photo to see who it is, or delete it. The next face scan (see Re-scan faces) cuts its thumbnail from the photo again.

Sometimes the face recognition might find a face that is not actually a face. To remove it, select the face and click on the trashcan symbol, or choose Delete face in the face's ⋮ menu; a confirmation dialog appears first. The face is then hidden everywhere in LibrePhotos — it disappears from the face dashboard, from the person's face list and from the photo's face list — and it is no longer used for training, clustering or classification. Note that hiding a face does not free disk space: the cropped face image and its embedding are kept, so the same region is not detected again on a later scan, and so the face can be restored. New in 1.5.0 Up to 1.4.0, deleted faces were still grouped by clustering, so a painting or a pattern you deleted could still merge or split the clusters of real faces. If Write face tags to image files is on, deleting faces also takes them out of the files: each affected photo's face regions are written again from the faces it has left, in a background job, and the deleted person's name is removed from the photo's keywords. Deleting the last face of a photo clears its regions, including ones another photo manager such as digiKam wrote and LibrePhotos imported: the media file loses XMP-mwg-rs:RegionInfo, and with Save to sidecar the sidecar gets an empty region list, which hides the regions still stored in the original. A name you also added to the photo as a tag stays a keyword. Only XMP MWG regions are changed: Microsoft Photo regions (XMP-MP:RegionInfo) and digiKam's People/… entries in XMP-digiKam:TagsList stay in the file. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, deleting a face left its region and name in the file. A face that was saved twice on the same photo (two overlapping boxes, for example from an old scan and from face regions read from the file) can be cleaned up for the whole instance by an admin with Remove duplicate faces.

New in 1.4.0 The message that confirms a delete, a label (Label as…, the tag button, the check-person buttons) or a wrong match (Not name, the person-off button) has an Undo button. It stays for 8 seconds, longer while you point at it. Undo puts the faces back exactly as they were: deleted faces come back to their person, and labelled faces go back to the tab they came from, with the suggestion they had (a face you confirmed on the Inferred tab is a suggestion on the Inferred tab again). When you act on several faces one after the other, the message adds them up, and its Undo takes back all of them.

The Deleted tab lists every face you deleted, grouped by the person each face had; deleted faces that had no person are under "Unknown - Other". To bring faces back: select them and click Restore N faces in the toolbar, click the restore button next to a person's name to restore all of that person's faces, or choose Restore face in a face's ⋮ menu. A restored face goes back to its person (or to the unknown faces), counts for that person again and is found by search under their name. If Write face tags to image files is on, the face's region and the person's name are written to the photo again.

Re-scan faces looks through all your photos again and adds any face it finds that does not already have a face record. This will take a while, because it has to look up all the photos again. New in 1.4.0 Every face scan, the one after a photo scan as well as Re-scan faces, first gives each face whose thumbnail is missing a new one, cut from the photo where the face was found. A face whose photo has no thumbnail keeps the grey person icon until the photo has one. Note A re-scan will not bring back faces you removed with the delete face action. Deleting a face marks it as deleted but keeps its region on record, and the re-scan skips any newly detected face that overlaps an existing record — including deleted ones. To get a deleted face back, restore it from the Deleted tab (see Restore deleted faces).

New in 1.4.0 Re-scan faces on the Library page looks at every photo, which takes hours on a large library. To look at a few photos or one folder only: Some photos: select them, open the ⋮ (Photo actions) and choose Detect faces again in the Files group (up to 1,000 photos). In the photo viewer it is in the ⋮ after the rotate buttons, and on a photo's page under More. A folder: on the folder's page (open it from Folders), open the ⋮ (Folder actions) and choose Detect faces again in this folder. It covers the folder and its subfolders and asks first, saying how many photos that is. New in 1.5.0 For a single photo (from the photo viewer or the photo's page), the photo's People section follows the scan: it says "Looking for faces again…" while the scan runs, then marks the faces it found with New, or says No new face found. The scan uses the same detector as before, so a face it missed stays missed: use Draw the face there to draw a box around it (see Add a face the scan missed). It works like Re-scan faces for those photos: faces already found and named stay as they are, and a face you deleted is not found again; restore it from the Deleted tab instead. The other photos are not touched, and the next face scan after a photo scan still looks at every photo whose faces have not been looked for yet. Only your own photos can be scanned, and a folder must be inside your scan directory or upload folder.
documents.s: Detect faces again in some photos or a folder

documents.t: After the first scan finished, go to the face dashboard. Label a couple of faces per person. Then train the faces with Train faces. Check if the inferred faces are accurate and add a couple of the inferred faces to the labels. Train the faces again. You will get the best results if all the persons in the pictures are known and when every label has at least a couple of faces.

Faces are detected with InsightFace. Its detector (SCRFD) finds the faces in each photo and returns a bounding box for every face it sees. This replaced the older dlib detectors, so there is no longer a separate hog / cnn choice — a single detector is used for everyone. Photos that already carry XMP RegionInfo face regions in the file or its XMP sidecar, for example ones written by digiKam, Lightroom or XnView, are read first. Any region marked Type="Face" with usable coordinates is taken as-is, and if the region carries a Name, the matching person is created and the face is labelled automatically. The InsightFace detector then still looks at the photo, because other photo managers usually store regions only for the faces someone tagged there. A detected face that overlaps a region is the same face: it is not added again, and it gives that face its ArcFace embedding. Every other detected face is added as usual. Regions without an overlapping detection get their embedding during the next train or re-scan, so clustering and classification work on them normally. New in 1.5.0 The detector saves every face it finds unless you set a Minimum face size under Settings → Face options: faces lower than that share of the photo's shorter side are then skipped on new scans. Face regions from the file are always kept.

New in 1.5.0 A video is not read only on its first frame, the one its thumbnail shows. The face scan also reads up to 8 frames spread from 5% to 95% of the video (one per second at most, so a short clip gets fewer) and looks for faces in each. A person seen in several frames gets one face for the video, the largest one found: a face that looks like a face the video already has (its first frame's, or one an earlier scan found) is the same person and is not added again. The video then shows up in that person's album once the face is labelled or recognised. Videos shorter than 2 seconds, or whose length the scan could not read, are read on their first frame only, as before. Up to 1.4.0, only the first frame of a video was read. After updating, the next face scan (after a photo scan, or Scan faces on the Library page) reads the other frames of every video once; the faces the videos have already stay as they are. Reading the frames costs a few seconds per video, and at most two minutes for a long one. To scan videos on their first frame only, turn off Faces in videos under Face detection in the Features card (see Feature Toggles). Open a video where a face appears​ New in 1.5.0 A face found in a later frame shows its time in the video, for example ▶ 0:42, in the corner of its thumbnail on the face dashboard. Opening the photo from that face (Show photo in its menu) starts the video a second before that moment, and a note over the video says so for a few seconds: "Started at 0:42, where Anna appears", with a Play from start button. On a person's page, a video where the person appears later shows that time in the corner of its tile and opens there too. A video opened anywhere else, from the timeline or an album, starts at 0:00 as before. In the People list of the sidebar, a face from a later frame has a time button next to its name: click it to play the video from there. If the video is being converted while it plays (see Seeking in videos), the player cannot jump ahead; the note then says where the face is and that the video can only play from the start. A face from a later frame has its thumbnail and embedding from the scan, since the frame itself is not kept: Train faces does not encode it again, a thumbnail that went missing is not cut again, and Write face tags to image files does not write it into the video as a face region, because its box is in another frame than the one other apps would show. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, a photo with even one face region was not given to the detector at all, so the other people in it were never found, not even by Re-scan faces. Run Re-scan faces once after updating to find them. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the face regions of a HEIC or AVIF photo whose EXIF Orientation disagrees with the file's own rotation (for example one turned with Save to media file in an earlier version) were read from, and written to, the wrong part of the photo.

At the moment no matter, which detection methods we use, there will be face detected, which are not actually faces. The user has to manually delete these faces. In the future, we will have a new classifier, which determines if it is a face and how likely it is a face.

Creates a 512-dimension ArcFace embedding for each detected face, which is what makes faces comparable to one another. You can choose which model is used in Admin area → Site settings → Face recognition model: smaller packs (like the default buffalo_sc) are faster and lighter, while larger packs (buffalo_l, antelopev2) are more accurate but use more memory. Switching the model later Changing the model only affects faces that do not yet have an embedding. Faces that were already encoded keep the embedding produced by the previous model: Train faces re-encodes only faces that have no embedding yet, and Re-scan faces skips faces that overlap ones already stored. Embeddings from different InsightFace packs are not comparable even though they are all 512-dimensional, so until every face is re-encoded, clustering and classification will mix two embedding spaces. To fully switch packs today you have to delete the affected faces and re-scan them. Upgrading from an older version Older versions of LibrePhotos used dlib with 128-dimension encodings. When you upgrade to the ArcFace engine, those old encodings and the existing face clusters are cleared automatically because they are not compatible with the new 512-dimension embeddings. Just run Train faces / Re-scan faces once and your faces will be re-encoded with the new model.

Clustering solves the issue of a system, which has no labelled persons yet. Users can get clusters they can name instead of going through a lot of faces and naming them. Clustering is stable, which means that you will get the same clusters out, when you put the same data in. Labels are not fed into the clustering algorithm itself — the encodings are grouped the same way no matter which faces you have already named. They do change the clusters that come out of it, though: any group that contains at least one labelled face is split into one cluster per labelled person, instead of producing a new unknown cluster for you to name. If you want to change how the grouping itself is done, add images, delete wrong faces, or change the clustering settings under Settings → Face options: Minimum cluster size (default Auto) — the smallest group the algorithm will treat as a cluster. Auto also applies when the stored value is 0 or 1, and grows from 2 to 4, 8 and 16 as your library passes 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 encoded faces. Minimum samples (default 1) — how conservative clustering is; a higher value is more conservative and leaves more faces unclustered. Cluster selection epsilon (default 0.95, shown as "Normal") — how readily nearby clusters are merged; a higher value merges more clusters together. Clustering compares face encodings scaled to length 1, so two faces are 0 to 2 apart and two photos of one person about 0.9. Small to Very high (0.9 to 1.05) merge more and more of one person's clusters; Very high can also put look-alikes, such as siblings, into one cluster. Steps which could be done to improve clustering are combining very similar faces from e.g. a serial recording or photo shoot, to prevent from too many small images to be clustered.
We could train a classifier to merge faces, based on previous merge decisions, which could improve the clusters even more.

Classification matches unknown faces against already known persons. Unlike clustering (which groups all faces from scratch), classification respects your previous labelling input and only tries to match faces to people you've already identified. This makes it much more accurate for large datasets where most persons are already known. You can filter between cluster and classification results in the face dashboard, and see the label probability for each inferred face. Classification probabilities are saved alongside clustering probabilities, so you can compare both approaches.

Yes. Version 1.0.0 came out in June 2026, and new versions have followed every few weeks since. Each release is described in the blog and on the GitHub releases page. Reviews and comparison articles written before 2026 often describe an older LibrePhotos; the feature comparison shows what it does today.

Not an official one yet. The official app, LibrePhotos Mobile, is being developed and can be tried by running it from the source code. Until it is released, UhuruPhotos is a third-party Android app for LibrePhotos. See Mobile Apps.

Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) No. The photo editor stores your edit as a list of settings and shows an edited copy that LibrePhotos makes in its own folder. The original file stays as it was, you can download it with Download original, and Revert to original... removes the edit.

documents.t: Your scan crashes with a Fatal Python error: Illegal instruction on a Proxmox guest, usually after only a few images have been imported. The traceback below is an example from an older LibrePhotos release, which used dlib / face_recognition on Python 3.9. This is a problem with proxmox, More specifically with the way the CPU was emulated. By default, QEMU in Proxmox uses its own CPU type kvm64, which has a reduced CPU flags set, to guaranteed that it works everywhere. This means that necessary flags like SSE and AVX are absent, which causes the Fatal Python error: Illegal instruction error. To fix this, one must either manually edit the .conf file and add the flags needed to the kvm64 CPU type, or pick a different method of CPU emulation. To add the flags, edit the xxx.conf file located in /etc/pve/qemu-server/ where xxx is the ID of the VM. The manual can be found here: https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Manual:_qm.conf If you don't care about live migration and moving VMs between nodes, the much easier option is to just change the CPU type to Host. With the Host option, the VM will match the CPU type of the host machine.
Select your VM and then Hardware tab. Then double-click on Processors or select it and click Edit:
This error usually means, that you forgot to rename the librephotos.env to .env

documents.t: You can set the scan directory as read-only, but then a couple of features will not be available. List of impacted features are: Writing back metadata to media files Uploading images Deleting images This is not yet handled gracefully for uploads and deletions, which means, you will probably just get non-descriptive errors there. A metadata write that fails keeps your edit in LibrePhotos and is reported instead: see Writes that fail.
documents.s: Why is the scan directory not mounted read-only?

documents.t: No. Every photo belongs to exactly one user, so LibrePhotos refuses a scan directory that overlaps another user's. To share photos within a household, keep them in one library and share albums or photos from there, or let each person share their whole library read-only with the others; Sharing photos in a family compares the setups.
documents.s: Can two users share one photo folder?

documents.t: A page fails now and then with "Something went wrong on the server", most often the Admin area, the statistics or the Things and Places lists, and the backend log shows: psycopg.errors.DiskFull: could not resize shared memory segment "/PostgreSQL.…" to … bytes: No space left on device Your disk is not full. Postgres keeps the shared memory of parallel queries in /dev/shm, and Docker gives every container only 64 MB there. On a large library a few such queries at once need more, and the one that asks last fails. The same page usually works again a moment later. New in 1.5.0 The bundled Compose files give the db service shm_size: 256mb, and the Kubernetes manifest mounts a memory-backed emptyDir at /dev/shm. Both are ceilings: memory is used only for what Postgres actually allocates, so a small library pays nothing. 1.5.0 also stopped the pages above from needing that much shared memory in the first place. If you run your own Compose file, or a release up to 1.4.0, add the setting to the db service and recreate it with docker compose up -d db: services: db: shm_size: 256mb To check it took effect, docker exec db df -h /dev/shm should show 256M.
documents.s: "could not resize shared memory segment ... No space left on device"

documents.t: The video may be in a format your browser cannot decode, most often H.265 (HEVC) in Firefox, or in Chrome on a machine without a hardware decoder for it. LibrePhotos converts such a video for your browser as it plays, without any setting (see Videos your browser cannot play). On 1.2.1 and older, enable "Always transcode videos" under Experimental Settings instead; it converts every video, so it is quite CPU heavy.

The issue could be caused by incorrect file permissions. You can resolve this by adjusting the permissions using the following commands: find . -type d -exec chmod 755 {} + find . -type f -exec chmod 644 {} + These commands will ensure that directories have permissions set to 755 and files have permissions set to 644, which should resolve any permission-related issues causing the 404 error.

In some cases you might want to enable or disable certain LibrePhotos features to preserve hardware resources or make use of some more advanced features. You can do that by referring to the following table. Feature toggles are implemented as environment variables you would have to configure before starting up backend. Feature Description Status Environment variable Embedded media Extract embedded media from "live photos" 🟢 FEATURE_PROCESS_EMBEDDED_MEDIA=true Video Import video files during a scan 🟢 FEATURE_VIDEO=true Animated video previews New in 1.4.0 Play a short silent clip of each video in the photo grid 🟢 FEATURE_VIDEO_PREVIEWS=true Face detection Find faces in your photos 🟢 FEATURE_FACE_DETECTION=true Faces in videos New in 1.5.0 Find faces in a few frames across each video, not only in its first frame 🟢 FEATURE_FACE_DETECTION_IN_VIDEOS=true Face clustering Group the faces that were found into people you can label 🟢 FEATURE_FACE_CLUSTER=true Image captioning Describe photos with an automatically generated caption 🟢 FEATURE_IMAGE_CAPTIONING=true Reverse geocoding Turn GPS coordinates into place names 🟢 FEATURE_REVERSE_GEOCODING=true Things (scene classification) Detect what is in photos (beach, kitchen, sunset, ...) for the Things albums 🟢 FEATURE_SCENE_CLASSIFICATION=true All of these default to on. See Advanced docker-compose usage for what turning each one off actually stops, and for the matching .env keys of the bundled Compose setup. Turning off face detection, image captioning or Things also keeps the matching machine learning service from starting, so its model is never loaded and never restarted by the watchdog. That is where the memory these switches save actually comes from. (Since 1.2.0; on 1.1.0 the switches stop the processing, but the services still start.) New in 1.4.0 Turning off face detection or image captioning also skips their model downloads: the Download models job no longer fetches the face recognition model or the captioning model, and a scan no longer waits for them. That saves the disk space, and an offline server no longer fails a download for a model it never uses. Turning the feature back on downloads the model then: saving the site settings starts the download, and so does the next scan or a click on "Generate caption". Models that were already downloaded stay on disk; delete their folder under data_models/ by hand if you want the space back (see Offline Usage for where each one lives).

New in 1.4.0 Every feature in the table except Embedded media also has a switch in the Features card, under Account menu > Admin area > Site settings, which an admin can flip without restarting anything. The two layers combine like this: An environment variable set to false is a hard off. The feature stays off whatever the site settings say, and its switch in the Features card is disabled, with a Locked badge and the name of the variable. To turn the feature on, change the variable in your Compose file or .env and restart. While the environment variable allows a feature (the default), its switch decides. All of them start on. Feature Name in the Features card Site setting Video Videos VIDEO_ENABLED Animated video previews Animated previews, under Videos VIDEO_PREVIEWS_ENABLED Face detection Face detection FACE_DETECTION_ENABLED Faces in videos Faces in videos, under Face detection FACE_DETECTION_IN_VIDEOS_ENABLED Face clustering Face clustering FACE_CLUSTER_ENABLED Image captioning Image captioning IMAGE_CAPTIONING_ENABLED Reverse geocoding Place names REVERSE_GEOCODING_ENABLED Things (scene classification) Things SCENE_CLASSIFICATION_ENABLED A switch saves as soon as you flip it, like the other site settings. A change applies to the next file, photo or job. Background workers take up to a minute to see it, and so does the watchdog that starts and stops the face recognition and captioning services. Turning a feature off does not delete the faces, captions, Things or place names it already produced.

New in 1.4.0 By default the photo grid plays a short silent clip of each video while you point at it, and a scan encodes two such clips per video (500 and 250 px high, VIDEO_PREVIEW_SECONDS long). On a large library of high-resolution videos that encoding is most of the scan time and of the thumbnail space videos take. Turn off Animated previews, the switch under Videos in the Features card, and a scan makes two WebP stills of each video's first frame instead, from the big thumbnail it makes anyway: no ffmpeg run, and tens of kilobytes per video where the clips often take hundreds. The grid then shows the still with the play icon and length in its corner, so a video still looks like a video, and opening it plays the whole video as before. The switch is disabled while Videos is off. Videos that already have an animated preview keep it: turning the switch off changes nothing on disk. Rescan (in the dropdown next to Scan) gives every video the kind of preview the switch asks for, so a rescan after turning the switch off deletes the clips and frees their space, and one after turning it back on encodes the clips again. New in 1.5.0 Up to 1.4.0, every video in view loaded its clip, and the stills were only made with the switch off. With the switch on, a scan makes the two WebP stills as well, and the grid shows a video's still with its length until you rest the pointer on it (or reach it with the keyboard): only then does its clip load and play, and it stops when you move on. A page full of videos so loads small pictures instead of a video player for each of them. Phones and tablets show the still, since there is no pointer to rest, and with reduced motion set on your device the grid never plays the clips. The videos added before 1.5.0 get their stills from the Make Video Posters job, which runs by itself after the update; until then they play their clip as before. Face detection, image captioning and Things run on a machine learning model. Under each of these switches a line says whether its model is ready. When a model is missing, saving a switch starts the Download models job, and the line shows its progress with a link to the job. If the download fails, the line says so and offers Retry. Embedded media The Embedded media switch is checked only the first time a file is imported. Enabling it on a library that has already been scanned extracts nothing for the photos that are already there, not even with Rescan all photos, which skips extraction for files it has already imported. Only files added afterwards are affected. Turning it off never removes clips that were already extracted; those stay on disk under protected_media/embedded_media/. Legend​ 🟢 Implemented 🔴 Planned, not implemented 🟡 In progress ⚪ Not planned

Besides the Features card above, some features are switched by a model choice in the app, under Account menu > Admin area > Site settings. A change there takes effect without a restart. Captioning model: None turns automatic captioning off. New in 1.4.0 It also keeps the captioning service stopped and the captioning model from being downloaded; picking the model again downloads it when you save. See Image Captioning. The FEATURE_IMAGE_CAPTIONING variable above switches it off for the whole deployment instead. Text recognition (OCR) model: None, the default, keeps text recognition off and its service stopped. Text that was already read stays searchable. See Text Recognition (OCR). Map tiles: None (hide map) hides the maps, so map backgrounds are never loaded from an outside server. See Site settings. Single sign-on is not a feature toggle: it is switched on in the Single sign-on group of the same Site settings card, once an identity provider is set up. See Single Sign-On.

New in 1.4.0 On a small server, or one without Internet access, you can turn off the machine learning you do not need. Set these in your .env (or the site settings switches above): FEATURE_FACE_DETECTION=false: no face detection, no face recognition service, no face recognition model download. FEATURE_IMAGE_CAPTIONING=false (or Captioning model None): no automatic captions, no captioning service, no captioning model download (about 370 MB). FEATURE_SCENE_CLASSIFICATION=false: no tags for the Things albums. Leave Text recognition (OCR) model at None, the default: no OCR service and no OCR model download. What still runs and is still downloaded: OpenCLIP ViT-B/32 (about 600 MB). It makes the embeddings behind semantic search and similar photos, so the tags service keeps running even with Things turned off, and there is no switch for it. The thumbnail, EXIF and similarity services also keep running; they hold no large models. There is no separate image without the machine learning runtime.

Each app's source code, documentation and release notes were read on 2026-11-13; for the closed-source apps (Google Photos, Synology Photos, PhotoStructure) only their official help pages were used. The version that was looked at is in the tooltip of each app's name. Cells with an i carry a note: hover over them, or turn on Show notes. Apps change quickly, and some answers depend on configuration, hardware or a paid tier. If you find a cell that is wrong or out of date, edit src/data/feature-comparison.json and open a pull request with a link to the source that shows it.
When you first access LibrePhotos, you'll be greeted with a guided setup wizard that walks you through the initial configuration in four steps: Account, Settings, Errors and Library.

The first step is to create your administrator account. Fill in the following details: Username – Your login name (will be converted to lowercase) Email – Your email address First name – Your first name Last name – Your last name Password – Choose a secure password Confirm password – Re-enter your password to confirm Click Create admin account to create your account. You'll be automatically logged in and taken to the next step.

In this step, you can configure important site-wide settings: Allow uploads – Enable or disable the ability for users to upload photos directly to LibrePhotos Allow user registration – Enable or disable public user registration (new users can create their own accounts) These settings can always be changed later in the Admin area. Click Continue to proceed.
New in 1.6.0 Choose whether error reports are shared with the LibrePhotos maintainers. Nothing is sent unless you turn it on; see Error reporting.

This is where you tell LibrePhotos where your photos are stored: Scan directory – Select or type the path to your photos folder. If you haven't modified the default docker-compose.yml, your photos are under /data, which corresponds to the folder you configured as scanDirectory in your .env file. If you will be the only user, /data itself is fine. If you plan to add more users later, pick a subfolder for yourself instead, for example /data/admin (create it on the host first). Scan directories of different users cannot overlap, so once your account scans /data itself, no other user can be given a folder under it. See Managing users. The directory picker shows a visual tree of available folders that you can click to select, or you can type the path directly. Click Save to save your settings and start the initial photo scan, or click Skip if you want to configure this later. Once complete, you'll be taken to the main LibrePhotos interface and your first scan will begin automatically if you configured a scan directory. If you shoot RAW+JPEG, the scan keeps the two files of a shot together as one photo with a RAW variant when they are in the same folder and have the same name. See Stacks & file variants.

The basic idea is this: For scanning photos that reside in the local file system Only the admin user can change the "scan directory" of the users, including that of the admin themselves. Normal users cannot change their own "scan directory" Each user needs a scan directory of their own: it cannot be the same as, inside, or above another user's scan directory. To show the same photos to several users, share them instead. Only the admin can find the page to control this: Account menu > Admin area For scanning photos that reside in external Nextcloud instances Any user can change their own Nextcloud endpoint, and choose a top level directory in the Nextcloud account.

New in 1.5.0 The login page has a Remember me checkbox under the password. Leave it off and you are signed out when you close the browser, or after 7 days at the latest. Tick it and this browser keeps you signed in for 30 days, also after a restart; when you tick it, the page says for how many days. Only tick it on your own device, not on a shared computer. Log out (in the menu under your avatar) ends a remembered sign-in on that browser right away. A remembered sign-in does not get longer by using it: after the 30 days you sign in again. Some browsers restore your last session when they start, and keep you signed in even without Remember me. That is a browser setting. Single sign-on (the buttons under "or") always works like a sign-in without Remember me. An admin can change both lifetimes, or remove the checkbox, with REFRESH_TOKEN_DAYS and REMEMBER_ME_DAYS (see Sign-in sessions).
Open Account menu > Admin area. On this page, it will show a list of users. Manually set the Scan directory for the desired user. Only an admin can do this.
documents.s: How to Change Your Scan Directory

documents.t: Open Account menu > Library. Under Scan library, click the Scan button. The chevron next to it opens a menu with Rescan, which reprocesses your entire library. See the auto scan page if you would like to set up automated scanning for new photos. For more details on the Library page and all available actions, see Library Management.

If you have a Nextcloud instance, you can also input login details for it on the Library page (Account menu > Library). The Nextcloud section is hidden until an admin enables it in Admin area > Site settings > Enable Nextcloud integration (see Library Management). Fill out the server address, username and app password for the Nextcloud section. Once the connection succeeds, the Status badge at the top of the Nextcloud section turns green and reads Connected. You can then click Browse next to Nextcloud scan directory to pick a top level directory in your Nextcloud account. Once this has been configured, you can click the blue Scan button at the bottom of the Nextcloud section (the one with the Nextcloud icon). This will copy the contents of the specified Nextcloud directory — images, videos, RAW files and XMP sidecars — to the local filesystem, and then index them the same way a regular file system scan does.
documents.s: How to Import Photos from an External Nextcloud Instance

documents.t: Open Account menu > Profile. Click Change photo next to your picture and choose Upload image to pick a file from your computer, or Choose from a face to start from the cover face of one of your people. A face you pick shows in the editor like a file would, so you can still move and zoom it. Click Upload to save it. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, an avatar could only come from a file on your computer.

Release notes and update steps use a few words that are not obvious if you do not run servers for a living. This page explains them in plain words and says where to find each thing in the app. Release notes link a word to its entry here the first time they use it. This page is for people who use LibrePhotos. If you write code for LibrePhotos, the developer glossary lists the names used in the code and the API.

The menu behind your profile picture in the top right corner. It opens Library, Profile, Settings, My jobs and, for administrators, the Admin area. On a phone, tap your picture at the right end of the bar at the bottom of the screen: the same pages open from a sheet, together with Trash and the colour scheme. Update steps write a path through the app like this: Account menu > Library.

The page where administrators change settings for the whole server: Site settings, Users, Admin tools, the Services and the Server logs. Open it with Account menu > Admin area. Only administrators see it. A step that starts with "Admins:" is done here, and other users can skip it. See Settings.

A copy of your LibrePhotos database, taken before an update so you can go back if something goes wrong. The database holds your albums, people, captions and settings. Your photo files are not in it and are never changed by an update. Docker: see Upgrading for the one command that writes the backup. Windows app: quit LibrePhotos from its tray icon, then copy the folder %LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos (or the folder you pass with --data-dir) somewhere safe.

LibrePhotos on Docker runs in containers: small, separate environments that hold the program and everything it needs. The standard setup runs several containers (the app, the database, the web server), and the single container deployment runs all of it in one. Update steps for Docker run their commands in the folder that holds your docker-compose.yml. If you use the Windows app, you have no containers and can skip these steps.

A new version sometimes changes how LibrePhotos stores its data. Developers call these changes migrations. LibrePhotos applies them by itself the first time the new version starts, so you do not have to do anything. The first start after an update can take longer because of this. Very old installs sometimes have to update in two steps, which the release notes then say. See Upgrading.

Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) The changes you make to a photo in the photo editor: a crop, a filter, brighter light and so on. LibrePhotos stores them as settings with the photo and shows an edited copy of the picture; your original file is never changed. Revert to original... in the editor removes an edit. See Editing photos.

Two common kinds of metadata. EXIF is written by the camera or phone into the photo file: the date and time, the camera and lens, the settings, and often the GPS position where the photo was taken. XMP holds details that people and programs add later, such as keywords, ratings, people and captions. It is stored in the photo file or in a separate .xmp file next to it. See Exif Data.

Work that LibrePhotos does in the background, such as a scan, finding faces, or reading the text on photos. You can keep using the app while a job runs. Follow your jobs under Account menu > My jobs. While a job runs, a progress ring is shown around your profile picture. Administrators see every user's jobs in the Worker logs of the Admin area. See Job System.

Information about a photo, as opposed to the picture itself: when and where it was taken, with which camera, who is in it, its keywords and its rating. LibrePhotos reads it from your files and can write changes back to them. See EXIF and XMP.

A file that lets LibrePhotos recognise things in photos: faces, the things and scenes in a photo, the text in a photo, or a caption. Models run on your own server, so your photos are never sent anywhere to be analysed. LibrePhotos downloads the models it needs by itself, which shows up as a Download models job. Administrators pick some of them in Site settings.

A web address that shows an album or a photo to anyone who has it, without an account. You create one from the album's Sharing dialog, or with the share link button in the photo viewer. A public link can be turned off again at any time. See Sharing.

A scan that reads every photo again, not only the new and changed ones. It takes much longer than a normal scan. Start it with Account menu > Library, then the arrow next to Scan > Rescan. Release notes ask for a rescan when a fix only applies to photos once they are read again. See Library Management.

LibrePhotos looking through your photo folders for new and changed files, and adding them to your library with thumbnails, dates, places, faces and things. Start it with Account menu > Library > Scan. Many installs also scan by themselves on a schedule, see Auto Scan.

Search by what a photo shows rather than by the words stored with it. Searching "dog on a beach" finds such photos even when no caption or keyword says so. A model compares your words with the photos, so after an update that changes this model, LibrePhotos reads all photos again in the background, and search slowly finds more photos while that runs. See Semantic Search.

A helper program that runs next to LibrePhotos and does one kind of work, for example making thumbnails or finding faces. LibrePhotos starts and restarts its services by itself. Administrators can see them under Services in the Admin area. See Service Management.

A smaller copy of a photo that LibrePhotos makes during a scan, so the grids and the photo viewer load quickly. Thumbnails are stored by LibrePhotos, apart from your photos. Changing or removing a thumbnail never changes your original photo file.
The release you are running, for example 1.3.0. After you log in, it is shown at the bottom of the sidebar as Version: 1.3.0. It says dev when you run a development build.

LibrePhotos as a program for one Windows PC, without Docker: you unzip a folder and double-click librephotos.exe. The docs call it the Windows standalone build. Release notes have separate update steps for it under "Windows app".

New in 1.4.0 Up to version 1.3.0 LibrePhotos skipped the JSON files of a Google Takeout export, so photos whose own metadata was missing ended up without a date, location or description. Google Takeout exports your Google Photos library as zip files. Next to each photo or video it puts a small JSON file with what Google Photos knew about it: when it was taken, where, and the description you gave it there. Many exported files lack some of that in their own metadata: screenshots and images saved from other apps never had it, and a location or date you changed in Google Photos lives only in the JSON. LibrePhotos reads these JSON files during the scan. It never changes your photos: the JSON is one more, lowest-priority source next to the file's own metadata.

Export Google Photos from Google Takeout and download every zip file of the export. Unzip them all into one folder inside your library (your user's scan directory, see Library Management), for example Takeout. Keep each JSON file next to its photo: LibrePhotos finds the JSON by its name and its folder. Run a Scan on the Library page. You do not need to run a tool that copies the JSON values into the files first.

In LibrePhotos From the JSON When Date and time photoTakenTime When none of the file's own tags has a date. The JSON's time is in UTC and is shown in the time zone of the photo's position, or in your Default timezone when it has none (see Date rules). It wins over a date in the file name. Location geoData, else geoDataExif When the file has no GPS position. A position of 0, 0, which Google writes for "no location", is ignored. The place name is then looked up as for any photo. Altitude the altitude of the same position With the location from the JSON. Caption description When the file has no description of its own (XMP, IPTC and EXIF come first). It becomes the caption as a description in the file does, see How a rescan treats your edits. A location or caption you set in LibrePhotos is kept, as for any photo. Albums, people, favorites and the other fields of the JSON are not read. A JSON file larger than 512 KB or one that is not valid JSON is skipped with a warning in the logs, and the scan goes on. A JSON without photoTakenTime, such as an album's metadata.json, is not a photo's JSON and is ignored.

Google names the JSON after the file, and LibrePhotos follows its naming: IMG_1234.jpg.json, or IMG_1234.jpg.supplemental-metadata.json in newer exports; for a long file name, the name before .json is cut to 46 characters, for example IMG_20180214_171835513.jpg.supplemental-metada.json or PXL_20230715_181512345.PORTRAIT.ORIGINAL-01.jp.json; for a second file of the same name, IMG_1234(1).jpg, the number moves to the end: IMG_1234.jpg(1).json; an edited copy, IMG_1234-edited.jpg, uses the JSON of the original, IMG_1234.jpg.json. A file whose JSON cannot be told apart from another file's (two long names that Google cut to the same text) gets none, so no photo takes the date of another.

A scan reads a photo again when its JSON was changed or added after the last scan (by its modified time), as it does for an XMP sidecar. Unzipping keeps the times the files had in the export, so a JSON unzipped later can look older than that scan. To read every JSON again, use Rescan (the arrow next to Scan). The JSON files are not photos: they do not show in your library and do not count as errors.

The JSON's date is read by two date rules, right before the file name rule: "Google Takeout JSON capture time in UTC + figure out timezone using GPS coordinates" (ID 20); "Google Takeout JSON capture time in user default timezone (can't find out actual timezone)" (ID 21). New accounts have them. After the update, an account whose rule list is still the default one of its LibrePhotos version gets them too; a list you changed (rules added, removed or moved) is left as you set it: add the two rules with Add rule, or use Reset to defaults. For photos you scanned before, use Apply date rules to existing photos for the dates, or Rescan for dates, locations and captions.

The goal of automatic image captioning is to understand the content of an image and then produce a coherent and contextually relevant sentence or phrase that describes what is happening in the image. To use the feature, open one of your own photos and click the information icon (Show info panel, or i) in the top bar to show the details panel; on a phone the icon is in the bar at the bottom. In the Caption section, click the pencil icon in the top-right corner of the caption box to start editing, then click the wand icon that appears in its place. Once a caption has been generated, it appears as a suggestion just above the caption box — click it to drop the text into the caption field, then press the green tick below the box to save it. (If a caption has already been generated for this photo, the suggestion appears as soon as you start editing.) The wand, cancel and tick controls are only shown while you are editing, and captions cannot be generated on publicly shared photos.

New in 1.4.0 To caption many photos at once, open Account menu > Library. Under the Captions heading is the Generate captions row: Generate captions the photos that have no generated caption yet. The first time, that is all of your photos; after that, the photos added since. A run you cancelled continues where it stopped the next time you click Generate. The arrow next to Generate opens Generate captions again for all photos, which writes a new generated caption for every photo. It asks first, because on a large library it runs for hours. Both start a Generate captions job, which you can follow under Account menu > My jobs and cancel there. It captions photos only, not videos, and skips photos in the trash and photos that have no thumbnail yet. Each user runs it for their own photos. A caption you wrote yourself is never changed: the job only writes the generated caption, which search finds next to yours. The job does not run by itself after a scan. When you have added new photos, click Generate again. It takes the time of one caption per photo (see below), so a library of 30,000 photos at about 2 seconds a photo keeps the job queue busy for around 17 hours; other jobs, such as a scan, wait until it has finished or you cancel it. A job that keeps making progress is not stopped by the stuck-job check, however long it runs. The Captions section is only shown while captioning is on: the Image captioning switch in the Features card is on and Captioning model is not None. When the captioning model is not downloaded yet, the job downloads it first and then starts captioning.

Captions come from LFM2.5-VL, a small vision-language model from Liquid AI that runs on ONNX Runtime like every other model in LibrePhotos. There is nothing to pick: the files (about 370 MB) are fetched with the other models while captioning is on. New in 1.4.0 With captioning turned off they are not downloaded; turning it on again downloads them when you save the site settings or ask for a caption. The model needs about 0.9 GB of RAM while it captions and takes a few seconds per photo on an older desktop CPU, under a second on a recent one. It writes one natural sentence, for example "A rocket is taking off from a launch pad at night, with two tall metal towers flanking the launch site." Because it is a vision-language model it also takes instructions, which is what the caption context settings below use. To turn automatic captioning off, set Captioning model to None in the Admin area; an administrator can also switch the feature off for the whole deployment with the FEATURE_IMAGE_CAPTIONING environment variable. The earlier captioning models (im2txt, BLIP, Florence-2 and Moondream) and the separate Mistral language model were retired; an install that had any of them selected is moved to LFM2.5-VL automatically.

A caption is better when it can say who is in the photo and where it was taken. LibrePhotos already knows both, from face recognition and reverse geocoding, and passes them to the captioning model in its prompt. Each user controls this in their own Settings, under Caption context: Tell the captioning model what LibrePhotos knows about a photo turns the context on. Default On. Use the names of recognised people in captions adds the recognised, named person to the prompt. The model is asked to use the name directly, as a friend tagging a photo would ("Grace in a simple gray shirt, standing against a blue background"). Only has an effect when the photo has a recognised, named person. Default On. Mention where the photo was taken in captions adds the photo's geocoded location. Only has an effect when the photo has one. Default On. With the context switched off, the model is simply asked to describe the photo.

There are a lot of log files in this folder. The most important one is librephotos.log, with its older parts in librephotos.log.1, librephotos.log.2 and so on. Here should be possible error traces you can report to the GitHub repository. LibrePhotos 1.3.0 and older call it ownphotos.log. The first start of a newer release renames it and its older parts; see Upgrading. LibrePhotos 1.3.0 and older also keep secret.key here, so do not zip this whole folder for a bug report; see secret.key below.

⚠ Do not delete this file, and do not share it. Django signs every session, login token and password-reset link with a secret key, and encrypts the SMTP password stored in the Admin area with it. On the first start LibrePhotos generates the key and keeps it in this file, which is then used every time you start it: /protected_media/secret.key inside the backend container, which the shipped Docker Compose file maps to ${data}/protected_media/secret.key on the host (%LOCALAPPDATA%\LibrePhotos\protected_media\secret.key for the Windows standalone build). Back it up together with the rest of this folder. If you delete it, a new key is generated: every user is logged out and the SMTP password has to be entered again. Anyone who has a copy of the file can forge a login to your instance. If you set shhhhKey in your .env file (SECRET_KEY for the backend container), that value is used as the secret key instead and this file is never created or read. LibrePhotos 1.3.0 and older keep the file in /logs instead. The first start of a newer release moves it here and logs a warning saying so. If both files exist, the one in /protected_media is used. An old file holding the same key is the rest of an unfinished move and is removed; one holding a different key is left untouched with a warning in the log: delete it once you have checked that you can log in.
When you upload an avatar for a user, you can find it in this folder.
Very small thumbnails and not actually square. Can be static or animated. These are used to show a blurred preview or the pictures while loading the bigger ones.
The thumbnails and not actually square. You see them in the overview, when you scroll through your timeline. Can be animated or static.

In order to make all files viewable, we create thumbnails for them. These are only static, as they are also used for all ML algorithms and face recognition to have a consistent format. These are the files you actually see in the lightbox.

Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) The edited pictures of photos you edited in LibrePhotos: <hash>.jpg is the edited photo at full size, which the photo view, downloads of one photo and shares show, and <hash>.preview.jpg a smaller render the thumbnails are made from while the full size is being made. Your original files are never changed. A photo's files here go when you undo its edit or delete the photo. The edits themselves are in the database: if you delete this folder, the thumbnails are rendered again when they are next made, but the full-size view shows the original until the photo is saved again in the editor.
When you upload a file, it gets uploaded in chunks. While the upload is incomplete, the files are saved in that folder.
Here we save the thumbnails of all the faces, so that viewing them is faster.

All the machine learning models live here: the LFM2.5-VL captioning model, OpenCLIP ViT-B/32 for tags and semantic search, and the InsightFace face recognition models. Rather than being baked into the image, they are downloaded by the "Download models" job, or when you pick a new model in the Admin area (for example the Captioning model setting). Because of that, this folder only grows as you enable features, but it is usually by far the largest folder in /protected_media — several GB in total. Deleting it is safe: the models are simply downloaded again the next time they are needed. If your server has no Internet access, see Offline Usage for how to place the files by hand.

Some phones store a short video inside the JPEG of a motion photo (Google and Samsung both do this). When such a file is scanned, LibrePhotos extracts that video and saves it here as <hash>_motion.mp4 — this is what plays when you view the motion photo, while the original JPEG still keeps its embedded copy. This is controlled by the FEATURE_PROCESS_EMBEDDED_MEDIA setting, which is on by default.

When you download several photos at once, LibrePhotos builds the archive here and serves it back to you. Each archive is deleted automatically about a day after it is created, so this folder normally stays small and needs no manual cleanup.
New in 1.5.0 No longer used: it held a font cache for matplotlib, which came along with the face recognition code up to 1.4.0. Safe to delete.

This is the folder of the Postgres database. You should not move it, if you want to migrate, but login into the database and do a pgdump instead and imported it when mounting to a different location. Postgres does not like moving folders.

The job system gives you information about the long-running jobs, including which job is running, in a queue, how far it progressed and when it started and stopped. Here are the available long-running jobs:

Scan photos will look at all media files in your scan directory and will add them to the library. A normal scan only reads the files that are new or changed (the file or one of its sidecars) since the last successful scan of the whole scan directory started. A scan that was cancelled or failed before it reached every file does not count, and neither does a scan of a few selected files or a Nextcloud scan. A full scan reads every file again. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, any finished scan counted, including cancelled ones and Detect stacks runs, and a file edited while the last scan ran could be skipped. The first normal scan after the upgrade therefore checks every file once.

This job will look at all media files that already exist. It tries to find common events by looking at the timestamp and grouping the images. If the media files are in a 1 day and 12 hour interval, they will appear in the same event album.

This will create a title for the event album based on the information of the media files in the event album. Since 1.3.0, titles leave out faces in "Unknown - Other" and no longer contain a double space where a part is missing. Run this job once to fix the titles of albums made by an older version. It also stores what each title is made of, so the web app can show it in your language. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, titles were always English.
This will look at all faces and its groups and will give us a certainty value for the image in the group.
Finds all missing media files and removes them from the database.

Goes through every photo in the database and flags the ones whose file can no longer be found on disk. It does not delete anything — use Delete missing photos for that. It runs automatically after a full scan and after any scan of your configured scan directory; it is skipped when you scan a different directory or only a specific list of files, and when the scan had to skip a folder it could not read. It checks every photo before it changes anything. New in 1.4.0 It fails without changing anything when the scan directory looks unmounted or more than the Missing photos limit of your photos would be marked missing. See Missing Photos.

Calculates the OpenCLIP search embedding of every photo that has none, then rebuilds the similarity index. This is used for semantic search and for finding similar images. Find things stores the embeddings as it tags, so with tagging on this job only fills the gaps. After an upgrade from a release with another model, it re-embeds those photos in place and gives them their tags from the same run. New in 1.5.0 Uploads start it too: a few minutes after your last upload, LibrePhotos embeds the uploaded photos that have no embedding yet and rebuilds the similarity index, then runs Generate face embeddings for faces without one. A burst of uploads gets one run. Up to 1.4.0, uploaded photos only appeared in semantic search after the next scan or restart. The first start after the upgrade does this once for every user with photos. Turning semantic search back on in your settings (Semantic search max results from Disabled to a number) starts it for your photos too, so search has embeddings to answer from. Changing between two numbers of results starts nothing.

Finds the things in your photos (beach, dog, sunset, ...) with OpenCLIP, for the Things albums and for search. It runs automatically after each scan and covers every photo that has no things yet, including the ones an earlier run did not reach because it was cancelled or failed. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, a normal scan only covered photos added since the last run, so photos a cancelled run left behind stayed without things until a full scan. New in 1.5.0 You can also start it from Account menu > Library, under the Things heading: Find covers the photos without things, and Find things again for all photos (the arrow next to it) labels every photo again with the current list of things, replacing the things it found before. Your own tags and keywords are never changed. See Things Albums. Up to 1.4.0 this job was called Generate Tags.

Looks up place names for each photo's GPS coordinates (reverse geocoding) so they appear in the places view and location search.
