To hand the photo back to the rules, open it, edit its date and click Remove timestamp; the rules then decide its date again, so the photo keeps a date read from its file if it has one. New in 1.4.0 Up to version 1.3.0 a hand-set date only applied through a rule called Timestamp set by user, and it stopped sticking once that rule was deleted or moved below another; that rule is gone from every saved list after the update.

Some sources of data might give us very rich information, e.g. timestamp + timezone, but others only allow getting local time (without knowing real timestamp). For historical reasons, it is expected to have a timestamp and a timezone. In some cases, it is known that the local time the rule would obtain is not in the desired timezone. E.g. video date time tag QuickTime:CreateDate is by standard written in UTC rather than local time. For such cases, each rule can optionally have setting "transform_tz" set to "1" - in that case this rule should also specify "source_tz" and "report_tz" settings where "source_tz" is describing the timezone that the rule is getting and "report_tz" is describing the timezone of the location where the photo/video was taken. Both "source_tz" and "report_tz" should be one of the following: "utc" - UTC timezone "gps_timezonefinder" - the timezone of the GPS location associated with the photo/video "user_default" - the Default timezone set in your user settings; several of the built-in rules rely on this, including "Video creation datetime in user default timezone" "server_local" - the local timezone of the machine running LibrePhotos (in Docker this is normally UTC unless you set a TZ for the container) "name:<timezone_name>" - the timezone with the name <timezone_name>, e.g. "name:Europe/Berlin" The predefined rules use "utc" for "source_tz" and "gps_timezonefinder" or "user_default" for "report_tz". New in 1.5.0 A rule you write yourself (see Writing your own rules) can also convert to a time zone you pick; "server_local" only works in a rule list saved through the API (the datetime_rules of your user). Up to 1.4.0 the settings page could not change a rule at all. If either "source_tz" or "report_tz" could not be obtained, the rule is considered to be not applicable.

Videos keep their date in other tags than photos, and the default rules read three of them: Phone videos (iPhone, many Android phones) state the local time they were recorded at, with its UTC offset, in QuickTime:CreationDate. The rule "Local time from the video's QuickTime:CreationDate tag (phones)" uses that time as is, so no time zone has to be guessed. It is ranked above the rules that convert the UTC QuickTime:CreateDate. Other MP4 and MOV files only have the UTC QuickTime:CreateDate, converted with the time zone of the video's position or, without one, your default time zone. MKV and WebM files have a UTC Matroska:DateTimeOriginal, converted the same way by the two "MKV/WebM creation date" rules. New in 1.4.0 After the update, accounts whose rules still contain both "Get Video creation tag in UTC + figure out timezone using GPS coordinates" (ID 2) and "Video creation datetime in user default timezone" (ID 4) get the three new rules (IDs 17, 18 and 19) next to them; a list without either of those two is left as you set it, and Reset to defaults adds them. Videos already in your library get the new dates with Apply date rules to existing photos or a Rescan.

Once a rule succeeds, LibrePhotos stores the local time the camera recorded — the time you would have read off the camera when you took the shot. This is deliberate. A photo taken at 14:00 in Tokyo and one taken at 14:00 in Berlin are both shown as 14:00, because that is the time each one was actually taken. LibrePhotos does not re-cast your library into the timezone you happen to be browsing from; if it did, every photo would shift whenever you travelled, and photos from a holiday abroad would no longer line up with the day you remember them on. New in 1.5.0 Next to the local time, LibrePhotos stores its UTC offset when the rule that read it knows one: the offset written after the time (2024:04:03 03:00:00-07:00), else the offset tag that goes with the date tag (EXIF:OffsetTimeOriginal for EXIF:DateTimeOriginal and XMP:DateCreated, EXIF:OffsetTime for EXIF:ModifyDate), or for a rule that converts a UTC time the offset of the time zone it converted to, on that day. The info panel shows it after the time, for example "Sunday, 23:30 (UTC-07:00)". A date read from a file name or a file's modified time, and a date you set by hand, have no offset. Photos already in your library get it with Apply date rules to existing photos or a Rescan. Note Under the hood the local time is tagged as UTC before it is saved. That is an internal storage detail, not a claim that the photo was taken in UTC — it is what keeps the wall-clock time stable for every viewer. If you query the database directly, read the timestamps as-is and do not convert them.
documents.s: What gets stored, and why times are not converted for you

documents.t: Currently, supported rule types: "exif" - local time is taken using exif tag params["exif_tag"] as obtained with exiftool. An XMP sidecar next to the photo wins over the file (see Which sidecars are read). For EXIF:DateTimeOriginal and Composite:GPSDateTime the sidecar is also read under its XMP name (exif:DateTimeOriginal, exif:GPSTimeStamp); any other EXIF tag in a rule is not looked up in the sidecar, so to use a property that only a sidecar holds, name its XMP tag directly (for example XMP:<tag>). XMP:DateCreated, where LibrePhotos writes the dates you set when Write edits to files is on, is the first rule of the default list. Accounts created before 1.1.0 do not have that rule unless they add it with Add rule or Reset to defaults. New in 1.5.0 These date tags hold local time: XMP:DateCreated, EXIF:DateTimeOriginal, EXIF:ModifyDate and QuickTime:CreationDate. Some apps still write them in UTC, with a trailing Z (2025:06:02 06:30:00Z); such a value is turned into local time with the date's offset tag (see above), else the time zone of the photo's position, else your default time zone. Up to 1.4.0 the Z was ignored, so such a photo was off by its UTC offset and could land on another day; apply the rules again to fix the photos already in your library. A rule with "transform_tz" says itself which zone its tag is in and is not changed by this. "path" - time is taken from the filename using a regular expression matching. With "path_part" set to "full_path" the whole path is searched instead of the file name. New in 1.5.0 A rule you write yourself names where the date is with a "date_pattern" such as YYYY-MM-DD HH.mm.ss (see Writing your own rules). An older rule saved through the API with its own regular expression ("custom_regexp") keeps working, but a new or changed rule cannot set one any more. "filesystem" - time is taken from a file property. params["file_property"] must be "mtime" (file modified time) or "ctime" (file created time). Since these are UNIX timestamps without timezones they are always translated to local time using UTC. "takeout_json" - the capture time in the Google Takeout JSON next to the file (photoTakenTime). It is a UTC timestamp, so the predefined rules convert it to the time zone of the photo's position (ID 20) or to your default time zone (ID 21). They sit right before the file name rule. See Importing a Google Takeout export. New in 1.4.0 After the update, an account whose rule list is still a default list (default rules only, in the default order) gets both rules before the file name rule; a list you changed is left as it is. "user_defined" - the old Timestamp set by user rule. It no longer matches anything, since a date you set by hand always wins (see above), and the settings page no longer offers it.

To add a new rule, go to settings and navigate to the date time parsing rules. Click on the Add rule button. You can now add optional rules, such as using the file's modified or created time. To remove a rule again, click the X (Delete rule) at the right-hand end of its row. The Reset to defaults button next to Add rule puts the list back to the rules LibrePhotos ships with; it is greyed out while your list already matches the default rules in their default order.

New in 1.5.0 When no predefined rule reads your files' dates, write your own. Click New rule next to Add rule, or Duplicate and edit (the copy icon) on a predefined rule to start from it. A rule you wrote has an Edit rule pencil instead; the predefined rules stay as they are. In the form: Read the date from: a Metadata tag, the File name or the File time. Tag: one of the date tags LibrePhotos can read, such as EXIF:CreateDate, QuickTime:MediaCreateDate or Composite:SubSecDateTimeOriginal. Tags that usually hold the time in UTC say so. Other tags cannot be picked: a tag name ExifTool does not know reads nothing, and a rule on it would never apply. Where the date is (file name): anywhere in the name, a WhatsApp name, or My own pattern, written with YYYY (year), MM (month), DD (day), HH (hour), mm (minute), ss (second) and ? (any one character); every other character stands for itself. For files named 2023-01-01 12.00.00 (2).jpg that is YYYY-MM-DD HH.mm.ss, and DD.MM.YYYY reads a day-first date. The year, month and day are required. Try it on a file name shows the date the pattern reads. Match the full path searches the folders too, for example YYYY/MM/DD. Time zone: As recorded keeps the time as the local time it is, Recorded in UTC converts it to the time zone at the photo's location, your default time zone or one you pick. Only when...: apply the rule only when the folder path, the file name or a tag (the camera model, for example) contains a text. Name: filled in from your choices until you write your own. Save rule checks the rule with the server first and shows anything it refuses next to the field; the rule is then added at the end of the list. Like every change to the list, it is stored once you confirm Save changes?, and photos already in your library get its dates with Apply date rules to existing photos.

New in 1.5.0 Open a photo of yours and click Why this date? under its date in the info panel. It lists every saved rule in order with what it reads from that photo (a date, Does not apply, or why it cannot run), and marks the one a scan takes the date from with Used. It also says when the photo shows another date now, which applying the rules or a rescan would change, and when the date was set by hand, which wins over every rule. Nothing is changed; save the rules first to test a change.
documents.s: Seeing why a photo has its date

documents.t: The top rules are applied first and the bottom rules last. To change the order, drag and drop the rules. Adding, deleting, reordering and resetting rules only take effect once you save your settings — LibrePhotos prompts you with Save changes? and you confirm by clicking Update.

The date rules are applied on each scan, so photos scanned after a change use the new rules. New in 1.4.0 To apply them to the photos already in your library, use Apply date rules to existing photos. Right after you save changed rules, the date rules card shows Your date rules changed with an Apply to existing photos button. At any time, open the Library page (from the profile menu in the top-right corner, choose Library; or press Ctrl+K and search for "Library") and click Apply in the Dates section. Both start the same background job, Apply date rules. It reads the date of every photo again with your current rules and moves each photo whose date changed to its new day. It does nothing else: no thumbnails, faces or other metadata are redone, and nothing is written to your files. A date you set by hand is never changed. When it is done, a message says how many photos moved to another day and how many keep the date you set by hand; the job list has the photos whose date could not be read. Event albums are not rebuilt by it: click Generate under Generate event albums on the Library page afterwards so your events follow the new dates. Up to version 1.3.0 the only way was a full Rescan: in the Scan library section, click the arrow next to the Scan button and choose Rescan (or Rescan all photos in the command palette). It still works, but re-processes every file, which takes much longer. A plain Scan does not apply changed rules to photos it has seen before: it only looks at files that are new or changed since the last scan.

Every photo is off by the same number of hours. If your whole library is shifted by a constant amount — and that amount happens to match your own UTC offset — no date rule will fix it, because the rules are not what is wrong. This was a display bug: the times were stored correctly, but the web interface converted them into the timezone of the browser you were viewing from, so a viewer at UTC+3 saw every photo three hours late. It is fixed in current versions; update and reload the page, and the stored times will show as they always were. No rescan is needed. A rule change had no effect at all. Check that you applied the rules to the photos already in your library with Apply date rules to existing photos or Rescan, not a normal scan (see above), and that the rule you expect to win is above the one currently matching — the first rule that can produce a time is the one that is used. A rule that names an EXIF tag your files do not carry is silently skipped, so it is worth confirming the tag actually exists in your photos: Why this date? on one of them shows what each rule reads. One particular photo ignores every rule. If you once corrected that photo's date by hand, LibrePhotos remembered it, and a date set by hand wins over every rule (the info panel shows Set by you under it). To hand the photo back to the rules, open it, edit its date and click Remove timestamp.

LibrePhotos can hand login over to an external identity provider that speaks OpenID Connect — Keycloak, Authentik, Authelia, Zitadel, Okta, Google, Entra ID and so on. After the provider confirms who someone is, LibrePhotos issues its own normal session, so everything downstream behaves exactly as it does for a password login. Username-and-password login keeps working alongside it. Turning SSO on does not take anyone's existing way of logging in away.

Your server's public URL, set as the FRONTEND_BASE_URL environment variable (for example https://photos.example.com). This one is not optional. The reverse proxy in front of the backend rewrites the Host header, so LibrePhotos genuinely cannot work out its own public address from an incoming request — it has to be told. Without it the login button reports that SSO is not fully configured. An email provider configured in Site settings, if you want LibrePhotos to create accounts on first login. See the email settings page. Without email configured, LibrePhotos will not create accounts over SSO, because it has no way to act on the provider's claim that an address is verified.

Create a confidential client (one with a client secret) at your provider and give it this redirect URI: https://your-librephotos-url/api/accounts/oidc/<provider_id>/login/callback/ <provider_id> is a short name you choose in the next step — keycloak, authentik, google, whatever you like. It must match exactly. Note down the client ID, the client secret, and the provider's issuer URL (the one whose /.well-known/openid-configuration document describes it).
documents.s: Registering LibrePhotos with your identity provider

documents.t: In the Django admin (/api/django-admin/), under Social applications, add one: Field Value Provider OpenID Connect Provider ID the <provider_id> you used in the redirect URI Name what the login button should say, if you add more than one provider Client id from your provider Secret key from your provider Settings {"server_url": "https://your-idp/realms/example"} — the issuer URL Sites pick your site Then, in the app, open Admin area > Site settings and find the Single sign-on group. Each change saves at once. New in 1.5.0 Up to 1.4.0 these switches were only on the Constance page of the Django admin, under the names in brackets. Show the single sign-on button (OIDC_ENABLED): the on/off switch. While it is off, the login button is hidden and the SSO endpoints are inactive, so switching it off is a real way to stop SSO logins. Button label (OIDC_BUTTON_LABEL): the text on the login button, e.g. "Sign in with Keycloak", at most 64 characters. With more than one provider each button shows its provider's name instead. Allow sign-ups over single sign-on (OIDC_ALLOW_SIGNUP): whether a first-time SSO login may create a new LibrePhotos account. Off by default; also requires email to be configured. The provider itself is only added and changed in the Django admin, as above. The group lists the providers it finds, and warns under the switches when SSO cannot work yet: no provider attached to this site, no public URL (FRONTEND_BASE_URL), or, for sign-ups, no email set up.

On a first SSO login, LibrePhotos looks for an existing account whose email matches the one the provider reports: A single matching account, and the provider says the address is verified → the two are linked, and from then on the provider's stable user id identifies that person. The provider has not verified the address → refused. Otherwise anyone able to register your email address at the provider could claim your account. Two or more accounts share the address → refused, whether or not sign-ups over SSO are on, because there is no single right answer. LibrePhotos does not create yet another account with the same address either. The matching account is deactivated → refused, also when it was linked before, and no new account is made for its address. Turn the account back on to let it sign in. Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) Up to 1.6.0, a deactivated account was linked, and signed in as soon as it was turned back on. The provider sends no address → refused, since there is nothing to match on and no verified address to create an account with. No matching account → a new one is created only if OIDC_ALLOW_SIGNUP is on and email is configured. Otherwise create the account first (or set its email to match) and let the user sign in again. Accounts created through SSO are never administrators. Grant that in the admin afterwards if you want it.

LibrePhotos does not connect to an LDAP directory itself. Instead, point your identity provider at the directory and LibrePhotos at the provider: people then log in with their directory username and password at the provider, and LibrePhotos gets the result over OpenID Connect. Every common self-hosted provider can do this. Authelia: set up the LDAP authentication backend (it works with LLDAP, OpenLDAP and Active Directory), then add LibrePhotos as an OpenID Connect client. Authentik: add an LDAP source that syncs your directory, then an OAuth2/OpenID provider with an application for LibrePhotos. Keycloak: in your realm, add User Federation with an LDAP provider, then a confidential OpenID Connect client. Turn on Trust Email on the LDAP provider, or Keycloak reports directory addresses as unverified and LibrePhotos refuses them. What this means for accounts: LibrePhotos matches people by the email address the directory holds, and only when the provider says it is verified (see How accounts are matched up). Either give each LibrePhotos account the same email as in the directory, or turn on sign-ups over SSO so that a first login creates the account. The mobile app logs in with a username and password, not with SSO. A user who only ever signed in through the provider has no LibrePhotos password yet; they can set one with Forgot your password? on the login page (this needs email to be configured).

A failed attempt returns to the login page with an explanation. The usual causes: Message What to change Account not known to LibrePhotos Create the account, or turn on OIDC_ALLOW_SIGNUP Email address not verified Verify the address at your identity provider More than one account uses this email address Give each LibrePhotos account its own email address (or clear it on the ones that should not log in over SSO) Sign-in was cancelled at your identity provider Nothing to fix: the user pressed Cancel or declined access. Try again Your identity provider could not complete the sign-in Look in the server log for the line starting SSO login via; it names the reason (for example an expired login, or the provider refusing the client secret) This LibrePhotos account is turned off The matching account is deactivated: turn it back on Public URL not configured Set FRONTEND_BASE_URL Provider-side "invalid redirect URI" The redirect URI at your provider must match the callback URL above exactly, including the trailing slash
LibrePhotos offers multiple ways to share your photos and albums — with other users on your instance, or publicly with anyone via a link.

The Sharing page (Sharing in the sidebar, or the Sharing tab at the bottom of the screen on a phone) is your central hub for all sharing activity. It provides an overview of: Your library: who you share your whole library with, and what each of them sees (Sharing your whole library) Libraries shared with you: the libraries other users share with you. This row only shows once someone does. Public photos — Other users on your instance who have made their profile public Shared with you — Photos and albums that others have shared with you You shared — Photos and albums you have shared with others Public links — Albums and photos you've shared publicly via link. An album card shows the album's title and number of photos; a photo card says Share link and when you made the link, or Public photo and the day the photo was taken. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, photo cards had no caption.

You can share any user album with other users on your LibrePhotos instance: Navigate to the album you want to share Open the ⋮ (Album actions) at the right of the album's header and choose Sharing Search for users and pick a role for each: No access, Can view or Can add photos You can also open the same dialog from the share action on the album's card under Albums, or, while selecting photos, from the selection bar's three-dot menu (⋮) under Album actions. Shared albums show up in the recipient's sharing area: they open Sharing, click the Shared with you tile, then the Albums tab (the page is titled Albums others shared). New in 1.5.0 Up to 1.4.0, each user had an on/off switch instead of a role, and everyone you shared an album with could only view it.

New in 1.5.0 A user you give Can add photos becomes a contributor: they add photos from their own library to your album, for example when you both photograph the dog. Their photos stay theirs. The album only links them, so nothing is copied or moved, and taking a photo out of the album never deletes it. Adding photos. A contributor selects photos anywhere in their library, opens the + menu and chooses Album. Under Shared with you, you can add they pick your album. The next step says who will see the photos and what of them (see below), and Add to adds them. Hidden photos cannot be added, and nobody adds photos while the album is locked. What each person can do Owner Can add photos Can view See the album and its photos ✓ ✓ ✓ Add their own photos ✓ ✓ Take photos out of the album any photo only the photos they added Rename, set the cover, lock, delete the album ✓ Share it with others, change roles, public link ✓ On the album page a contributor clicks Select, selects the photos they added and chooses Remove from album. A photo someone else added says why it cannot be removed. Leaving and roles. When a contributor leaves the album, or you set them to Can view or No access, the photos they added leave the album at once. They stay in their library. The share dialog asks first and says how many photos leave.

Members always see the photos and their dates. Each of these details shows only where both sides allow it: Location, Names of people, Camera information, Captions and Original files. The album's owner sets what members may see under What members see in the share dialog. All are on by default, so your own photos look to members as they did before. A contributor sets what the others see of the photos they add: in the step before adding, or later with What others see of my photos in the album's ⋮. All are off until they turn them on. The table shows the album's choice, theirs and the result. Names of people on the owner's photos also need Show the names of people on photos you share. Some things are never shared through an album: the file name and folder, ratings and favourites, whether the photo is hidden or in the trash, the photo's other albums and its edit history. A photo its owner hides or moves to the trash disappears from the album for everyone else. Without Original files, a member who downloads a photo, or plays a video, gets a full-size copy without the file's metadata instead of the original, as with a shared library: the original carries everything the camera recorded, including where it was taken. The same choices hold under Shared with you: the album's photos appear under its members' places only with Location on, under their things only with Captions on and under their people only with Names of people on, and each photo there shows only what the album allows. A photo the owner also shared with you on its own shows what that share shows. When the photo's owner also shares their whole library with you, that share's choices decide what you see of their photos, in albums too.
documents.s: What members see of each photo

documents.t: New in 1.5.0 Everyone in a shared album, its owner included, can comment on its photos and like them. Open a photo from the album's page and open the details panel (Show info panel, or i): under Comments you see the comments, the heart and who liked the photo, and a box to write in. Enter sends, Shift+Enter starts a new line. Comments belong to the album, not the photo: the same photo in another album has its own comments, and only the people in that album see them. A comment is plain text, at most 1000 characters. Links and formatting are shown as typed. You edit and delete your own comments from their ⋮. The album's owner can delete anyone's comment, and turn comments and likes off with Members can comment and like in the album's Sharing dialog. While they are off, the existing comments stay visible and nobody can add one. When a photo leaves the album, or a contributor leaves and takes their photos with them, the comments and likes on those photos are deleted. To keep one person from flooding an album, each user can post at most 30 comments or likes a minute.

Only in the album itself. They are not in the album owner's timeline, search, places or downloads, not in anyone's Shared with you places, things and people, and never on the album's public link, which shows only the owner's own photos. An album only holds photos its owner or a current contributor added. Since 1.5.0, old links in an album to other users' photos are removed when you upgrade.

New in 1.5.0 You can share one of your people, for example your child with the grandparents, without sharing an album or your whole library. Open the person under People, open the ⋮ (Person actions) and choose Share…. Turn on each user who should see the photos; they can only look. Face recognition can be wrong, and a wrong match would hand someone a photo that has nothing to do with the person. So the people you share with see a photo only when both of these are true: You labelled a face on it with the person. A face that face recognition only suggested, or a face group such as Unknown 012, never counts. Only people you named can be shared. You approved it for sharing. The photos you labelled before you first share the person are approved at once: that is what you chose to share. Photos you label afterwards wait, also when you turn a user off and on again. The person's page then says how many wait; Review shows them, each ticked, and the ticked ones are shared when you confirm. An unticked photo is kept back for good. Taking the label off, hiding or trashing a photo takes it away from them at once, and turning a user off in Share… ends their access to all of the person's photos. They see each photo and its date. Two switches in Share… add more, both off by default: Where the photos were taken and Names of the other people on these photos. Camera details, captions and original files are never shared this way (a download is a copy without the file's metadata). The people you share with find the person under Shared with you, on the People tab, with whose person it is (Mila, shared by Anna).

You can share individual photos (or a selection of photos) with other users: Select one or more photos from any view Click the three-dot menu (⋮, Photo actions) and choose "Sharing". On a wide screen the share button in the selection bar does the same. Search for users and toggle sharing on or off for each Shared photos show up in the recipient's sharing area, grouped by the person who shared them: they open Sharing, click the Shared with you tile, then the Photos tab (the page is titled Photos others shared).

New in 1.5.0 You can share your whole library with another user, read-only. They see your photos and videos as you add them, without you sharing albums or photos one by one. Nothing moves and nothing is copied: the photos, their people, albums and edits stay yours, and you can stop at any time.

Open Sharing. The Your library section is at the top. Click Share my library. Under With, pick the user. Under What they see, turn on what you want them to see. Every switch starts off. Click Share with Ben (with their name).

They see it Photos and videos, and their dates Always Location: GPS position, place names, the map and Places Only with the switch on People names: the face boxes and names of the people you named Only with the switch on. Faces you have not named and face groups such as Unknown 012 are never shown Camera information: make, model, lens and exposure Only with the switch on Captions and descriptions: your descriptions, generated captions and text found in photos Only with the switch on. A generated caption can name the person and the place, so it also needs Location and People names Download original files Only with the switch on. Off, a download is a full-size copy without the file's metadata New in 1.5.0 The photo's copyright, creator and license Always, also without a license Hidden photos, the trash, albums, tags, favourites and ratings, edit history, file names and folders Never Caution An original file keeps its GPS position, camera serial number and keywords inside it, whatever the Location switch says. Turn on Download original files only for someone you would also show where your photos were taken. With it off, downloads and videos are copies without that metadata; thumbnails never carry it. Search follows the same rules. With Location off, searching a place name does not find your photos for them; with People names off, searching a person's name does not either, and the same goes for captions and cameras. Searching for what is in a photo, such as beach or dog, works, because they see the photo. They can open, search and download your photos. They cannot edit, delete, favourite, rate or hide them, add them to their albums, or change their people. The switches also apply to the photos and albums you share with that user one by one: once you share your library with someone, its switches decide what they see of every photo of yours.

Every person you share your library with is listed under Your library, with a line that says what they see (for example No location, People, Copies only) and whether they show your photos in their timeline. Click What Ben sees (with their name) to: turn a switch on or off. It is saved at once. Preview a photo as Ben: your newest photo, with what you see next to what they see. Stop sharing. They lose access at once, including photo links they already opened. Photos and albums you shared with them one by one stay shared.

When someone shares their library with you, Sharing shows it under Libraries shared with you. Click it to open the library, read-only, as a timeline of its days. The page says what the owner shares; a day shows no place when they do not share locations. Turn on Show in my timeline to see their photos between yours on the Photos page, in your search and in their day groups. Their photos carry a small avatar in the corner, and the title says whose photos it includes. It is off when a share starts, and only you can turn it on or off. Archived photos stay out of your timeline, as in theirs, but are in their library page. The details panel of their photo says whose photo it is and, for each field they do not share, that they don't share it with you. The photo's own controls are not there: it is read-only. To leave a library, open it, click the ⋮ at the right of its title and choose Leave Anna's library (with the owner's name). LibrePhotos asks first. The owner can share it with you again.

New in 1.5.0 When you share an album or a photo with another user, they see each shared photo with its date, its place and its things (what the photo shows, such as beach or tram). They find the shared photos under the places and things in their Shared with you area, counted from the photos you shared with them only: your other photos of the same place never show, not even in a count. The people on a photo are different, because a name is personal. The users you share with see people only if you allow it: Open Settings and, under Sharing with users, turn on Show the names of people on photos you share. It is off by default. Even then, they only see the people you named. Faces you have not named, face groups such as Unknown 012 and the suggestions face recognition makes are never shown to them. The setting applies to everything you share with other users, albums and single photos alike. The sharing dialogs say the same in one sentence under the list of users. When you also share your whole library with someone, its People names switch decides for them instead of this setting. Public links do not use this setting: what a visitor of a public album or photo link sees is set by the Photo details of the link, and Share detected faces there also shows only the people you named.
documents.s: What the users you share with see

documents.t: Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) When you share a photo you edited, everyone you share it with sees and downloads the edited picture, never your original file: users you share it or an album with, album members, people you share your library with and visitors of a public link. This holds even with Original files or Download original files on, and while the full-size edited picture is still being made. See Downloads and sharing.
You can create a public link for any user album, making it accessible to anyone — even people without an account on your LibrePhotos instance.

Navigate to the album you want to share publicly Open the sharing dialog (three-dot menu → "Sharing") Toggle "Public sharing" on A unique URL slug is generated automatically The public album is accessible at https://your-instance/public/s/{slug}. On your public profile, https://your-instance/public/<username>?album={slug} shows the same album. A link always needs the slug: the album's number alone opens nothing for a visitor. The dialog shows it as the Album link, with buttons to copy it and to open it in a new tab.

Under the album link, the dialog also shows a Slideshow link: the same address with ?slideshow=1 added (https://your-instance/public/s/{slug}?slideshow=1), with its own copy and open buttons. Whoever opens it sees the album start as a slideshow from its first photo, in the lightbox, instead of the photo grid. It is handy for a photo frame, a TV or a party screen. The slideshow link is the album link with a different start: it shows the same photos and the same Photo details, expires with the album link, and stops working when you turn public sharing off. There is no separate link to revoke. Visitors have no LibrePhotos settings, so a photo stays on screen for 5 seconds. They can change the interval in the lightbox, pause with the play button or s, and step through with the arrow keys. The slideshow stops at the last photo. Closing the lightbox shows the album's photo grid, and the address goes back to the plain album link. When the visitor's device asks for reduced motion, photos cross-fade instead of zooming in. Only whole albums can be shared as a slideshow: there is no slideshow link for a hand-picked selection of photos. Put the photos in an album and share that. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, a public album link always opened on the photo grid.

Toggle "Public sharing" off again and the link stops working immediately. The slug is burned at the same time, so turning public sharing back on generates a brand-new URL rather than reviving the old one. Anyone who still holds the withdrawn link, including someone you shared it with by mistake, keeps getting a "not found" page. This also means a custom slug is not kept across a revoke: set it again after re-enabling the link if you want it back.

When public sharing is enabled, click Show settings in the sharing dialog to expand the configuration panel. From there you can configure: Custom Slug​ Change the URL slug to something memorable — 3–64 characters using only lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. Capitals you type are converted to lowercase automatically; spaces, underscores and other punctuation are rejected. Slugs must be unique across the instance, and the field checks availability as you type. For example: summer-vacation-2025 → /public/s/summer-vacation-2025. Expiration​ Expiration is optional. Pick any expiry date and time with the date picker (down to the second), or use the built-in 7 days, 30 days or 90 days presets in the picker's dropdown for a quick choice. Click Never (or clear the field) to remove the expiry so the link never expires. After expiration, the link no longer works. Photo Details​ The Photo details panel fine-tunes what information visitors can see when they open a photo in a public album: Setting What it controls Share photo timestamps Whether photo dates and times are visible. Without it, photos are not grouped by day and are listed in an order that says nothing about when they were taken. Share location information Whether GPS coordinates and place names are shown Share camera information Whether camera model, lens, focal length, aperture, ISO, and shutter speed are shown Share captions Whether captions are visible: yours, and the tags. A caption written by the captioning model can name the person and the place (see Caption context), so it is shown only when location information and detected faces are shared too. Share detected faces Whether the names of the people you named are displayed. Faces you have not named and face groups are never shown. New in 1.5.0 A photo's copyright, creator and license follow none of these settings: a photo with a license shows them on every public page, so visitors know what they may do with it. A photo without a license shows visitors none of them, not even a copyright or creator its file carries. Each of these settings can be toggled independently per album. When left unset, the user-level defaults from your settings are used; you can configure those in Settings → Public sharing defaults. All five are off by default — both as the built-in fallback and as the initial value of your user-level defaults, following a privacy-first, opt-in approach. So on a brand-new public link, visitors don't see any of these per-photo details until you turn the relevant options on. These settings cover what the page shows, and the files behind it. Thumbnails are stored without the photo's EXIF and XMP (GPS position, camera serial number, keywords), keeping only the colour profile. Thumbnails created by 1.2.1 and older may still contain it. An admin cleans them once after upgrading, with Remove photo details from old thumbnails in Admin area > Admin tools or the strip_thumbnail_metadata command; see After upgrading from 1.2.1 or older. An original file carries all of its metadata at once (location, camera, date, keywords, people), so a visitor gets the original file of a photo or video only when all five settings are on. Otherwise a download is a full-size copy without metadata (a photo as a JPEG keeping only its colour profile, a video with its streams as they are but without the recorded location and other container metadata), and the video of a motion photo is not available. The text LibrePhotos searches in, file names and folders, ratings, favourites and stacks are never shown to visitors, whatever the settings. The same rules apply wherever a visitor can reach the photo: the public album page, a photo made public, your public profile, and a photo link. Users of your instance who open a public photo that is not shared with them see it as a visitor does. Caution Changes to the slug, expiration and Photo details settings are not applied until you click "Save link settings" at the bottom of the settings panel. That button stays disabled until you change something; the Public sharing toggle itself only saves the on/off state.

Visitors to a public album link see: A photo grid with the album's photos A Play slideshow button above the grid (a play icon on a phone), which starts the same slideshow as the slideshow link A lightbox viewer for browsing individual photos; the open photo is in the address, so a visitor can link to one photo of the album Photo details (subject to the album's Photo details settings) No login required

Besides sharing whole albums, you can make individual photos public without putting them in an album: Select one or more photos from any view Click the three-dot menu (⋮, Photo actions) and choose "Make public" When you select photos individually, direct image links (https://your-instance/media/photos/<hash>.jpg) are copied to your clipboard so you can paste them straight away. In select all mode the photos are still made public, but no links are copied. These are raw image-file URLs, so they behave differently from public album links. There is no album page, no custom slug and no expiration — anyone with the link can open the image file directly. What it shows follows your Settings → Public sharing defaults: the original file only when all five details are shared, otherwise a copy without its metadata (see Photo details). If you need per-link controls, share a public album instead. Public photos appear under the Photos tab of your Public links page, on your public profile at https://your-instance/public/<username>, and in your own My Public Photos view. Your public profile shows the details your Public sharing defaults allow; without Share photo timestamps its photos are one group without a date instead of days. To reverse this, select the photos again and choose "Make private" from the same menu.

The Share link button in the lightbox (the share icon, shortcut P; on a phone it is in the bar at the bottom) does something different from the bulk Make public action above: it creates a share link for that one photo and opens a dialog showing it, with a button to copy it. The link looks like https://your-instance/public/p/{slug}, where the slug is 12 random characters that belong to the share rather than to the photo. Creating a link does not make the photo public: it does not appear on your public profile or under Make public, and the photo's own /media/... URLs still require a login. Because the slug is random, the link can be withdrawn: Replace link mints a new slug. The previous URL, and the image and video URLs behind it, stop working at once. Revoke switches the share off and burns the slug, so anyone still holding that link gets a "not found" page. Sharing the photo again creates a brand-new link rather than reviving the old one. Your active photo links are listed under the Photos tab of your Public links page, each with its own copy, replace and revoke buttons. What a visitor with the link can see: The photo as a large preview image (not the original file). For a video, the video itself, so it can be played: the original file only when all five Public sharing defaults are on, otherwise a copy without its metadata. The photo details you allow in Settings → Public sharing defaults (date, location, camera, captions, people's names). Photo links have no per-link settings of their own. What they cannot see: the original file of a photo, face thumbnails, any other photo, or anything that identifies the file's content hash. While the photo is hidden or in the trash, its link shows "not found" as well. Expiring links and password-protected links are not available for photo shares yet. Caution Making a photo private stops it from being served through the public views, but it cannot retroactively invalidate a direct link that someone has already opened or saved a copy of the image from.

Open Sharing and click the You shared tile (the pages are titled Photos you shared and Albums you shared) to see: Photos tab — All photos you've shared, grouped by recipient Albums tab — All albums you've shared, grouped by recipient

Open Sharing and click the Shared with you tile (the pages are titled Photos others shared and Albums others shared) to see: Photos tab — Photos others have shared with you, grouped by sender Albums tab — Albums others have shared with you, grouped by sender Places tab: the places of the photos shared with you, directly or in an album. A place several people shared photos of is one tile, so Lisbon holds everyone's Lisbon photos. Its count only covers the photos shared with you. Things tab: the things the shared photos show, the same way. People tab: the people their owners named on the photos shared with you, each with whose person it is (Mom, shared by Alice). Two people's Mom stay two tiles. You only see someone's people if they allow it. Click a place, thing or person to see the photos shared with you under it, grouped by sender. When nothing is shared with you under it any more, the page says so. In the details panel of a photo someone shared with you directly, you see its people (if the owner shares their names), its things and who shared it. You cannot change them; that is for the owner. New in 1.5.0 Up to 1.4.0, there were no Places, Things and People tabs, and the details panel of a photo shared with you showed only its date and place.

An album someone shared with you stays in your list until you leave it. Open the ⋮ on the album's cover under Albums others shared, or the ⋮ (Album actions) at the right of the album page's header, and choose Leave album. LibrePhotos asks first; after you confirm, the album and its photos are no longer shown to you under Sharing, and on the mobile app it disappears at the next sync. Only you leave: the owner keeps the album, it stays shared with everyone else, and the owner no longer sees you under Albums you shared for it. They can share it with you again at any time. You cannot leave an album you own; delete it or stop sharing it instead. New in 1.5.0 If you could add photos, the photos you added leave the album with you. They stay in your library. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, only the owner could take an album off your list, by unsharing it.
documents.s: Leaving an album shared with you

documents.t: Open Sharing and click the Public links tile to see everything you've made publicly accessible. It has two tabs: Albums (albums with a public link) and Photos (individual photos you've marked public). The Public links row on the Sharing page shows your latest public photos and counts all of them. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, public photos rarely showed or counted on the Sharing page or the Photos tab, and the Photos tab also listed other users' public photos.

Users can make their profile publicly accessible by enabling Public sharing in their profile settings (Account menu > Profile). Other users on the instance can then find them in the Public photos section of the Sharing page, which lists every user with public sharing enabled along with their public photo count. A user's public photos are browsable at https://your-instance/public/<username>. New in 1.5.0 That page, and the API behind it, only work while the user's public profile is on (the user still sees their own public photos under Public links). Up to 1.4.0 the API also answered without a username, with every user's public photos together, whatever their profile setting; everyone's public photos together are now the public gallery, which is off until an admin turns it on and shows only users who take part.

New in 1.5.0 The public gallery puts the public photos of everyone who takes part on one page, at your server's address. It is off until an admin turns it on under Admin area > Public gallery (settings): Members only shows it to every signed-in user under Sharing, Everyone opens it at the server's address for visitors without an account. While it is off, the server's address opens the login page as before. Nobody takes part by default. To show your public photos there, turn on Settings > Public gallery > Show my public photos in the public gallery. Only you can turn it on or off for yourself; an admin cannot do it for you. The card lists what visitors see of your photos. Turning it off takes them out of the gallery again; they stay public on their own links and your public profile either way. Only photos you made public (Make public) are shown, never photos that are only in a public album or behind a photo link. The gallery has four tabs: Timeline: the days of everyone's photos, newest first, each photo marked with whose it is. Photos of people who do not share dates (or that have no date) come last, in one group without a date and in no particular order, so the order does not tell when they were taken. A day names its town only when every photo of the day is of someone who shares places. Places: the towns the photos were taken in, with the photographers who took them. Only towns, never a street or a spot on a map, and only for people who share where their photos were taken. A town opens its photos on the timeline. People: the people each photographer named, for photographers who share the names of the people on their photos. Two photographers' Mia stay two tiles, each saying whose photos they are. A person opens their photos on the timeline. Unnamed faces never show. Photographers: everyone who takes part, each opening their photos on the timeline. The chips above the tabs narrow the timeline, places and people to one photographer. The address keeps the tab and the filters, so a link shows the same view to anyone. What a visitor sees of each photo follows its owner's Public sharing defaults, owner by owner, as on a photo link: the photo, its owner's name, and dates, town names, named people, camera details and captions only where the owner shares them. The gallery's lists never carry a photo's coordinates or address, even for owners who share their location. File names and folders, hidden, archived and private photos, albums, tags, favourites and ratings never show. A signed-in user sees the gallery exactly as a visitor does, their own photos included. Search engines are asked not to index the gallery unless the admin allows it.

LibrePhotos has no shared library yet, where several people own the same photos together (#395). Every photo belongs to exactly one user, with its own faces, albums, ratings and edits. That is why two users cannot scan the same folder: LibrePhotos refuses a scan directory that overlaps another user's (see Manage multiple users). A household can still share its photos today, in one of these setups.

Create one account for the shared family archive and give it the family folder as its scan directory. Everyone also gets a personal account for their own photos. The family account names the people, makes albums and shares them with each person's account. Everyone sees the family photos under Shared with you, with their places, things and, if the family account shares names, their people. Only the family account can edit the family photos, name people or change albums. Someone has to sign in as it to do that.

Each person scans their own folder and shares albums or single photos with the others. Each person keeps their own favourites, faces and private photos. Under Shared with you, everyone sees the others' places and things merged, and their people per owner. A trip both partners photographed stays in two libraries. One makes an album and gives the other Can add photos, so both halves end up in one album.
documents.s: Setup 2: everyone shares their own photos

documents.t: New in 1.5.0 Each person scans their own folder and shares their whole library with the others, choosing what they see. Everyone turns on Show in my timeline for the libraries they want between their own photos. Each person keeps their own favourites, faces, albums and hidden photos. New photos show up for the others without sharing anything again. The others can look, search and download, but not edit: for photos several people should change, use Setup 1.
documents.s: Setup 3: share your libraries with each other

documents.t: Everyone signs in with the same account. It is the simplest setup, but nobody has favourites, ratings or private photos of their own, and everyone sees everything, including what someone meant to keep to themselves.

Each person keeps their own library and shares the people the others care about, for example the children with both grandparents (Sharing a person). New photos of them reach the others once you approve them.
documents.s: Setup 5: share the people who matter

documents.t: Owning photos together, or one library that several users scan and change: #395. Sharing your whole library shares it read-only. Adding the people someone shared with you to your own People page: #632.

LibrePhotos can automatically detect and group related photos together. There are two distinct concepts: file variants (same capture in different formats) and stacks (different captures grouped together).

File variants represent the same moment captured in different file formats. Instead of showing duplicate entries in your timeline, LibrePhotos treats them as a single photo with multiple files attached.

When you shoot in RAW+JPEG mode, your camera creates two files for each shot (e.g. IMG_001.CR2 and IMG_001.jpg). LibrePhotos groups these automatically during scanning — you'll see one photo in your timeline with a RAW badge overlay indicating that a RAW variant is available. This happens whenever both files are in the same folder and have the same name, like IMG_001.CR2 and IMG_001.jpg, and there is no setting for it: both files stay in your library, as one photo with a RAW variant. A RAW in another folder, for example on a second memory card, becomes a photo of its own. The Stack RAW+JPEG pairs switch that 1.2.1 and older showed on the Library page and in first-time setup did nothing, and is gone since 1.3.0. Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) The photo editor works on the photo's main file, so a RAW+JPEG pair is edited from its JPEG. A RAW file that is a photo of its own is edited from its RAW data.
Live Photos (common on iPhones) consist of a still image and a short video clip. LibrePhotos detects these and groups the image and video as file variants of a single photo.

LibrePhotos uses a two-phase scan to group file variants: Phase 1 — Grouping: Before processing, all image and video files are grouped by their directory and base filename. For example, IMG_001.jpg and IMG_001.CR2 in the same folder become one group. XMP sidecars are set aside at this stage. Phase 2 — Processing: Each group is processed together, creating one Photo entity with all files attached as variants. The main display file is chosen automatically by priority: JPEG → Video → RAW. Once all image groups have finished, any XMP sidecars are processed and attached to the photo they belong to. Metadata is read from the main file and from the XMP sidecars of every variant. A sidecar named after the RAW file (IMG_001.CR2.xmp, as darktable and other RAW editors write it) counts as well, so a rating, keywords, a description or face regions set in the RAW editor reach the photo. When both exist, a sidecar named after the main file (IMG_001.xmp or IMG_001.jpg.xmp) wins over the RAW's. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, only sidecars named after the main file were read; a Rescan from the Library page picks up the others. After each scan, a Repair file variants job runs automatically. It looks for RAW files that ended up as their own photo and merges them into the matching image photo (same folder, same base name — JPEG, HEIC, PNG or TIFF), and corrects the main display file when a RAW file is still marked as the main one. Live Photo videos that were already scanned as separate photos are not merged by this job.

When viewing a photo that has file variants: A RAW badge appears on the thumbnail in the photo grid In the lightbox sidebar, next to the filename (beside the dimensions and file size), a photo with extra formats shows a +N format(s) link. Expanding it lists the non-primary variants, each with a format badge (JPG, RAW, VIDEO, META, or FILE). When you download photos as a zip, all file variants of each photo are included automatically. New in 1.4.0 So are their XMP sidecars, see Sidecars in a download.

Stacks group different but related captures together. Unlike file variants (same shot, different format), stacks contain separate photos that belong together logically. Note Once photos are stacked, only the stack's cover photo appears in your timeline — the other photos stay in your library but are collapsed behind the stack. Open the stack to reach them, use Set Cover to change which one is shown, or Unstack to bring them all back.

Type Description Detection Burst A rapid sequence of photos taken in burst mode Automatic (rule-based: EXIF burst/sequence tags and filename patterns by default) Bracket Exposure brackets for HDR Reserved — not currently created; there is no bracket detection, and Create stack always makes a Manual stack Manual Any photos you want to group together Manual

Burst detection runs a list of rules stored per user. Enabled by default (hard criteria): EXIF Burst Mode Tag — camera burst / continuous-drive flags EXIF Sequence Number — sequence metadata written by the camera Filename Burst Pattern — file names that say "burst": Google and other Android cameras (IMG_20151009_143426_BURST1), Pixel (00001IMG_00001_BURST20200302155220435) and Samsung (20200115_123456_001, the cover ..._COVER). Frames with the same burst name in one folder are one stack The two EXIF rules build one burst from consecutive frames of the same camera (model, and serial number when the photo has one; a frame scanned before LibrePhotos read serial numbers has none and still joins the other frames of its model when they all come from one body) taken at most 2 seconds apart, using the sub-second capture time (SubSecTimeOriginal). A burst that crosses a second boundary stays one stack, two cameras shooting at the same moment get one stack each, and a sequence number that starts again begins a new burst. A frame whose sequence number says "single shot" (0) is not a burst frame. Frames are ordered by capture time, and the stack's cover is the middle frame. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, these rules grouped frames by the whole second, and a Canon photo shot in continuous drive mode made Detect stacks fail. Run Detect stacks again to regroup existing bursts. A camera's file counter (IMG_0001, DSC_0815) or a download copy (photo (1)) does not make a burst by default: every camera numbers its files. A filename rule set to a counter pattern (sequence_suffix, bracketed_sequence, iphone_burst) or to a custom pattern still matches them, but then its frames also have to come from the same camera, count up by one and follow each other within the rule's interval (2 seconds by default). New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0, the default filename rule took every IMG_xxxx file of a folder for one burst. Run Detect stacks again to regroup existing bursts. Available but disabled by default (soft criteria — these estimate, and can group unrelated photos): Timestamp Proximity — photos taken within a configurable interval of each other (2 seconds by default, measured to the sub-second) on the same camera Visual Similarity — perceptual-hash comparison of consecutive photos Open Settings and use the Burst detection rules panel to enable, disable, reorder, add or remove these rules (including extra presets such as a looser 5-second timestamp rule or a custom filename pattern). Changes apply the next time you run Detect stacks. You can trigger stack detection from the Organizing → Photo stacks page by clicking "Detect photo stacks" and choosing which types to detect.

The Organizing page is your central hub for managing stacks and duplicates. Open it from the dropdown of the Photos page title, under Organizing (Duplicates or Stacks). It has two tabs, Duplicate photos and Photo stacks: Stacks Tab​ Browse all detected stacks Filter by stack type — the dropdown offers All types plus each type you actually have stacks of Click a stack to open the Stack Modal showing all photos in the group with details (resolution, file size, camera, date) Set as cover — Choose which photo represents the stack in the timeline Unstack photos — Remove the grouping. It asks first: the photos stay in your library, a burst or bracket stack comes back with the next detection, but a manual stack has to be built again by hand View full size — Browse stack photos in the full lightbox viewer Creating Manual Stacks​ Select multiple photos from any view Open the selection actions menu (three-dot menu) Click "Create stack" The selected photos are grouped into a manual stack, and only the cover photo remains visible in your timeline Managing Stacks​ From the selection actions menu, you can also: Merge stacks — Combine multiple stacks into one Break apart stacks — Remove the selected photos from every manual stack they belong to (a stack is deleted automatically if fewer than 2 photos remain)

When viewing a photo that belongs to a stack: The Stacks section in the sidebar shows thumbnail previews of other photos in the stack Click any thumbnail to switch to that photo Click "View full stack" to open the Stack Modal If a photo is in multiple stacks, they are shown in an accordion grouped by type

LibrePhotos includes a Statistics section with several interactive visualizations that help you explore patterns in your photo library. It is not in the sidebar: open it with View statistics at the top right of the Library page (Account menu > Library), or press Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on macOS) and search for "Statistics". You can also go straight to /statistics. The page starts with the same counts as the Library page, then a tab bar to switch between the five views: Timeline (where it opens), Place tree, Word clouds, Social graph and Face clusters.

The Place Tree shows all your photo locations organized in a hierarchical tree — from countries down to regions and cities. This gives you a bird's-eye view of everywhere you've taken photos. Multiple layouts — Switch between the tree layout (shown horizontally or vertically) and a radial layout Link style — Switch the connectors between curved, step and straight lines Expand / collapse — Click on any node to expand or collapse its children Pan — Drag anywhere on the canvas to move around the tree Zoom — Scroll to zoom, or use the zoom in / out / reset buttons; the keyboard shortcuts +, - and 0 (reset) also work Hover — Hover over a node to see its full name and photo count
The Timeline view provides two charts that show how your photo-taking habits have changed over time:
A bar chart showing how many photos you took each month. This makes it easy to spot busy months (vacations, events) vs. quieter periods.

A single horizontal stacked bar spanning your whole library, laid out chronologically. Each colored segment is one continuous stay at a location, and the segment's width shows how long that stay lasted. Hover over a segment to see the location name and the month-and-year range it covers; the color legend underneath lists every segment. Note that each stay gets its own color, so a place you visited more than once appears more than once. This is great for seeing travel patterns at a glance.

Three interactive word clouds generated from your photo library: Cloud Based on Places Place names from reverse geocoding (postcodes and points of interest are skipped) Things What OpenCLIP detected in your photos. These are also what populate your Things albums. People Names of recognized people in your photos Each cloud shows at most the top 100 terms, and larger words appear more frequently in your library. Click on any word to search for photos matching that term.

A force-directed graph showing the relationships between people in your photos. Each node represents a person, and edges connect people who appear together in the same photos. Nodes are all drawn the same size and labeled with the person's name; a node's outline turns orange when you hover over it Edges connect people who appear together in at least one photo — the graph is unweighted, so every node and edge is drawn the same size Drag nodes to rearrange the layout Zoom to explore dense areas of the graph This is a fun way to see who shows up in photos together.

A scatter plot of every detected face in your library. Each dot is one face, positioned by a projection of its face embedding, so faces that look alike land close together — this gives you an overview of how well face recognition has separated people. Color identifies the person; unlabeled faces are drawn as small gray dots Hover over a dot to preview the face thumbnail and the person's name Click a dot to open that photo in the lightbox Filter by person — Click a name badge above the plot to highlight that person's faces and dim everyone else's. The badges list the people with the most detected faces, plus All to clear the filter and Unknown for faces not yet assigned to anyone (shown only when you have unlabeled faces). Click the active badge again to deselect. Summary — The cards below the plot show how many people were identified and the total number of faces in the plot. Useful for spotting clustering errors or finding unlabeled faces

Text recognition (OCR, optical character recognition) reads the text it can find on your photos: receipts, letters, signs, screenshots, whiteboards, book pages. LibrePhotos stores that text with the photo, so you can search for it and select and copy it in the photo viewer. It also helps LibrePhotos tell documents apart from ordinary photos. Text recognition is off on a new install. An administrator turns it on for the whole server, and then each user starts it for their own photos.

When an administrator picks a model, LibrePhotos asks them to confirm, under the heading Text recognition reads everything: Text recognition stores all readable text of every photo in the database as plain text. That includes documents, receipts, letters and IDs that happen to be in your library. Larger models are more accurate, but need more time and memory per photo. Some things to know before you turn it on: The text stays on your server. The model runs locally, like every other model in LibrePhotos. The text is not encrypted. Anyone who can read your database or a database backup can read it. Only the owner of a photo sees its text. People you share a photo or an album with, and visitors of a public link, do not get it, and search only ever looks at your own photos. Turning it off again does not delete the text that was already read. See Turning it off again.
documents.s: Privacy: what turning it on means

documents.t: An administrator turns text recognition on in Account menu > Admin area, under Site settings, with Text recognition (OCR) model: Model Download When to pick it None Text recognition is off. This is the default. PP-OCRv6 Tiny (fastest) about 6 MB Older or low-power machines, or when speed matters more than every word. PP-OCRv6 Small about 26 MB A balance between speed and accuracy. PP-OCRv6 Medium (most accurate) about 100 MB Small print and difficult photos, when the machine has memory and time to spare. Picking a model opens the confirmation described above. Cancel keeps the previous choice. After you click Save: A Download models job fetches the model if it is not on the server yet. The ocr service starts within about a minute, with no restart. You can see it under Services in the Admin area (see Service Management). Nothing is read yet at this point. Each user starts the reading from their Library page, as described next.

Open Account menu > Library. Under the Text Recognition heading is the Extract Text row: Extract reads the photos that have not been read yet. The first time, that is all of your photos. After that, it reads the photos still without text: new ones, and ones an earlier run could not read. New in 1.5.0 Up to 1.4.0, it read the photos added since the last run, so a photo that failed or whose thumbnail was not ready yet could be left out for good. The arrow next to Extract opens Extract text again for all photos, which reads every photo again, also the ones that already have text. Both start an Extract text (OCR) job, which you can follow under Account menu > My jobs. It reads photos only, not videos. Each user runs it for their own photos, so on a shared server every user clicks Extract for themselves. New in 1.5.0 While a model is selected, the job also starts by itself after a scan and a few minutes after an upload, for the photos still without text. Selecting a model therefore reads your whole library after the next scan or upload, a little at a time. Up to 1.4.0, it only ran when you clicked Extract. A photo the text recognition service failed on three times is no longer read by these automatic runs. Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) Extract tries it again, and so does Extract text again for all photos. Up to 1.6.0, only Extract text again for all photos did. When the service could not be reached at all, that does not count as a failure. If the administrator changes the model later, Extract also reads again the photos that were read with the previous model. When no model is selected, the buttons are disabled. Administrators then see "Choose a text recognition model in the admin area to enable this.", and other users see "Text recognition is turned off on this server. Ask your administrator to choose a text recognition model."

Once a photo's text has been read, a normal search also looks at that text. Searching invoice or Main Street finds the receipt or the street sign that shows those words, together with the photos that match by caption, place, person and so on. See Text Search. On PostgreSQL (the Docker setups) the text is matched word by word. On SQLite (the Windows app and the single container's internal database) any photo whose text contains your search term matches, also in the middle of a word.

When LibrePhotos found text on one of your photos, the photo viewer shows an extra toolbar button, Select text in photo (T). Click it, or press t, and the recognised text is laid over the photo, so you can select it with the mouse and copy it like text on a web page. Press t again, or click Stop selecting text (T), to go back to the plain photo. The button only appears on your own photos, and only when text was found on them.
documents.s: Selecting text in the photo viewer

documents.t: LibrePhotos uses the recognised text, together with the things it sees in the photo (the same labels as the Things albums), to find documents: receipts, letters, forms and book pages. A photo is marked as a Document when it shows a thing such as a receipt, an invoice or a book page, or when two hints come together, for example a lot of text, an amount next to a word like "total", or a thing such as a menu or a whiteboard. The Extract text (OCR) job checks this for every photo it reads. You can then hide documents from the timeline with the Filter button (see Filtering the timeline), browse them on the Documents page, or pick Documents only with the media button of a list such as Favorites or an album. Without text recognition, LibrePhotos has nothing to go on and no photo is detected as a document. You can still mark photos as documents yourself, see Category.

Set Text recognition (OCR) model back to None. The ocr service stops being started within about a minute, and Extract is disabled for everyone. This only stops reading new text. The text that was already read stays in the database, and search keeps finding it. If you turned text recognition off for privacy reasons, keep this in mind. LibrePhotos has no button to delete the stored text yet. For the other switches that live in Site settings rather than in environment variables, see Feature Toggles.

Mark file as "deleted". Select the image you want to delete, open the selection actions menu (⋮) and click Move to trash (on a wide screen, the trash button in the selection bar does the same). Open Trash in the sidebar. On a phone it is in the account menu: tap your picture at the right end of the bar at the bottom of the screen. Select the images you want to delete forever (click Select at the right of the header, or tick a photo's checkbox; the selection bar appears under the header). Click the red trash icon in the selection bar (tooltip Delete permanently, or Delete N photos permanently when more than one is selected), then confirm in the Delete N photos permanently? dialog by clicking its red button. This cannot be undone. You can also restore a photo instead of deleting it: select it in Trash and click the blue undo-arrow icon (tooltip Restore photo) to remove the "deleted" status. New in 1.5.0 While a photo is in the trash, its faces are not on the face dashboard and face training does not use them. Restoring the photo brings them back. Deleting the images from the file system only works, if LibrePhotos has the access to the images. If it is read only, files will not be deleted. Not released yet (comes after 1.6.0) A photo is deleted with all its files or not at all: when one of its files cannot be deleted, the photo stays in the trash with every file it had. A photo you restore while Empty trash runs stays restored, files and all. Info New in 1.4.0 This applies to the trashed-on date, the Empty trash button and the automatic deletion described below.

LibrePhotos records the moment a photo goes to the trash, whether you moved it there yourself or resolving a duplicate did. Restoring the photo clears that date, so moving it to the trash again starts over. Photos that were already in the trash when you updated count as trashed on the date they were last changed. Open a trashed photo and its details say Moved to the trash on that date: in the lightbox's info panel, under the photo's date, and on the photo page, in the red "This photo is in the trash" box above the actions. When an administrator has turned on automatic deletion, a second line says Deleted for good in N days, on the date the cleanup removes it (red from three days before), or Deleted for good at the next daily cleanup once that date has passed. The subtitle of the Trash page says which rule applies: Photos in the trash are deleted for good after N days, or Photos stay in the trash until you empty it while automatic deletion is off.
documents.s: When a photo was moved to the trash

documents.t: The red Empty trash button in the header of the Trash page (a red icon on a phone) permanently deletes every photo in your trash in one go. The photos of other users are never touched. Click Empty trash. The Empty the trash? dialog says how many photos and videos are in the trash. The count is always the whole trash: when the Photos/Videos filter hides some of them, the dialog says how many of them it includes. Click the red Empty trash button in the dialog to start, or Cancel. Like Delete permanently, it deletes the original files from disk, and it cannot be undone. It runs as a background job, so a large trash no longer runs into a timeout the way selecting everything and deleting it does. While it runs the button says Emptying the trash; the job shows up in the job list with how far it got. When it is done, a message says how many photos were deleted. A photo that cannot be deleted (for example on a read-only library) is skipped and stays in the trash; the job then ends as failed, and the message says how many photos are left.

An administrator can have LibrePhotos empty the trash on its own: in Admin area > Site settings, Delete photos from the trash after takes a number of days. A daily task then permanently deletes every photo that has been in the trash for longer than that, for all users. Automatic deletion removes your original files The automatic cleanup deletes photos the same way Delete permanently does: the original files are deleted from disk, together with their thumbnails, faces and everything else LibrePhotos knows about them. It cannot be undone. Only turn it on if your library has a backup, or if you are sure that what lands in the trash can go. The setting is 0 days by default, which keeps photos in the trash until their owner deletes them. Updating LibrePhotos never turns it on. While it is on, a red box under the field says that original files are deleted. Turning it on, or making the number of days smaller, asks first: the Delete old photos from the trash automatically? dialog says how many photos, in how many users' trash, the next daily cleanup would delete. Making the number larger, or setting it back to 0, saves without asking. A photo the cleanup cannot delete is skipped and tried again the next day. Apps and scripts can read the setting as trash_retention_days from GET /api/sitesettings and change it (administrators only) with POST /api/sitesettings.
documents.s: Deleting photos from the trash automatically

documents.t: Missing images can happen, when you moved files outside of the LibrePhotos photo folder or if you deleted them with a third party tool like the filesystem. In this case the metadata, thumbnail and faces still exist, but the actual file is not known to LibrePhotos. There are two ways to deal with that: Move the files back to the LibrePhotos folder and do a rescan Delete the metadata of the missing images. On the Library page, whenever missing files have been detected, a red Missing Photos badge (showing how many) appears next to the Photos heading. Click it and confirm in the Remove missing photos dialog. This permanently deletes those photos from the database, along with their metadata, faces, ratings, captions and album assignments, and cannot be undone. See Missing Photos for more on how missing files are detected and resolved.

In the top right corner of the web interface, there is an upload button. Clicking it will open a file picker. You can select multiple files and upload them. You can also drag photos and videos from your computer onto any page of the app. New in 1.4.0 Up to 1.3.0 only the upload button took dropped files.
